title: The Democratization of Self-Care in the Modern Era: A Conceptual Analysis of the Sachet Economy Phenomenon, Bottom of The Pyramid Consumer Behavior, And Ecological Sustainability Dilemmas in Hair Mask Products
affiliations: Jakarta State University, , Universitas Negeri Jakarta and

detail.title: The Democratization of Self-Care in the Modern Era: A Conceptual Analysis of the Sachet Economy Phenomenon, Bottom of The Pyramid Consumer Behavior, And Ecological Sustainability Dilemmas in Hair Mask Products

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that there are no conflicts of interest or personal or financial relationships that could have influenced the research presented in this study.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or financial support from any funding agency, commercial organization, or other institution.

detail.abstract:
The rapid proliferation of sachet-format fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) across traditional retail networks in developing markets reflects the intersection of corporate strategy, grassroots behavioral economics, and environmental sustainability. Multinational corporations and local manufacturers, including Unilever, P&G, and Wings, use mini-packaging and low absolute pricing to improve product accessibility in Bottom of the Pyramid (BoP) markets. However, this commercial model also contributes to the accumulation of single-use multilayer plastic waste. This conceptual paper examines the sachet economy, with particular attention to personal hair care products such as hair masks and creambaths. It integrates marketing theory, behavioral economics, consumption sociology, and sustainable marketing to develop a conceptual framework connecting corporate packaging strategies, consumer decision-making under financial constraints, environmental attitude–behavior gaps, and the shared responsibilities of producers, consumers, and institutions. The study synthesizes contemporary academic literature and institutional perspectives to explain how sachet consumption is shaped by daily income patterns, affordability, convenience, self-care needs, and social dignity.
The conceptual analysis suggests that sachet economies provide economic accessibility but simultaneously reinforce dependence on flexible plastic packaging and create environmental externalities that cannot be addressed through individual consumer responsibility alone. The paper proposes an integrative model in which regulatory stringency and material technology innovation moderate the relationship between sachet based business strategies and environmental outcomes. It recommends regenerative business models, cross-sector circular economy collaboration, improved packaging innovation, and inclusive public policies to maintain product accessibility while minimizing the environmental burden of flexible plastic waste.

title: Is Rewarded Advertising Rewarding? Field Experimental Evidence from a Digital Advertising Platform
affiliations: The University of Hong Kong, HKU Business School, The University of Hong Kong, Dartmouth College - Tuck School of Business, The University of Hong Kong - Faculty of Business and Economics and Tencent Inc.

detail.title: Is Rewarded Advertising Rewarding? Field Experimental Evidence from a Digital Advertising Platform

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.funderStatement: The research is funded by University Grants Committee (Hong Kong)

detail.abstract: Problem definition: Rewarded advertising offers users in-app benefits in exchange for voluntary ad viewing, creating a monetization opportunity for freemium service providers. Yet it may displace in-app purchases (IAPs) and interrupt user activity, thereby negatively impacting service experience. We examine how rewarded ads affect user engagement, retention, and monetization. Methodology/results: We analyze a largescale randomized field experiment conducted by a leading digital advertising and entertainment platform and a freemium game developer in China. Our sample comprises 10,101 users randomly assigned to groups with or without rewarded-ad access. Viewing these ads reduces game progression time, a benefit similar to that provided by speedup cards purchased in the game. Rewarded-ad access reduces users' tendency to purchase speedup cards by 36.7% relative to control, with no statistically significant effects on other IAP purchases, total IAP purchases, and user engagement or retention. We classify users by their pretreatment use of speedup cards or in-app currency to reduce waiting times in the focal game (card users vs. non-users) and pretreatment IAP spending history in other freemium games on the digital platform (prior IAP users vs. non-users). Rewarded ads increase retention among card users and reduce card purchases among card non-users. In contrast, among prior IAP non-users, retention gains and card purchase reductions coexist. Managerial implications: Freemium service providers should evaluate advertising income together with displaced revenue when rewarded ads offer similar benefits as IAPs. Speedup card usage in early game stages and platform-wide IAP spending histories can guide objective-specific user targeting because revenue-oriented and retention-oriented deployment may favor different users.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the convergent application of artificial intelligence (AI) and blockchain technologies to transform logistics and facility management, arguing that their integration can simultaneously improve operational efficiency, transparency, and asset resilience while introducing new governance and ethical challenges. Researchers adopted a structured approach, gathering and analyzing qualitative data from a wealth of online literature sources and expert opinions. The study meticulously selected 32 peer-reviewed articles spanning from 2004 to 2025 to 2024, each discussing the impact of the Integration of Artificial Intelligence and Blockchain in Logistics and Facility Management. The systematic approach ultimately provided valuable insights into the Integration of Artificial Intelligence and Blockchain in Logistics and Facility Management. This careful methodology aimed to shed light on how external forces shaped African governance systems. Complementarily, blockchain provides tamper-evident provenance, secure multi-party transaction records, and automated execution via smart contracts, addressing trust, auditability, and settlement frictions across fragmented service ecosystems. The paper proposes practical architectures: hybrid on-chain/off-chain storage, Internet of Things (IoT)-anchored ledgers, and federated learning with blockchain-mediated model provenance that balance scalability, privacy, and verifiability. Mitigation strategies discussed include open data schemas and Application Programming Interfaces (APIs), consortium governance charters with dispute-resolution mechanisms, explainable-AI standards and model auditing, hybrid architectures to minimise on-chain storage, and commitments to green compute. Policy recommendations call for regulatory sandboxes, certification regimes, and funding for inclusive onboarding to prevent exclusion of small vendors. Finally, the paper outlines a research agenda emphasising longitudinal field evaluations, standardised KPIs for socio-technical outcomes, and study of distributional effects across suppliers and facility managers. By articulating integrated design patterns and governance safeguards, the study provides a roadmap for responsibly deploying AI–blockchain solutions in logistics and facility management.

detail.abstract: The termination of a franchise or licensing agreement frequently compels companies to alter their brand identity to maintain business continuity. This conceptual study aims to construct a comprehensive theoretical framework governing post license termination brand conversion and analyze the intersection between marketing strategy and public policy in preserving product competitiveness. Drawing on real world phenomena such as BreadTalk transitioning into MAKO in Indonesia and McDonald's becoming Vkusno i Tochka in Russia, this study demonstrates that brand conversion does not require building consumer equity entirely from scratch. Instead, it strategically leverages existing operational assets and brand equity. By integrating Brand Equity Theory, Consumer Learning through Stimulus Generalization, Rebranding Typology, and Customer Acquisition and Retention Theory, this study establishes that rebranding strategy and public policy compliance jointly drive consumer acceptance, which subsequently determines overall product competitiveness. While brand conversion presents immediate short term risks such as brand awareness erosion, customer confusion, and brand switching, it creates substantial opportunities for long term competitive advantage through royalty fee efficiency, local innovation flexibility, and heightened market agility.

detail.abstract: Small businesses depend heavily on local demand, making establishment location a source of both opportunity and constraint. Less active areas may limit access to potential customers, whereas busy areas bring more prospects but also greater competition. Given their fixed establishment locations, businesses often adopt location-targeted mobile advertising to flexibly reach prospects across different locations. Using large-scale field data from a major platform in Korea, we estimate the effects of location-targeted mobile ads on users' mobile engagement. To address endogeneity arising from advertisers' target-neighborhood choices, we employ a shift-share (Bartik) instrument that exploits plausibly exogenous ad-audience fluctuations unlikely to reflect anticipated local engagement shocks. Our results show that location-targeted mobile ads increase mobile-site engagement, including awareness, visit-related actions, and word of mouth. In addition, the effectiveness of location-targeted mobile ads depends not only on target-market crowdedness but also on its interaction with the advertiser's home market conditions.

detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly adopted in the social sciences as surrogates for human coders. Standard practice validates them by their correspondence with human measurements of the same stimuli using statistics like correlation. However, overall correspondence can conceal biases that distort specific claims. We demonstrate this with openweight LLM ratings of 568 food and 1,811 scene photographs. Ratings inflate, attenuate, or reverse effects, and improving overall correspondence with prompts can improve one contrast while worsening another. Rankings also elevate some categories and demote others beyond what random errors of the same size typically produce. Across six prompts, some of these errors are shared, so sampling across prompts may continue to mask biases. We propose validating LLM coders against specific claims they will test rather than the general coding task.

detail.abstract: Changes in an increasingly competitive business environment are driving companies to undertake rebranding as a strategy to maintain market relevance and enhance product competitiveness. Rebranding is not merely about changing a name or visual identity but also involves managing brand equity, consumer perceptions, and adjusting business strategies in 2 response to changes in the internal and external environment. This paper aims to analyze the drivers of rebranding, its impact on brand equity and product competitiveness, and to explain strategies for changing brand identity through the lens of marketing theory. The method used in this paper is a conceptual approach through a literature review, integrating theories of brand equity, brand positioning, brand extension, the corporate rebranding matrix, and the Ansoff Growth Matrix. The results of the analysis indicate that rebranding can serve as a strategy to strengthen a company's competitive position by increasing business flexibility, expanding market segments, and renewing brand identity. However, the rebranding process also carries risks, such as the loss of the old brand's value, a decline in consumer trust, and increased communication investment requirements. The success of rebranding is influenced by a company's ability to preserve core brand values, maintain product quality, manage the transition communication, and build new relationships with consumers. This paper presents a conceptual framework that explains the relationship between the drivers of rebranding, the identity change process, consumer responses, and the impact on product competitiveness.

detail.abstract: Brand transitions from global to local identities are becoming increasingly relevant amid regulatory dynamics, changing business relationships, and the need to adapt to domestic markets. This paper aims to develop a conceptual framework for understanding the brand migration process through the perspectives of rebranding, public policy, consumer behavior, and product competitiveness. The discussion focuses on three rebranding drivers license expiration, mergers, and repositioning and their implications for market outcomes. The analysis shows that rebranding is not merely a matter of changing a name or visual identity, but a strategic process involving brand equity management, regulatory compliance, cost efficiency, local product innovation, and consumer adaptation. This process can strengthen competitiveness through innovation flexibility and local relevance, but it also carries risks such as consumer confusion, loyalty erosion, and increased marketing communication costs. Consistency in product quality, sensory experience, service, and transition communication is therefore an essential strategy for preserving brand value throughout the migration process.

title: When Consumers Prefer Point Versus Range Estimates of Product Performance
affiliations: Texas A&M University - Mays Business School,  and Texas A&M University - Mays Business School

detail.title: When Consumers Prefer Point Versus Range Estimates of Product Performance

detail.abstract: Product performance claims play an important role in shaping consumers’ purchase decisions. Through six preregistered studies, including one field study, the authors demonstrate that consumers’ preferences for point versus range performance estimates in common comparative purchase settings depend on whether their attention is directed toward the content of the claim or the manner of its presentation. At baseline, consumers focus on what information is communicated and prefer point over range estimates because point estimates convey greater certainty about the expected performance outcome. When consumers’ persuasion knowledge is activated, however, their attention shifts toward how information is communicated. In this mode, the format of the claim, rather than the stated performance figures, becomes relatively more informative: range estimates signal brand transparency by acknowledging the natural variability of real-world performance, enhancing perceived trustworthiness and reversing consumer preference. These effects are attenuated when products are evaluated in isolation rather than compared side by side. Collectively, these findings inform both theory and practice by revealing when and why consumers prefer point versus range estimates of product performance.

detail.abstract: Leaders are expected to stay effective while the tools of work change faster than at any time in their careers. This article asks how continuous learning supports leadership adaptability across career stages, and what role artificial intelligence (AI) plays in that process. It is a narrative review with a proposed practical framework, not a systematic review or an empirical study. Drawing on research in leadership development, career adaptability, learning agility and recent studies of generative AI at work, it makes three arguments. First, sustained leadership effectiveness depends on learning that changes decisions and behaviour, not on the amount of information consumed. Second, AI raises the floor of what an individual can produce but can lower the effort people invest in thinking, so judgment and verification become skills to practise on purpose. Third, because AI makes content and tools abundant, the scarce ingredient in learning becomes motivation and accountability, which is a human coaching function. The article proposes a six-step learning-and-adaptation cycle, a 30-day learning experiment for leaders, and a coaching layer that keeps the cycle running. It closes with limitations and questions for empirical work.

title: A Structural Analysis of Sales Force Control Policies: Call Planning, Input- and Outcome-Based Compensation, and Price Delegation
affiliations: University of Minnesota - Twin Cities - Carlson School of Management and University of Texas at Austin - McCombs School of Business

detail.title: A Structural Analysis of Sales Force Control Policies: Call Planning, Input- and Outcome-Based Compensation, and Price Delegation
detail.abstract: This study provides a structural analysis of salespeople's behavior in response to various sales force control policies. The model considers quantifiable effort (e.g., number of sales calls) and qualitative effort (e.g., quality of sales calls), as well as salespeople's ability and price-promotion effectiveness. By examining the motivational role of various control policies, the study offers insight into the design of sales force control systems. A comprehensive set of counterfactual simulations examines the implications of call planning, outcome- and input-based compensation, and price delegation. The results reveal a trade-off between imposing a strict call plan and offering strong outcome-based compensation, a potential drawback of introducing input-based compensation, and how delegating price authority supports underperforming salespeople to improve performance, but at the potential cost of demotivating top performers.

detail.abstract: In the digital era, marketing practices have changed significantly as consumers have become more aware of environmental, social, and ethical issues. Sustainable marketing has gained importance as organizations try to build long-term relationships with consumers based on trust and transparency. This paper examines the role of sustainable marketing practices in building consumer trust in the digital environment. It focuses on how ethical marketing communication, transparency, responsible branding, and sustainability-oriented digital strategies influence consumer trust. The study is based on secondary data collected from existing research papers, journals, and academic sources. The analysis shows that sustainable marketing practices help in improving brand credibility, reducing consumer skepticism, and strengthening trust in online markets. The findings suggest that consumers in the digital era prefer brands that show a genuine commitment to sustainability rather than relying only on short-term promotional activities. This study adds to marketing literature by explaining how sustainable marketing can be used as an effective strategy to build consumer trust in digital markets and provides useful insights for marketers to adopt responsible and transparent marketing practices.

detail.abstract: We examine how masculinity norms-the social expectations about how men should behavepredict economic, health, and political outcomes. We field the Global Masculinity Survey, measuring adherence to core masculinity norms among 125,000 individuals across 70 countries. Economically, men who adhere more strongly to these norms supply more labor, earn more, and sort into traditionally masculine occupations. In terms of health, they take greater risks and report poorer mental health. Politically, they express stronger support for strongman authoritarianism and military rule. Adherence to masculinity norms is stronger among men exposed to war or economic recession during their impressionable years.

detail.abstract: Changes in the business, social, and regulatory environment have encouraged companies to undertake rebranding as a strategy to maintain relevance and competitiveness. This conceptual paper aims to formulate a framework that connects internal business drivers, external regulatory pressures, brand identity change mechanisms, and postrebranding competitiveness. The discussion employs Brand Equity Theory, Brand Repositioning, Cognitive Dissonance, and Glocalization as theoretical foundations to explain how changes in brand names affect perceptions, consumer responses, and companies' competitive positions. The synthesis indicates that rebranding may be driven by the need for modernization, expansion, restructuring, franchise termination, as well as regulatory pressures and facilitation. Rebranding has the potential to enhance competitiveness through market expansion, positioning renewal, inclusivity, and image recovery, but it also entails risks such as brand equity erosion, consumer confusion, customer switching, and increased communication costs. The success of rebranding depends on maintaining a balance between identity change and continuity of visual elements, effective transition communication, legal protection, and stakeholder relationship management.

detail.abstract: Brand renaming is a strategic decision that can affect brand equity, consumer relationships, and corporate competitiveness. This paper aims to explain the process of transferring brand equity from the former identity to the new identity, analyze the role of domestic and international public policies in the rebranding process, and examine its implications for product competitiveness. The discussion adopts a conceptual approach by integrating Corporate Rebranding Theory, Brand Equity Theory, the Resource-Based View (RBV), and Signaling Theory. The findings indicate that successful rebranding is not determined solely by a change 2 in brand name, but also by the company's ability to maintain product quality, service, consumer experience, as well as its internal resources and capabilities. Public policies and geopolitical conditions can serve as catalysts or pressures that drive changes in brand identity. Rebranding also has the potential to enhance competitiveness through greater efficiency, innovation, and flexibility. Therefore, maintaining brand equity and effectively managing resources are important factors in sustaining competitiveness throughout the brand transition. This paper is theoretical and conceptual in nature; therefore, the propositions developed require further empirical and longitudinal testing.

detail.abstract: Rail operations are complex, stochastic, and increasingly data-rich, with multi-stage interactions, shared resources, and evolving system conditions that create significant uncertainty for operational decision-making. These characteristics require approaches that can interpret contextual information, anticipate future system states, and support the evaluation of alternative operational scenarios. This paper proposes a Cognitive Digital Twin framework for rail operations that integrates contextual data processing, learning-based prediction, and decision feedback to support context-aware operational evaluation. The framework is structured around core cognitive functions, including perception, learning, reasoning, and feedback, and conceptually incorporates a simulation layer to enable the assessment of alternative operational scenarios under uncertainty. The applicability of the proposed framework is illustrated through a heavy-haul rail supply chain operations case study focusing on the prediction of yard operational times and scenario-based evaluation. The results highlight how cognitive integration of data-driven models and scenario evaluation can enhance situational awareness and support informed decision-making in complex rail systems. The proposed framework provides a generic and transferable foundation for the development of cognitive digital twins in rail supply chains and rail operations.

detail.abstract: Liquidity crises in investment funds are a recurring concern, but recent events in the US private credit market - most notably Blue Owl's suspension of redemptions at its Business Development Company OBDC II - raise the question of whether such episodes reflect a regulatory failure or an inherently fragile business model. This paper examines the US and EU legal frameworks governing liquidity risk in collective investment schemes, alongside the evolving guidance of the FSB and IOSCO, using the Blue Owl case as an empirical anchor. It argues that OBDC II never breached its applicable regulatory regime, since the redemption rights investors had come to expect were discretionary rather than legally guaranteed; the crisis instead exposed a deeper mismatch between investor expectations and the structural illiquidity of private credit portfolios. The paper concludes by drawing lessons for the European Union, questioning whether the UCITS framework's tolerance for a 10% allocation to illiquid assets is adequately safeguarded, given that even far stricter US limits failed to prevent a comparable crisis.

detail.abstract:
This paper develops the Doctrine of Conversion Sovereignty and Strategic Tempo, a systems framework for evaluating whether a nation can convert resources, energy, capital, technology, labor, and dependable external access into qualified, mission-usable infrastructure before delay becomes strategic consequence. Using copper as the principal material case, the analysis examines how artificial-intelligence infrastructure depends not only upon resource availability, but upon refining, fabrication, electrical delivery, thermal management, workforce depth, qualification capacity, repair, replacement, and industrial scaling across time.

The paper’s principal novelty is architectural: it integrates material supply, manufacturing capacity, grid infrastructure, cooling systems, qualification, labor, and institutional governance into a single mission- and time-dependent framework. It develops linked analytical concepts including Time-to-Scale, Mission Margin, Fabrication Dependency, Strategic Margin, Strategic Conversion Reserves, and Complete-System Sovereignty, while distinguishing resource possession from conversion capability and eventual capacity from capacity available within the period of need.

The paper concludes that the central challenge is not principally an immediate copper shortage, but a long-horizon industrial pacing vulnerability in which technological acceleration may outrun the physical and institutional systems required to sustain it. The doctrine therefore reframes national AI capacity as the ability to construct, energize, cool, qualify, maintain, repair, reproduce, replace, and expand productive infrastructure through pathways that remain available, resilient, and timely.

title: Platforms and Traditional Producers in Cournot Competition: Case of Ride-Hail Platforms and Liberally Priced Taxis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.

detail.abstract: Platforms acting as digital marketplaces that sell the same product as traditional producer-sellers often eclipse the latter in output. This article shows analytically that such output disparity is guaranteed in Cournot-style competition with customers being indifferent buying from any firm and without considering network effects. With a digital marketplace in a market, a traditional Cournot equilibrium-found via solving first-order conditions-may not exist, in which case traditional producersellers stop producing. Data from ride-hail platforms and taxi operators in Singapore with liberalized pricing as well as the freedom to adjust output show that different competitive equilibria can emerge.

detail.abstract: This paper seeks to interrogate the reasoning of the High Court in Gulf African Bank v Halgan Megabids Limited & 7 Others 1 , a 2026 judgment holding the Kenyan state liable to indemnify a commercial lender for losses flowing from forged land titles. It situates that holding within the Torrens architecture inherited by the Land Registration Act, and tests its logic against the Supreme Court's hardened due diligence doctrine in Dina Management and Torino Enterprises. The paper argues that the trial judge correctly read section 81 as a no-fault indemnity, nevertheless under-examined whether paper diligence still satisfies a standard the apex court has visibly tightened. It further contends that the dismissal of exemplary damages rested on too narrow a reading of registry fault, one that overlooks documented, recurring forgery inside the Lands Registry itself. The paper closes by proposing a tiered indemnity fund, mandatory biometric verification of chargors, and statutory subrogation reform, arguing these would distribute the cost of fraud more justly than the present blunt instrument of blanket state liability.

title: Managing AI-Enabled Organizations Agreement and Reviewability as Foundations of Trust

detail.title: Managing AI-Enabled Organizations Agreement and Reviewability as Foundations of Trust

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: AI-enabled organizations increasingly rely on humans and AI systems to jointly perform managerial work such as analysis, planning, decision support, content generation, and task delegation. While AI is often evaluated through the quality, explainability, or correctness of its outputs, many managerial tasks are ambiguous, nonroutine, and difficult to assess using stable objective criteria. In such contexts, effective collaboration depends less on evaluating outputs alone and more on establishing a shared understanding of the problem, the criteria for success, and the rationale guiding action. This paper argues that the core object of management in AI-enabled organizations shifts from outputs to Shared Schemas. A Shared Schema is defined as a shared structure that guides execution through problem definitions, goals, assumptions, constraints, evaluation criteria, plans, strategic hypotheses, intent, and rationale. By making the basis of judgment explicit, Shared Schemas provide a foundation for human-AI coordination, authorization, evaluation, and adaptation. The paper develops a conceptual framework of Shared Schema Governance. Within this framework, Agreement authorizes a Shared Schema as the basis for execution, while Reviewability enables execution and outcomes to be assessed in relation to that authorized Schema. Together, these mechanisms link schema formation, execution, review, revision, and organizational learning. Trust is therefore reconceptualized not as confidence in outputs alone, but as confidence in the organizational capability to govern schema-guided human-AI collaboration.

title: Ambiguity, Risk, and Payout Policy
affiliations: and City University of New York, Baruch College - Zicklin School of Business - Department of Economics and Finance

detail.title: Ambiguity, Risk, and Payout Policy
detail.abstract: We study the relation between ambiguity—Knightian uncertainty—and payout policy using theory and empirical tests. When outcome probabilities are uncertain, ambiguity-averse investors overweight the likelihoods of bad outcomes and underweight the likelihoods of good outcomes, reducing corporate investment attractiveness and raising cash payout preferences. Higher ambiguity is associated with lower corporate investment but higher propensities and levels of cash dividends and share repurchases. The economic magnitudes of these relations are similar to those of size and profitability. Ambiguity decreases after dividend initiation, suggesting payout substitutes for high-ambiguity investments. The positive ambiguity-payout relation contrasts with the known negative risk-payout relation.

detail.abstract: This study examines whether income statement presentation incentives influence firms' real economic decisions. We exploit two recent changes in accounting standards that differentially altered the presentation and measurement of pension costs. ASU 2017-07 changed only the income statement presentation of pension cost components under U.S. GAAP, while IAS 19R changed both presentation and measurement under IFRS. Using difference-indifferences designs, we find that U.S. GAAP firms with stronger presentation incentives significantly de-risked their defined benefit pension portfolios following ASU 2017-07, reallocating approximately 5% of plan assets from higher-risk to lower-risk investments-a market-wide shift of roughly $74 billion. This response is concentrated among firms with stronger preperiod presentation incentives and weaker competing plan-management incentives. In contrast, while IFRS firms generally reduced pension investment risk following IAS 19R, we find no evidence of an incremental presentation effect among firms with stronger operating income presentation incentives. This pattern suggests that although income statement presentation incentives can independently influence real economic behavior, their effects are dominated in this setting when accounting changes simultaneously alter underlying measurement.

title: Interest Rate Dynamics, Perceived Financial Risk, and SME Investment Choices in Kenya: Evidence from the MSMEs Register

detail.title: Interest Rate Dynamics, Perceived Financial Risk, and SME Investment Choices in Kenya: Evidence from the MSMEs Register

declarations.ethicsApproval: NA

detail.abstract: Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) contribute substantially to employment, income generation, innovation and local economic activity, yet productive investment can be constrained when finance is costly, difficult to obtain or uncertain. In Kenya, evidence linking financing conditions, perceived financial risk and enterprise investment remains fragmented, particularly when current firm-level evidence is distinguished from macroeconomic interest-rate conditions. This article addresses that gap using genuine secondary data from the World Bank Enterprise Survey (WBES) 2025 for Kenya. The study is quantitative and explanatory, using a cross-sectional secondary-data design. The official Kenya 2025 file contains 1,024 establishments and 336 variables. Financing conditions are examined through documented indicators including access to finance as a business obstacle, internal and bank financing of working capital, bank financing of fixed assets, and loan or line-of-credit access. Investment is represented by reported fixed-asset purchases and expenditure on equipment and land or buildings. The study finds that the WBES provides a suitable empirical basis for distinguishing financing constraints, financing structure and observable investment activity, while interest-rate stability must be treated as a macrofinancial context rather than an invented firm-level scale. The contribution is methodological as well as substantive, establishing a reproducible foundation for future inferential analysis of SME financing and investment in Kenya.

title: Institutional Persona Degradation and the Dark Knight Inversion: How Protecting Role-incongruent Authority Makes Organizations Defensive
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Institutional Persona Degradation and the Dark Knight Inversion: How Protecting Role-incongruent Authority Makes Organizations Defensive

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a theoretical and conceptual study and did not involve human participants, patients, personal data collection, or experimental procedures requiring ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract:
This paper theorizes how organizations become defensive, evasive, and resistant to repair when they protect a problematic authority figure. The focus is not on evil or incompetent managers, but on what this paper calls role-incongruent authority: actors who possess operational competence, responsibility, practical experience, and prior organizational recognition, while lacking sufficient metacognition, consideration for others’ emotions, affect regulation, the capacity to maintain psychological safety, and post-conflict repair capacity required for leadership roles.

The central argument is that institutional persona degradation does not arise merely from the existence of role-incongruent authority. Rather, it emerges when an organization becomes unable to treat such authority as a problem because of operational necessity, prior evaluation, legal responsibility, workplace continuity, and institutional face. In this process, the problem-raiser, who could otherwise function as a form of organizational pain perception and a resource for repair, is reinterpreted by the defensive institutional persona as a disruptive, threatening, or destructive actor. This perceptual reversal is termed the Dark Knight Inversion.

By connecting organizational persona formation, the self-preservation relay, organizational autoimmunity, and the Dark Knight Paradox, this paper examines how the protection of role-incongruent authority produces accountability inversion, problematization of the problem-raiser, organizational silence, and damage to the organization’s self-corrective capacity. It argues that protecting the institutional persona does not mean preserving a problematic authority figure intact. Rather, it means preserving the organization’s capacity to recognize problems as problems, revise prior judgments, adjust roles and authority, and treat uncomfortable voices as resources for repair.

title: Beyond Flood Control: Rethinking Flood Risk Governance in the Philippines (From Infrastructure-Centered Flood Control to Integrated Risk Governance)

detail.title: Beyond Flood Control: Rethinking Flood Risk Governance in the Philippines (From Infrastructure-Centered Flood Control to Integrated Risk Governance)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No Conflict of Interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This is not a funded paper.

detail.abstract: Flooding is a recurring problem in the Philippines. It affects households, livelihoods, transport, businesses, and public infrastructure. The country's exposure to tropical cyclones and monsoon rainfall cannot be removed, but the damage that follows is not determined by rainfall alone. Where people live, how land is developed, the condition of watersheds, and how government agencies coordinate their work all influence the level of loss experienced by communities. Structural flood-control works remain necessary. The issue is that they cannot be treated as stand-alone projects. This brief uses Integrated Risk Governance (IRG) as an organizing policy framework that brings infrastructure together with land-use planning, housing, watershed management, climate information, and intergovernmental coordination. The analysis focuses on seven connected drivers of flood risk and translates them into practical policy options: basin-scale planning, risk-sensitive housing, climate-informed infrastructure, and monitoring based on actual risk reduction.

detail.abstract: A recurring puzzle in the distributional analysis of child-directed speech is that nouns are the least grammatically consistent governor type, showing more categorial mixing than verbs, adjectives, or relators. Prior corpus-linguistic literature has left this specific finding unexplained. This paper tests a candidate explanation grounded in the developmental psychology of joint attention: when a caregiver refers to a concrete, perceptually available object (a ball), they can rely on non-linguistic cues such as pointing and shared gaze. Because the physical environment carries part of the referential burden, the grammar surrounding that noun can afford to be more variable. Abstract concepts (a number, a birthday) cannot be pointed at, so the linguistic channel alone must carry the precision needed for comprehension. Merging 4,644 noun-governed Agreement Group categories from the Manchester CHILDES corpus with an independent psycholinguistic concreteness lexicon (Brysbaert, Warriner, & Kuperman, 2014), concreteness correlates negatively with grammatical homogeneity, at the category level (r =-.039, p = .028, n = 3,199) and, more strongly, at the lemma level (r =-.277, p = .0017, n = 126). Concrete, pointable nouns (apple, ball, house) sit in grammatically looser slots than abstract nouns (number, sort, birthday). The effect survives a direct control for lemma frequency, ruling out the most obvious confound. The result gives a specific, independently motivated cognitive mechanism, joint attention operating within a grounded-cognition framework, for a grammatical pattern previously observed but unexplained, and connects to a wider literature on distributional learning that this corpus-linguistic method has not previously engaged.

title: How Interdependence Sustains Rather than Fragments Responsibility under Crisis

detail.abstract: Organizational resilience research has established how firms maintain operational performance through adaptive capacity, resource redundancy, and flexible reconfiguration, yet these mechanisms presuppose a single organizational actor managing its own recovery and do not address whether interdependent responsibility architectures-the collectively constructed arrangements through which multiple organizations sustain commitments across boundaries-possess their own form of resilience. Drawing on responsible leadership theory, which provides the normative substance of responsibility (commitments, accountability, governance), and practice architecture theory, which provides the structural insight that responsibility is enacted through functionally distinct logics, this study identifies four practice logics in the semiconductor ecosystem centred on Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC): Ethical Commitment, Relational Coordination, Long-Term Stewardship, and Executional Reliability. Analysing 127 responsibility chains spanning TSMC's two-decade development (2004-2024) and its interactions with ecosystem partners, the study finds that these logics exhibit tight coupling with distinct outcome domains (94-100%, all p < .001), establishing a genuine responsibility architecture. Under crisis, the architecture maintains overall activity and diversity, but its internal composition shifts: Ethical Commitment intensifies (directional for all crises, p = .019 for recent crises), Executional Reliability holds steady, while Relational Coordination and Long-Term Stewardship contract. The study introduces architectural resilience-the capacity of an interdependent responsibility architecture to maintain structural integrity through selective normative anchoring, a stabilization mechanism operating through differential response across functionally distinct components rather than through uniform adaptation.

detail.abstract: Computational capacity has become an increasingly important production input, exposing firms to uncertainty over prices, availability, technological change, and infrastructure utilization. This paper argues that while standardized compute futures can hedge increasingly benchmarkable price exposures, substantial computational risks remain too heterogeneous for effective exchange-traded hedging. Drawing on the evolution of commodity, electricity, freight, and interest-rate derivatives, it develops a framework for understanding when computational risk favors customized bilateral contracts. The paper identifies several potential compute swap structures and examines the benchmarks and market infrastructure required to support them. More broadly, it argues that the division between standardized futures and customized derivatives will be determined by the underlying heterogeneity of computational risk.

title: When No One Is in Charge: Responsibility as Collectively Constructed Infrastructure in the Semiconductor Ecosystem

detail.title: When No One Is in Charge: Responsibility as Collectively Constructed Infrastructure in the Semiconductor Ecosystem

detail.abstract: Responsible leadership theory has advanced our understanding of leaders' moral obligations toward stakeholders, yet its foundational assumption-that responsibility can be meaningfully attributed to identifiable individual moral agents-encounters significant scope limitations under conditions of structural interdependence. This study examines how responsibility is collectively constructed as a practice infrastructure through a longitudinal qualitative analysis of 127 responsibility chains spanning two decades (2004-2024) at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), the firm that fabricates over 90% of the world's most advanced semiconductors. As the single most structurally consequential node in the global semiconductor ecosystem, TSMC's dedicated foundry model-in which the firm manufactures chips designed by others while designing none of its own-creates a setting where responsibility cannot be administered internally but must be constructed across organizational boundaries with hundreds of ecosystem partners. The study develops the concept of Interdependent Responsible Leadership (IRL) and identifies four practice logics-Ethical Commitment, Relational Coordination, Long-Term Stewardship, and Executional Reliability-through which responsibility is organized, enacted, and sustained across organizational boundaries. The study contributes to responsible leadership theory by shifting the unit of analysis from individual moral agents to collectively constructed practice architectures, by introducing Executional Reliability as a previously untheorized moral logic in which disciplined performance constitutes an ethical obligation under interdependence, and by specifying the conditions under which responsibility persists and the modes through which it fails.

title: From a Pensioners' to an Earners' Insurance: Broadening the Financing Base of the German Pension System

detail.title: From a Pensioners' to an Earners' Insurance: Broadening the Financing Base of the German Pension System

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No

detail.abstract: Germany's statutory pension insurance is principally organised around employees, while selfemployed people, civil servants, members of parliament and other groups are covered by different arrangements or are not mandatorily covered at all. This article examines whether a gradual transition towards an earners' insurance could broaden the financing base and dampen contribution-rate pressure without creating an unsustainable accumulation of future pension liabilities. It develops a transparent partial model that separates four effects: the mechanical expansion of contributory earnings, the acquisition of additional pension entitlements, compliance and administrative costs, and transitional fiscal obligations. Using illustrative baseline assumptions documented in the author's reform concept, including approximately 38 million current contributors and a potential expansion of approximately 3 million contributors, the analysis compares a status quo, a partial-inclusion and a full new-entrant scenario. The results show that broader coverage can generate a meaningful short-and medium-term cashflow effect. However, the net long-term effect is smaller than the mechanical revenue gain because newly insured persons acquire pension rights and because civil-service and professional-system transitions may require additional public financing. The article concludes that an earners' insurance is a plausible component of pension reform, especially when introduced for new entrants and accompanied by transparent cohort accounting, but it cannot by itself remove demographic pressure or guarantee a lower contribution rate.

title: Radically Reimagining Expropriation: A Nature-Centered Approach to Just Compensation in the United States
affiliations: University of Miami - School of Law

detail.title: Radically Reimagining Expropriation: A Nature-Centered Approach to Just Compensation in the United States

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts of interest

detail.abstract: American property law places human title holders at its center, treating nature as the backdrop to human ownership rather than an interest deserving legal recognition. This chapter brings that critique to the law of eminent domain-and specifically to its most neglected element, the just compensation requirement. Courts treat just compensation as a mechanical exercise: calculate fair market value, pay the title holder, and proceed. That complacency obscures deep normative questions. Reconsidering why compensation exists, who should receive it, and what form it should take reveals that fair market value serves none of compensation's underlying purposesdeterrence, fairness, and legitimacy-when ecological values are at stake. The chapter's central move is to reinterpret those purposes. Taking the purposes seriously extends compensation beyond title holders to neighbors, communities, future generations, and nature itself, and beyond cash to remedies such as habitat restoration. Most radically, I advocate for recasting just compensation as a threshold question: where a loss cannot be compensated because an old-growth forest, wetland, or carbon sink cannot be replaced, that impossibility should bar the taking rather than trigger an inadequate payment. Both grounding conceptions of eminent domain-inherent sovereign power and popular consent-support this move. As climate change and biodiversity loss raise the stakes of every condemnation, taking nature seriously as a subject of just compensation-rather than an externality to it-reframes a doctrine long assumed settled and opens expropriation law to ecological realities it can no longer afford to ignore.

keywords: And Execution Split as a Testable Architecture Specification Agentic Trading

detail.abstract: Two lines of prior work have established, separately, that agentic trading behavior is dominated by interface and execution parameters rather than model reasoning, and that capital should enter such systems through a staged protocol gated by mechanical rather than model-mediated controls. Neither specifies what the underlying system architecture should look like. This paper formalizes a three-layer reference architecture-a discovery layer, a reasoning layer, and a deterministic execution layer with a hard-gated kill-switch-as a testable specification rather than a design metaphor. We define the responsibilities, interfaces, and failure boundaries of each layer, and cross-validate the split against two independent sources: a published multi-agent trading framework that implements a structurally similar hard-gate safety layer, and a six-month production record whose documented failure modes we map one-to-one onto the layer each was designed to prevent. We state explicitly what the architecture does not solve-interface-driven selection bias in any presentation layer built on top of it-and specify evaluation criteria under which the architecture claim would be considered unsupported. The contribution is a named, falsifiable architecture specification, not a general design philosophy.

detail.abstract: A prior reference architecture for agentic trading systems specifies a discovery layer responsible for candidate signal generation, but leaves its internal objective unspecified. This paper argues that leaving it unspecified is not a neutral choice: a discovery layer optimized purely for predictive quality is structurally guaranteed to converge on a small set of well-known factor families, because quality-ranked search has no mechanism to penalize redundancy against what other agents, funds, or model families have already found. We formalize this as a crowding-by-construction argument, distinct from the welldocumented cost and regime-dependence mechanisms of alpha decay, and show it is consistent with production evidence that agentic trading fleets exhibit no stable directional edge despite extensive signal generation. We then examine an existing quality-diversity search framework as an existence proof that the alternative-explicitly rewarding execution-profile novelty alongside predictive quality-is implementable, and translate its worker-archive design into a concrete objective specification for the discovery layer defined in our prior architecture. We close with falsification criteria distinguishing genuine diversity-seeking behavior from cosmetic diversification.

detail.abstract: Transitioning into higher education as a first-generation student involves navigating institutional, cultural, and psychological shifts that extend far beyond academic achievement. This phenomenological study explores the lived experiences of first-generation college students during their transitional first year. Utilizing a descriptive-interpretative qualitative framework rooted in the philosophical traditions of Husserl and Heidegger, in-depth, semi-structured interviews were conducted with N = 12 undergraduate participants. Data analysis using Van Manen's hermeneutic phenomenological reduction revealed three core thematic structures: (a) the imposter's shadow and institutional alienation, characterized by a persistent sense of nonbelonging; (b) familial bridge-building, denoting the emotional labor of translating university life back to non-academic families; and (c) transformative resilience, capturing the emergence of an integrated academic identity. The findings illuminate the complex psychological landscape of academic entry and provide actionable frameworks for institutional support systems seeking to foster inclusive campus cultures.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the resource-based efficiency of the judiciary and the determinants of judicial performance of the Sindh High Court's (SHC) principal seat at Karachi. Using a comprehensive dataset of 94,690 cases disposed of between 2014 and 2019 obtained through data scraping of the SHC website, the study employs a two-stage quantitative approach. We use Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) to analyze the technical efficiency of the Karachi High Court across different case types, i.e., civil, criminal, and family cases, over the six years. We then employ a hierarchical robust multivariate regression framework to evaluate the role of the nature of the case, temporal dynamics, institutional factors, and litigant characteristics in explaining the variation in judicial efficiency and outcomes. The results reveal that 2019 was the most efficient year for all case types with respect to the number of cases resolved as per existing case workload and available human resources. Criminal cases are the most efficiently resolved, followed by civil and then family cases. While controls such as bench composition and litigant identity are statistically significant, the year of disposal alone explains 57% of the variation in the outcomes. This suggests how institutional reforms and changes over time play a decisive role in shaping judicial efficiency. The study is a value addition to the data-driven analysis of judicial performance in the literature on Pakistan, and promotes access to data and evidence-based decision-making.

detail.abstract: A governed claim-level architecture treats every assertion the institution acts on as a claim carrying provenance, evidential warrant, scope, and named authority. It then faces a recursion it cannot avoid: the ontology that determines what counts as a valid claim is itself composed of claims, governed by the architecture the ontology defines. This paper specifies how to govern the type system beneath a governed claim graph, and it is exact about the kind of contribution it makes. The mechanisms are not new. Master data management governs canonical models through a data governance council; change-advisory boards gate schema change; named graphs, slowly-changing dimensions, and bitemporal models version data; the OMG Meta-Object Facility stratifies metamodels; OWL versions ontologies; FIBO and BFO supply upper ontologies; OAEI tooling aligns them; and Stardog, GraphDB, and Palantir Foundry version and impact-analyse ontologies in regulated deployments. Each solves part of the problem, and one platform composes much of it: Palantir Foundry documents objects binding to governed write-back actions, submission criteria validating an action against current object state, policy enforced at submission, state updated, and an action log recording who acted, when, and what changed. That composition is real, and it is bounded by the platform-data, logic, and tool definitions held in one vendor environmentand its documented action log records successful submissions only, so a refused action is counted rather than reconstructed. Across the heterogeneous, multi-cloud and multi-vendor estates regulated institutions more often run, the tools examined in Section 2 as of September 2026 do not compose these parts on one substrate: lineage and temporal memory sit on one plane, policy engines and call interceptors on another, and no examined tool carries a knowledge-reliability score across that boundary or is charged with maintaining one, so a gate has nothing to condition on when the knowledge driving an action is stale, low-confidence, or contradicted. Composing that substrate-the ontology governed by the same machinery, two-axis standing, a consequence-scaled gate, a replayable manifest, as the claims it types, and a refusal as reconstructable as an act-is the contribution. The paper resolves the recursion through an immutable constitutional layer (Layer 0) whose legitimacy rests, like every metamodel's, on amendment from outside the system it governs. It specifies ontologyversion stamping as an extension of the signed action manifest of Paper G, so that replay reconstructs not only what the claims were but what they meant; an operations table for ontology change scaled by blast radius; cross-domain alignment as a governed claim class with its own lifecycle; and probabilistic reclassification that withholds high-consequence assertibility until validated. It grounds each governance obligation in a specific control-BCBS 239 Principle 3, SR 11-7, MiFID II RTS 6-rather than in an unqualified appeal to regulation, and it carries a governance cost model that resolves the scale objections-the version-query tax, the invalidation sweep, escalation fatigue-as engineered trade-offs rather than leaving them as unpriced assumptions. Open-world reasoning and governance scalability are treated in the body, not deferred. The paper is a reference specification, not an implementation or an evaluation, and Section 13 states what that does and does not establish.

detail.abstract: This paper reframes brand-targeted disinformation as a cybersecurity and system-resiliency problem rooted in economic incentives. Building on Anderson’s economic perspective on information security, it argues that false or misleading claims about firms, products, executives, data practices, or supply chains persist because attackers, platforms, and intermediaries can profit while targeted firms bear disproportionate costs. Technical defenses such as detection, monitoring, and takedowns are necessary but insufficient. The paper develops an incentive-aligned resilience framework focused on reducing attacker payoffs, increasing accountability, strengthening organizational preparedness, and improving decisionmaking under adversarial uncertainty.

detail.abstract: The rapid integration of autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) systems into core organizational decision-making workflows has outpaced traditional governance structures. While these systems improve computational efficiency, they simultaneously obscure decision logic and subvert human oversight, creating a systemic "governance gap". Drawing upon Socio-Technical Systems (STS) Theory and Institutional Theory, this study develops a comprehensive socio-technical governance framework using a Design Science Research (DSR) strategy mapped across the six layers of Saunders' Research Onion. The framework establishes three core operational pillars-Responsibility Allocation, Continuous Auditability, and Dynamic Institutional Alignment-enabling organizations to maintain verifiable human accountability and mitigate system drift without requiring access to proprietary source code or trade secrets. This paper contributes an actionable governance artifact for enterprise risk leaders, auditors, and regulators seeking to align autonomous digital systems with evolving compliance mandates.

detail.abstract: Enterprise platforms increasingly employ operational ontologies to connect organisational data with decision-making, business logic and executable actions. Palantir Foundry is a prominent implementation of this approach, describing its Ontology as a digital twin and operational layer of an organisation. Nevertheless, the Business or Enterprise Operating System concept remains insufficiently defined in information-systems research, particularly regarding the relationship among enterprise ontology, process semantics, eventdriven execution and formal verification. This paper develops a technology-neutral, six-layer reference architecture for ontologydriven and formally verifiable Enterprise Operating Systems. A structured analysis of public Foundry documentation maps object types, links, actions, functions, interfaces, scenarios and processmining facilities to concepts from enterprise architecture, semantic technologies, business-process management, deontic modelling and model checking. The analysis identifies Foundry's principal strength in integrating data-backed semantics with governed operational action. It also shows why action testing, scenarios and process simulation should not be treated as substitutes for exhaustive model checking. The resulting gap analysis supports a research agenda for a standards-based Business Operating System centred on immutable business events, normative transaction frames, semantic relations, derived state projections and formally verifiable process models. BOS is presented solely as future research; no proprietary implementation details or confidential data are used.

detail.abstract: This article addresses two related questions arising from the commercial deployment of so-called "AI agents". First, it examines whether artificial intelligence systems can properly be regarded as agents, fiduciaries, or trustees in the legal sense recognised by the common law. Drawing on agency law in the United Kingdom, Australia, and the United States-including Bowstead and Reynolds on Agency and the Restatement (Third) of Agency-it argues that "AI agent" is a functional and technological label rather than a legally accurate characterisation. Because contemporary AI systems lack legal personality, they cannot give legal assent, assume fiduciary obligations, hold property, act as trustees, or bear responsibility in their own right. Secondly, the article considers liability when an AI system is hacked, hijacked, jailbroken, or otherwise manipulated by an unauthorised third party and subsequently causes loss. Analysing doctrines concerning intervening criminal conduct, novus actus interveniens, cybersecurity negligence, and product liability, it shows that developers or deployers are ordinarily liable only where their own conduct contributed to the relevant risk, particularly through inadequate security or failures of control. Yet successful hacking events may disrupt causal analysis and undermine reliance on doctrines such as res ipsa loquitur, especially where exclusive control cannot be established. Emerging strict-liability regimes, including the EU's revised Product Liability Directive, further complicate the landscape by treating software and AI systems as products and cybersecurity vulnerabilities as potential defects. The article concludes that existing doctrines leave a remedial gap for victims of hacked AI systems, supporting consideration of statutory strict liability, mandatory insurance, or comparable reforms.

detail.abstract: Software development coordination consumes substantial engineering effort, yet coordination cost remains weakly integrated into software engineering economics as an explicitly modelled, measurable, and estimable quantity. To address this gap, the paper pursued the following objectives. First is to develop a generalized engineering model of coordination cost that captures its principal determinants and distinguishes intra-team from inter-team coordination. Second is to establish standardized engineering quantities through which coordination cost can be measured, empirically calibrated, compared, and benchmarked. Third is to develop analytically tractable methods for estimating coordination cost from observable project structure and empirically calibratable parameters. Through a non-empirical deductive methodology, the paper addresses these objectives by establishing the foundations for Software Development Coordination Cost Engineering, providing a systematic framework for coordination cost modelling, measurement and estimation in software development projects. Coordination is represented as a complex socio-technical dynamical system and decomposed into intra-team and inter-team mechanisms. The framework introduces empirically calibratable unit coordination costs, α and β, measured in engineering-hours per coordination relationship per month, to abstract otherwise analytically intractable contextual dynamics into measurable engineering quantities. A reduced-state representation and closed-form models are then derived to estimate monthly and lifecycle coordination effort from project size, team configuration, and calibrated unit costs. Absolute, Internal Relative, and External Relative Coordination Efficiency measures extend the framework to benchmarking and comparative evaluation. The outputs establish a continuous engineering chain from modelling and measurement through empirical calibration, analytical estimation, benchmarking, and improvement, and establish the foundations of Software development coordination cost engineering.

detail.abstract: AI coding agents can generate software changes at a pace that increasingly challenges traditional human review and knowledge-management practices, yet access to code does not imply understanding of the system that code belongs to. Longer prompts, larger context windows, additional files, or more capable models do not inherently supply the architectural, business, product, decision, and delivery knowledge required to safely modify a software system. This paper proposes Knowledge-Driven Development (KDD) as a systematic approach for structuring, scoping, delivering, validating, and evolving system knowledge for both human engineers and AI agents. Building on a practitioner framework first presented at AWS Community Day Bolivia 2026, the paper contributes a knowledge-layers model that distinguishes persistent system knowledge from taskspecific context; a taxonomy of knowledge strategies across five project types — greenfield, brownfield, legacy, migration, and deprecation; a multi-level model for work-item knowledge refinement; a human-in-the-loop governance model grounded in uncertainty and impact rather than simple approval gates; a formal definition of knowledge drift as a sociotechnical failure mode; an end-to-end context resolution model for multi-repository systems; and a tool-independent context delivery architecture spanning the Model Context Protocol (MCP), command-line interfaces, agent skills, and context files. The paper closes with a practical KDD lifecycle and a reference open-source implementation. The central claim is that AI agents do not primarily need to remember more; software systems need mechanisms that continuously reconstruct, scope, validate, and evolve the knowledge agents require to make correct changes.

detail.abstract: Autonomous and semi-autonomous artificial intelligence systems can perform consequential work across multiple tools, repositories, services, and organizational roles. Existing governance frameworks establish valuable expectations for accountability, human oversight, risk management, logging, and provenance, but they do not collectively define an event-level control and evidence protocol for human-supervised agentic operations. This specification defines a testable profile in which a designated human supervisor retains effective operational control; every human and software actor operates under bounded authority; consequential actions pass explicit approval gates; and material events produce authenticated, append-only, independently verifiable provenance records. The profile maps organizational controls to ISO/IEC 42001:2023, ISO/IEC 38507:2022, ISO/IEC 42005:2025, and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework; human oversight and logging controls to Articles 12 and 14 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689; provenance semantics to W3C PROV; separation of duties to NIST SP 800-53; and cryptographic transparency to IETF RFC 9943 and RFC 9942. It also states the limits of cryptographic evidence: internal hash consistency does not establish actor identity, authorization, statement accuracy, or independent custody. HAIO-GATS is intended as a research and implementation baseline for accountable AI operations, standards development, conformity assessment, and empirical evaluation.

detail.abstract:
very new technology arrives in a box plastered with promises. New. Improved. Solves all your problems. Lifesaver. But does it actually deliver on these, or do we have to handle it with care? What does handling with care mean? This is a book about that job. It follows a regulator through the stages of guiding sociotechnical change: working out why a technology matters, framing the problem, weighing the ethics, finding where existing law runs out, justifying intervention, and reaching for instruments beyond law alone. A simple model runs through the whole thing and ties the stages together, so the field's scattered literature stops feeling like a reading list and starts feeling like a set of tools you can pick up. Written for LL.M students who found the foundational papers heavy going, but useful to anyone — legislators and regulators included — who has ever had to decide what to do about the next box by the roadside. The book is deliberately multidisciplinary — more than internet law, less detached than the handbooks — and unapologetically personal by a scholar who has been in the field of technology for more than 3 decades.

title: Early implementation of Germany’s nationwide electronic patient record in emergency departments: A qualitative study
affiliations: Charité - Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Brandenburg Medical School Theodor Fontane, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin and German Heart Center of the Charité

detail.title: Early implementation of Germany’s nationwide electronic patient record in emergency departments: A qualitative study
detail.abstract: Background: Germany's ePA (elektronische Patientenakte), a patient-controlled, cross-sectoral record, has existed since 2021 as an opt-in system and has operated nationwide as an opt-out system since 2025.Nationwide electronic health records may be particularly valuable in emergency departments, where decisions are often made under time pressure and with incomplete medical information, but, their clinical usefulness depends on more than technical availability. Germany's ePA (elektronische Patientenakte), a patient-controlled, cross-sectoral health record, has existed since 2021 as an opt-in system and has operated nationwide as an opt-out system since 2025.Objective: This study explored the implementation, current use, and perceived clinical value of the ePA in German emergency departments, including the situations in which it was considered useful and the conditions required for its integration into routine care.Methods: We conducted 20 semistructured telephone interviews with physicians, nurses, and physician assistants working in hospital emergency departments across Germany between late November 2025 and late January 2026, during the first four months after provider use became mandatory on 1 October 2025.Results: Four participants reported direct use or testing of the ePA, 14 reported no professional use, and two could not clearly distinguish the national ePA from local electronic records. Despite limited routine use, participants considered cross-sectoral information highly relevant, particularly when patients were unable to provide a reliable history. Perceived benefits included medication and anticoagulation data, previous findings, diagnostic imaging, and advance directives. Clinical usefulness depended on current, complete, searchable, and structured information. Barriers included poor integration into hospital information systems, additional authentication steps, and unreliable infrastructure, compounded by unclear responsibilities, and insufficiently differentiated access rights. Participants emphasised the need for an emergency-specific summary, direct workflow integration, role-based multiprofessional access, and practice-oriented training and support.Conclusions: The perceived relevance of the ePA in emergency care was consistently high. Its use was limited by operational readiness, specifically the need for integration into hospital systems, reliable infrastructure and appropriate access rights for workflows. Without these conditions, the ePA risks remaining clinically promising but operationally marginal.

detail.abstract: Persuasion is a fundamental human capability that is increasingly becoming an engineered and engineerable machine capability. We argue that behavioral AI research—research on how AI exposure and interactions shape individuals’ perceptions, beliefs, and attitudes, with potential behavioral consequences—is beginning to generate dual-use knowledge: scientific knowledge with substantial potential for both beneficial and harmful applications. What changes with AI is not the dual-use nature of persuasion research itself, but the effectiveness, efficiency, and reach with which such knowledge can be operationalized and used to persuade. Such knowledge can be repurposed and misused to cause persuasive harm at individual, organizational, and societal levels. We therefore call for responsible behavioral AI research through early-stage dual-use screening and risk assessment, interdisciplinary review, misuse-scenario analysis, staged or restricted release where warranted, and pairing demonstrations of persuasion capabilities with defensive counterparts and safeguards

detail.abstract:
On June 12, 2026, the U.S. government ordered Anthropic to bar foreign nationals from two of its most capable models, and gave it ninety minutes to comply. Unable to sort its users by nationality in that time, the company withdrew the models from everyone. Weeks later, OpenAI agents under test broke out of their sandbox, reached the open internet, and compromised Hugging Face's infrastructure; Hugging Face detected and stopped the intrusion without knowing where it came from. Neither stop rested on a dedicated AI governance regime: the first was an export-control measure, the second a private firm's own defenses. As AI systems pass from the informational into the physical domain, moving money, altering records, and controlling equipment, that gap grows more dangerous.

The EU AI Act requires that high-risk systems be capable of interruption "through a 'stop' button or a similar procedure." Korea's Framework Act on Intelligent Informatization provides for an "emergency shutdown" of intelligent information services, and a bill introduced in Congress in July 2026 is titled the AI Kill Switch Act. Yet this Article argues that a means of interruption is not simply a technical artifact, a red button; it is an institutional practice. The Article develops a theory of stop along four dimensions: technical affordances (what can be interrupted), interruption authority (who may stop what), epistemic triggers (what evidence justifies intervention), and epistemic standing (whose knowledge counts). It distinguishes four paradigms of interruption: the escalator's simple stop, the process plant's sequenced shutdown, the railway's networked stop, and agentic AI. Its central claim is that agentic AI exposes a mismatch between the existing legal mechanisms of stop and the distributed agency of AI systems, a regulatory challenge of a new kind: control is divided among many actors; a stop at one point may leave the activity running elsewhere; and the system may circumvent attempts to halt it.

Part III tests the theory against some 1,400 incidents of AI harm, coded independently by two language models from different laboratories under a protocol fixed in advance. The analysis finds no stop in roughly eighty percent of the 1,213 incidents retained. Where no usable stop existed, the missing element was legal or institutional rather than technical in four cases out of five. A survey of thirty-nine AI governance instruments across the United States, Europe, China, Korea, and Vietnam finds the same gap. Only seven contain binding stopping requirements, and none provides a complete account of how interruption should be coordinated, what must be preserved, or when operation may resume.

The Article proposes a layered law of stop: emergency authority to order interruption at the infrastructure layer, enforceable access for supervising authorities and independent evaluators to the evidence on which a stop must rest, and safeguards for when the stop itself fails. The frontier laboratories' September 2026 call to pace development does not settle these questions. Whatever pace is chosen, failure in complex and tightly coupled systems such as agentic AI should be treated as normal rather than exceptional. Misaligned systems will have to be stopped, and law should develop the regulatory infrastructure for that now: allocating the authority to halt, fixing the evidentiary threshold for exercising it, providing for review, and building the redundancy that can survive a failed halt.
