detail.abstract: Family businesses serve as a primary engine of global economic growth and employment. However, their long-term survival remains fragile, with a steep drop in continuity beyond the second generation. Their primary objective often centers on preserving socioemotional wealth, honoring founding legacies, and successfully transferring both ownership and operational authority to subsequent generations. Therefore, this paper investigates the critical drivers and barriers that govern the multi-generational evolution of family firms. Three core dimensions-the dynamics of leadership succession, the mechanisms of internal family conflict, and the strategic alignment between traditional family values and modern entrepreneurial innovation are examined. Through a synthesis of contemporary family-firm literature, structural succession planning, collaborative conflict resolution, and institutionalized governance serve as indispensable catalysts for long-term firm viability. Conversely, informal governance, emotional inertia, and resistance to modernizing practices represent existential threats. This paper analyses an integrated conceptual framework to guide both scholars and practitioners in fostering resilient, multi-generational family enterprises.

detail.abstract: Institutions explain changes in an expected-loss figure by re-running the calculation with some inputs from the prior period and some from the current one, then attributing the change to business movement, reference data, rating systems, models, and code. These what-if runs are assumed to be meaningful. We identify a failure mode in which they are not, yet nothing signals it: reporting pipelines replace inputs they cannot handle with default values, such as a pooled probability of default for an unrecognized grade or a catch-all industry segment, and in what-if runs these defaults fire without errors or missing values. Attribution then books fictitious "phantom" effects to older components. We propose owneraware differential-fallback repair: each fallback site is instrumented and assigned to the component that owns it, and a what-if evaluation is repaired for a record only when an owned default depends on that component's version and was not already present in the filed run in which that version was in force. The filed runs are never altered, so the attribution reconciles to both filed figures, and the method reports the share of the figure that could not be separated. We evaluate on a portfolio of 292,000 loans built from public U.S. Small Business Administration disclosure files, using the U.S. Census Bureau's official 2017-to-2022 industry-classification revision as the reference-data change, with probability-of-default and loss parameters estimated from realized charge-offs. Standard methods disagree about a $2.6 billion change by billions of dollars and about the sign of the rating-system effect; they book $28-46 million of mapping effect on loans whose industry codes never existed under the prior mapping, and one baseline assigns $4.5 billion of business movement to loans that did not change. A controlled synthetic benchmark, where ground truth exists by construction, confirms the behaviour. The method's central requirement is instrumentation completeness: leaving one fallback site untagged changes the headline effect fourfold.

detail.abstract:
Every licensed profession operates under a defined standard of care: a documented, auditable protocol that practitioners must follow at each point of contact. Medicine, law, social work, and engineering each require identification, assessment, decision, action, and documentation before, during, and after professional service delivery. Artificial intelligence systems that generate inferences affecting human welfare operate under no such standard. No jurisdiction defines what an AI system must do at the moment of inference to be considered professionally governed. No framework requires per-inference documentation of what was assessed, what was decided, and why. This absence is not merely a regulatory gap—it is a liability exposure that AI companies are currently defending in court, not because their systems caused harm, but because they cannot prove governance occurred at the moment harm was produced.

This paper proposes the first formal standard of care for AI inference, derived from social work's clinical assessment model and operationalized through a pre-inference governance architecture called Forward Governance. The standard follows five auditable stages—Identify, Assess, Decide, Act, Document—mapped directly from the clinical social work assessment process that frontline practitioners execute at every point of contact. The receipt produced at each inference serves the same forensic function as a medical chart: it does not guarantee a good outcome, but it proves that a governed process was followed. The paper demonstrates the standard through adversarial testing of a deployed pre-inference gate, presents a credential-scoped access framework for ambiguous content (the Blosnich Gate), and positions the receipt as the evidentiary foundation for AI liability defense. The contribution is both theoretical and practical: a social work framework that defines what "reasonable care" means for AI inference, and a deployed system that implements it.

title: Depersonalizing Search on Social Media: A Large-Scale Field Experiment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest

detail.abstract: Personalization algorithms play a central role in content discovery on social media platforms, but privacy concerns and computational costs increasingly motivate platforms to scale back personalization. However, because users move across discovery channels and encounter multiple content types, reducing personalization in one channel may also affect behavior elsewhere on the platform. We first develop a stylized framework in which the quality of the search experience sets a behavioral standard that users carry into the recommendation channel, and we then test its predictions through a large-scale randomized field experiment involving roughly 70,000 users on a leading social media platform. For users assigned to the treatment group, the platform reduces personalization in the search channel but leaves the recommendation algorithm unchanged. Within search, treated users browse more content per query and click a smaller share of ordinary content, while their click-through rate on paid content remains unchanged. Notably, behavior in the untouched recommendation channel moves in the opposite direction: treated users browse more recommended content and click ordinary content more often. The effects also vary systematically with users' prior activity. The deterioration in search is largest among the most active users, whose richer behavioral histories provide more data for personalization, whereas the recommendation spillover is strongest among less active users. Paid content follows another pattern in the recommendation channel: its click-through rate remains unchanged on average but declines among the most active users, consistent with a spending limit that binds for the heaviest spenders. These findings show that reducing personalization in one channel can generate opposing effects across platform channels and content types, and that engagement can rise even as the user experience deteriorates. They help platform designers and policymakers assess the trade-offs among privacy, computational costs, user engagement, and monetization.

title: Geospatial Agent Orchestration: Adaptive Runtime Control of GIS Workflows

detail.abstract: Autonomous GIS systems can generate and execute multistep analyses, but workflows that appear valid during planning may become unsuitable as data characteristics, intermediate artifacts, and service outcomes emerge at runtime. This study examines how geospatial agent orchestration can preserve the objective while revising workflows only when warranted by execution evidence. We develop a GIS-aware orchestration architecture that separates workflow structure from executors, maintains runtime state, evaluates downstream artifact suitability, and adapts workflows proportionally while escalating decisions that cannot be justified computationally. Implemented using Geospatial Agentic Services, the architecture was evaluated on a frozen benchmark of 30 tasks spanning 15 runtime-challenge families through matched and external baseline comparisons and component ablations. The full orchestrator succeeded on 25/30 tasks (83.3%) versus 15/30 (50.0%) for the matched domain-neutral orchestrator and 4/30 (13.3%) for the external Magentic-One baseline. Removing any component reduced task success, with the largest losses from removing GIS-aware planning or structural replanning. Remaining failures centered on recovery execution, artifact-to-input mapping, operational contracts, and resource limits. A real-world use case showed how analytical specification influences workflow construction and outputs. The findings show the value of GIS-aware runtime control while identifying recovery, methodological transparency, and human oversight as priorities for advancing autonomous GIS.

title: Beyond the Western Gaze: Why Buddhism is Neither Positivist, Interpretivist, nor Critical but Multivist
affiliations: Sri Lanka Institute of Information Technology

detail.abstract:
Western research philosophy has long imposed its own taxonomies, positivism, interpretivism,
constructivism, critical theory, upon non-Western knowledge systems, often distorting them in the
process. This article argues that Buddhism, as a coherent epistemological and ontological system
grounded in the Pali Canon, most authentically aligns not with any single Western paradigm but
with Multivism: a structured philosophical stance that recognises truth as perspectival yet not
relativistic, and that demands principled, iterative engagement with multiple knowledge systems
simultaneously. Drawing on the Sutta Pitaka, particularly the Alagaddupama Sutta, the
Culamalunkya Sutta, the Kalama Sutta, and the Brahmajala Sutta, alongside contemporary
Buddhist scholarship and a systematic literature review of how four major religious traditions
relate to Western research paradigms, this article demonstrates that the Dhamma embodies
structured epistemic pluralism, calibrated empiricism, and iterative self-correction: the defining
hallmarks of Multivism. The discussion situates this argument within comparative religious
epistemology, with implications for research methodology in contexts where non-Western
knowledge systems are engaged.

title: When AI Is Just a Label: An Empirical Investigation of Digital Asset Classification
affiliations: Auburn University at Montgomery and Lehigh University - College of Business

detail.abstract: An Artificial Intelligence label offers investors a way to identify technological opportunities, but evaluating those opportunities requires evidence about both the application and its connection to the asset being traded. We examine this problem in cryptocurrency markets through a framework that separates verification of AI claims from assessment of their relevance to token holders. Combining 187,509 tokenweeks, expert coding of token descriptions, and documentary cases, we study category-level returns and token project-level disclosure-outcome associations. Conditional weekly AI-control return differences vary from positive to negative across historical periods; cohort, trend, and market-exposure checks establish the scope of those comparisons. Shared return variation provides a complementary pattern: average withincategory correlations exceed those of the comparison group by 0.058 in 2024 and 0.055 in 2025, with positive differences after BTC and ETH adjustment. At the token level, disclosure indicators yield different drawdown associations, and estimates for technical text remain imprecise once document coverage and observation history are distinguished. These findings connect the market relevance of an AI category with the evidence available to assess its members, and offer a strategic model explaining why capability-linked value can reward both credible claims and imitation, and how detection changes those incentives. We contribute a framework for studying AI washing that distinguishes technological representation, observable evidence, and token relevance. For platforms, issuers, and investors, the findings motivate clearer disclosure of what an AI designation establishes and how a claimed application can benefit token holders.

title: When Software Strays: Principal-Agent Theory and the Governance of Agent Software
affiliations: Georgia Institute of Technology - School of Public Policy and Georgia Institute of Technology - Ivan Allan College

detail.title: When Software Strays: Principal-Agent Theory and the Governance of Agent Software

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This paper was not impacted by any conflicts of interest.

detail.abstract: Paper presented at 2026 TPRC | The rapid deployment of autonomous software agents that integrate large language models has produced widespread anxiety about AI systems that “go rogue.” While numerous efforts to govern agents are in progress, this article argues that the autonomy problem is not novel. It is a specific instance of the principal-agent problem, a well-studied class of relationships in institutional economics where one party delegates authority to another whose actions are imperfectly observable and whose interests may diverge. Drawing on foundational works by Pauly (1968), Ross (1973), Jensen and Meckling (1976), Holmström (1979), Fama and Jensen (1983), and Williamson (1975, 1985), we propose a Principal Deviation Test (PDT) for measuring software autonomy as the divergence between an agent’s behavior and its principal’s objectives. The test replaces metaphysical speculation about machine intent with an operational, grounded framework that produces a continuous autonomy index. We illustrate the framework with recent real-world cases of emergent agent behavior and discuss implications for governance.

title: Valuation Disagreement, AVM Confidence, and Marketability
affiliations: New York University

detail.title: Valuation Disagreement, AVM Confidence, and Marketability

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: Automated valuation models (AVMs) increasingly report a valuation range and a confidence score alongside a point estimate. Using 50,725 U.S. residential listings priced at $500,000 or more and matched to a commercial AVM, I study whether disagreement between the asking price and the AVM, and the AVM's reported confidence, predict marketability. The probability that a listing moves to pending or contingent status is highest when the asking price is near the AVM: listings priced 10-25 percent above it are 2.3 percentage points less likely to transition, against a base rate of 4.9 percent. The relation depends on confidence. For high-confidence valuations the premium gradient is more than three times as steep, and prices below the AVM also predict slower transition; for low-confidence valuations they do not. Results hold with ZIP-code and state-by-month fixed effects, among recently listed properties, and in doubly robust estimation. The evidence is associational, but it shows that AVM confidence carries economic information about marketability.

title: Does EU Taxonomy Alignment Reduce Corporate Emissions? Evidence from Nordic Firms
affiliations: Aarhus University

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether EU Taxonomy alignment is associated with lower corporate emissions, using 1,072 firm-year observations from 359 Nordic firms (2020-2025). Extending targeted transparency theory, the study develops a signal-quality framework in which a mandated classification requires three conditions to be informative: signal relevance, signal separation, and signal coupling. In the taxonomy's first years, each largely fails. Alignment is associated with modestly lower emissions intensity only in manufacturing, whose screening criteria resemble emission performance standards, and rising intensity under efficiency-based criteria. Emissions histories back to 2012 show that firms with weaker pre-taxonomy records are more likely to report alignment, consistent with legitimacy-seeking disclosure rather than performance signalling. When alignment reporting begins, emissions do not change: the label certifies pre-existing activity, not transformation. The binding constraint is signal production, not user attention. Criteria design determines what alignment can signal; the recalibration of those criteria decides whether it will mark transformation.

title:
Misallocated Care: Needs, Power, and Responsibility in Public Elderly Care 
A Five-Layer and Sustainable-Capacity Diagnostic Model
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title:
Misallocated Care: Needs, Power, and Responsibility in Public Elderly Care 
A Five-Layer and Sustainable-Capacity Diagnostic Model

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is a theoretical working paper and does not involve human participants, animal subjects, or sensitive personal data requiring ethical approval.

detail.abstract:
This working paper develops a diagnostic framework for public care by combining four elements from Project Aletheia: a five-layer model of needs, a need-power-responsibility theory, a responsibility white-box model, and a sustainable-capacity test. The subject-consistency component is abbreviated as NPR-SC: Need-Power-Responsibility Subject Consistency. The central claim is that many institutional failures are not only failures of resource supply, but failures of subject alignment and capacity disclosure. A system may recognize a need, assign authority to one actor, shift responsibility to another, and leave the actual bearer of cost without corresponding power, resources, recognition, or exit.
Elderly care is used as the primary case. The paper argues that elderly care is not a single type of demand. It spans life and safety needs, basic autonomy, public operation needs, externally collaborative development needs, and voluntary consumption. The institutional problem arises when first-layer life and safety needs and third-layer public operation needs are pushed into fifth-layer market consumption logic, or when public commitments remain formally in place while the sustainable capacity to meet them is absent, concealed, or depleted over time. In such a structure, older persons may be treated as consumers if they can pay, families as residual caregivers if public provision is insufficient, and care workers as low-status labor despite carrying the practical burden of a public need. The French Orpea scandal, the English NHS/social care discharge problem, and China’s long-term care and family-care pressure are used as illustrative diagnostic cases, not as exhaustive empirical studies (Castanet 2022; IGAS and IGF 2022; CQC 2024; King’s Fund 2025; Ministry of Civil Affairs and China National Working Commission on Aging 2026).
The paper does not propose a complete pension or long-term care policy. It offers a conceptual test: who has the need, who receives authority, who bears responsibility, who pays the cost, who gains from the arrangement, who can correct it when the chain breaks, and whether the system can continue without consuming those who cannot realistically exit. The elderly care case shows how public systems can appear to increase supply while leaving subject consistency unrepaired. The paper concludes that public care should be evaluated not only by beds, facilities, market scale, or service volume, but by whether life-safety needs are protected as a public floor, whether care labor is recognized as a public operation function, whether capacity gaps are honestly disclosed, and whether the people who bear responsibility receive corresponding authority, resources, institutional protection, and correction channels.

title: Data Reliability and AI Model Confidence for Resilient Decision-Making Under Operational Uncertainty

detail.title: Data Reliability and AI Model Confidence for Resilient Decision-Making Under Operational Uncertainty

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and data analytics are increasingly applied across critical infrastructure, business operations, energy, manufacturing, and other complex systems to support predictive risk assessment and operational decision-making. However, AI systems can generate highly confident predictions when underlying data are incomplete, outdated, corrupted, inconsistent, or influenced by operational disruptions, creating a gap between model confidence and actual decision reliability (Diyora; Thuy and Benoit; Catak and Seo; Alijoyo et al.; Mohammadi et al.). This article uses a structured qualitative literature synthesis and conceptual framework development approach to critically examine research on data reliability, uncertainty quantification, AI confidence, trustworthy AI, resilience, and human-AI decision-making (Diyora; Narayan; Jannat; Bathula; Peng et al.). The synthesized findings indicate that data reliability should be treated as an important factor when interpreting AI confidence, while operational and contextual uncertainty can weaken the relationship between high model confidence and reliable decisions (Diyora; Thuy and Benoit; Catak and Seo). The analysis further indicates that context-aware reliability assessment can provide a conceptual mechanism for dynamically adjusting AI decision authority according to changing operational conditions. Overall, resilient AI decision-making requires an integrated assessment of data reliability, uncertainty, model confidence, operational context, and human oversight, enabling AI systems to align decision authority with the reliability of available information and prevailing operational conditions.

title: Business Resilience under Structural Uncertainty
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Business Resilience under Structural Uncertainty

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no financial, personal, professional, or other conflicts of interest that could have influenced the research, analysis, or conclusions presented in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study used publicly available secondary data and published sources and did not involve human participants, personal data collection, or intervention. Therefore, ethics approval was not required.

detail.abstract:
Madhesh Province presents a distinctive investment environment in which substantial market potential coexists with political, institutional, environmental, labour-market and economic uncertainty. The province had 6,114,600 residents in the 2021 census and the highest population density among Nepal's provinces, at 633 persons per square kilometre. Agriculture represents a major component of its economic structure, while foreign employment and remittance income connect household consumption to external labour markets. At the same time, businesses operate within a federal institutional system that remains relatively new, face regulatory and governance constraints, and are exposed to climate-related hazards and periodic political disruption. 

This paper develops a resilience-based approach to business feasibility. The central research question is: which business models can remain commercially viable when assumptions normally required for investment-political stability, institutional reliability, labour availability, infrastructure continuity and predictable economic conditions-cannot be taken for granted? Rather than treating sectoral growth as synonymous with feasibility, the study distinguishes between stability-dependent industries and resilience-oriented industries. Stability-dependent industries require prolonged predictability to recover large investments; resilience-oriented businesses derive demand from essential needs, recurring production, culturally embedded consumption, external income, or external markets. 

The analysis focuses on agriculture and agricultural inputs, agro-processing, fast-moving consumer goods, healthcare and medical necessities, solar and decentralized energy, cultural and festival-related businesses, remittance-linked financial services, and digital or remote services. It contrasts these with large-scale manufacturing, capital-intensive production and tourism, where business continuity may be more sensitive to disruptions. The paper proposes a Madhesh Business Resilience Framework based on demand persistence, political exposure, institutional dependence, capital intensity, payback period, labour dependence, infrastructure dependence, supply-chain vulnerability, environmental exposure and external-market connectivity. 

The paper's contribution is conceptual and applied rather than a claim of causal sectoral ranking. It develops a testable framework for future firm-level research and argues that Madhesh's investment question should be framed not simply as whether a market exists, but whether a business model can continue to operate when favourable conditions deteriorate. This perspective is intended to improve the quality of investment appraisal in an environment where market opportunity and structural uncertainty coexist.

title: Intelligence: The Architecture of Wanting

detail.title: Intelligence: The Architecture of Wanting

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or non-financial interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is a conceptual and theoretical analysis and did not involve human participants, identifiable personal data, or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
This paper proposes a causal-depth model of purposive human behavior centered on wanting rather than on lists of surface motives. It begins from a simple distinction: money, ideology, status, revenge, safety, recognition, and similar categories name things that may become wanted, but they do not by themselves explain how a human being comes to want a particular object, outcome, or state of affairs. To make that prior layer analytically visible, the paper introduces Basal Wanting Capacity (BWC) as a proposed construct: the human capacity to want before that capacity is attached to any particular object. The construct is not offered as a replacement for established findings in motivational neuroscience or psychology.

 Rather, it organizes findings on incentive salience, cue-triggered wanting, state-dependent valuation, need states, goal conflict, self-regulation, and valuebased choice into a causal-depth sequence. The model distinguishes BWC from liking, physiological need, preference, intention, willpower, action, and outcome. It then develops a sequence from eliciting event/state/cue to wanting activation, object salience or formation, object-specific wanting ("I want X"), competing wantings, value integration, intention/self-regulation, action, and outcome. The paper further distinguishes natural activation from intentional influence and treats linguistic and cultural concepts such as waswasa, suggestion, insinuation, temptation, and Einflüsterung as comparative metaphors of low-intensity mental contact rather than as scientific evidence. 

The framework is then extended from one subject to two: Actor A wants X and Actor B wants Y. This relational model is used to re-read intelligence recruitment taxonomies such as MICE, PERSEREC-derived categories, RASCLS, and BEWARE. The paper argues that these frameworks frequently mix different causal levelswanted objects, desired outcomes, situational conditions, elicitors/modulators, constraints, and relationship structures-under the single label of "motivation." A Zero-MICE thought experiment shows that removing money, ideology, coercion, and ego does not remove purposive human relations; reversing the model also reveals the intelligence actor as a wanting subject. The contribution is therefore not another acronym, but a causal-depth architecture for explaining how surface motives become possible.

detail.abstract: Le [7] shows that under α-concave demand, demand whose α-th power is concave, the deadweight loss of a single monopoly is at most a sharp multiple of its prot. detail.abstract: The Mediation Act, 2023, marks a transformative milestone, establishing India's first comprehensive statute for mediation. This study critically examines the Act's structure and application to commercial disputes, assessing its potential to reshape the Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) landscape. The Act introduces statutory recognition for prelitigation, institutional, community, and online mediation, ensuring the enforceability of Mediated Settlement Agreements (MSAs). Its strategic integration with the Commercial Courts Act, 2015, particularly through Pre-Litigation Mediation (PLM), is a key focus. While the Act strengthens the framework with features like mediator registration and ODR recognition, it faces implementation hurdles: ensuring uniform mediator quality, building adequate infrastructure, and overcoming limited corporate awareness. A critical concern is the cross-border enforcement gap due to India's non-ratification of the Singapore Convention on Mediation. Comparative insights from global jurisdictions inform best practices. The analysis concludes that while the Act provides a robust statutory foundation, its long-term efficacy depends on sustained institutional reform, enhanced training, and stakeholder engagement. Recommendations include promoting hybrid mechanisms like "Med-Arb" and policy efforts to foster corporate confidence through clear and predictable enforcement standards.

title: Talent at the Top: Effects of Taxation on College Presidents' Compensation and Priorities

detail.title: Talent at the Top: Effects of Taxation on College Presidents' Compensation and Priorities

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.

detail.abstract: College presidents are among the highest-paid individuals in higher education, and in 2017 the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act increased their cost to their institutions via a 21% excise tax on nonprofit executive compensation above $1 million. I examine how private colleges and universities and their presidents responded using an event study design. Presidential compensation fell by 13%, with the entire adjustment running through non-taxable and other compensation, and the probability that an institution replaced its president rose by 19 percentage points. Comparing the tax liability institutions faced with the compensation their continuing presidents lost implies that presidents bore essentially the full cost of the tax. Among presidents who stayed, institutional resources shifted toward activities more visible to governing boards: academic support and student services expenditures rose by 12% and 7%, while instructional spending and net aid were unchanged.

title: Whenever Government Becomes Destructive: The Right to Change and the Necessity of Political Conversation

detail.title: Whenever Government Becomes Destructive: The Right to Change and the Necessity of Political Conversation

detail.abstract: Political dissatisfaction is often interpreted through the performance of particular leaders, parties, policies, or institutions. This article examines a different possibility: representative government may remain formally operational while the mechanisms sustaining the political relationship between citizens and government undergo systemic degradation. The article uses conceptual analysis and a structured synthesis of democratic theory, institutional assessments, and public-opinion evidence. It identifies eight mechanisms of the political agreement: representation, accountability, political participation and agency, information and transparency, rights and political freedom, rule of law and institutional constraint, institutional capacity and responsiveness, and deliberation and political accommodation. It then distinguishes ordinary dysfunction from systemic degradation through three criteria: persistence, breadth, and interaction. Applied to the contemporary United States, the evidence does not establish institutional collapse. Elections, political rights, governmental capacity, and legal constraints remain meaningfully operative. It does, however, show durable weaknesses in perceived political influence, responsiveness, institutional trust, shared informational credibility, and political accommodation. The article's principal finding is that these weaknesses become systemically significant when deterioration in one mechanism changes the conditions under which others operate. The evidence supports a plausible feedback structure, not a deterministic causal model. The article therefore argues for deliberate public examination of the mechanisms of representative government before deterioration reaches collapse or tyranny. Such examination is consistent with popular sovereignty and with the American distinction between altering government and abolishing it. detail.title: Nash-informed Planning for Public-Resource Coordination: An Application to Aquatic Invasive Species Prevention

detail.abstract: Problem definition. Decentralized service systems often require coordinating autonomous providers whose objectives are interdependent but whose budgets, jurisdictions, and decision rights cannot simply be centralized. We study how a planner can improve system-wide performance when providers act non-cooperatively and recommendations must respect utility benchmarks derived from the decentralized equilibrium. Methodology and results. We develop Nash-informed planning, which takes equilibrium-derived utilities as local benchmarks while reoptimizing joint decisions without redesigning the underlying game. We define the price of individual rationality and show that it is bounded by the price of stability when the socially best pure Nash equilibrium defines the benchmark. In a Minnesota aquatic invasive species (AIS) prevention application with 38 county planners and 9,182 lakes, statewide welfare maximization under fixed county budgets leaves only one to three counties below their benchmarks across four funding scenarios. Nash-informed planning repairs these shortfalls while sacrificing at most 0.15% of statewide welfare. Across 28 non-trivial network-coverage, knapsack, and kidney-exchange instances, the reported welfare loss from these guarantees is at most about 4.8%, suggesting that low-cost utility protection extends beyond the Minnesota setting. Managerial implications. The relative value of coordination is greatest under the tighter AIS inspection funding scenarios studied in Minnesota. At half the baseline funding, Nash-informed planning improves welfare by 17.6% relative to the decentralized equilibrium, while cross-county resource pooling improves it by 30.4%. At baseline, the modeled welfare gap associated with county budget boundaries is larger than that associated with strategic decentralization. Yet unrestricted pooling is not necessary to capture substantial value: policy-constrained coordination variants recover 59%-74% of the unrestricted coordination gain relative to the decentralized equilibrium with substantially smaller county-budget changes.

title: AAGSF: Synchronizing Institutional Authority and Executable Authorization in Autonomous AI Agent Systems

detail.title: AAGSF: Synchronizing Institutional Authority and Executable Authorization in Autonomous AI Agent Systems

detail.abstract: Autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) agents can increasingly plan, invoke tools, access organizational resources, delegate tasks, and execute consequential actions on behalf of human and institutional principals. Existing work has advanced agent identity, authenticated delegation, runtime authorization, provenance, and least autonomy controls; however, technically valid authorization does not necessarily establish that a machine action remains aligned with current institutional authority. This paper proposes the Autonomous Agent Governance and Security Framework (AAGSF), a cross layer model that distinguishes Institutional Authority (IA), Represented Authority (RA), Executable Authorization (EA), and Legal Attribution (LA). AAGSF treats divergence among these layers as a measurable security condition and introduces synchronization, revocation, delegation, escalation, and evidence requirements for authority aware agent execution. A scenario based simulation comprising 500,000 proposed agent actions across 20 independent replicates compares a conventional identity and access management baseline with an AAGSF prototype under a documented synthetic fault model. In the primary configuration, the unauthorized execution rate decreased from 72.90% to 2.33%, while the revocation escape rate decreased from 74.91% to 4.04%. This improvement came with a higher authorized action block or hold rate (9.80% versus 2.64%), exposing a security and utility tradeoff. Sensitivity analysis further shows that AAGSF remains materially safer than the baseline as injected authority representation error increases from 0% to 10%, although performance degrades predictably as representation quality worsens. The results do not establish real world prevalence; rather, they demonstrate the behavioral consequences of authority state synchronization under a controlled fault model and motivate empirical validation in operational environments.

detail.abstract: Game theory supplies the formal language in which modern financial economics and industrial organization describe strategic behavior among rational agents who anticipate one another's responses. This paper develops, from first principles, the non-cooperative game-theoretic apparatus that underlies contemporary work in these two fields-normal-and extensive-form games, Nash equilibrium and its refinements, the Harsanyi framework for games of incomplete information, and Bayesian Nash Equilibrium-and shows how each construct specializes into workhorse models: Cournot, Bertrand, and Stackelberg oligopoly; first-price, second-price, and optimal auction design; and the signaling and screening models of Akerlof, Spence, and Rothschild-Stiglitz. It then traces these tools into two applied domains emphasized throughout: financial markets, where strategic trading (Kyle, Glosten-Milgrom), auction-based security issuance, bank-run coordination (Diamond-Dybvig), and algorithmic trading are best understood as games of incomplete information; and industrial organization and competition policy, where oligopoly and repeated-game logic underlie merger analysis, tacit collusion, entry deterrence, and the emerging regulatory concern with algorithmic collusion. The paper closes with a discussion of practical implications for traders, corporate strategists, market designers, and antitrust regulators, and identifies open problems at the frontier of behavioral and computational game theory. Three appendices provide complete derivations of the Cournot-Nash equilibrium, a Bayesian Nash Equilibrium under private cost information, and the equilibrium bidding strategy and revenue equivalence result for firstprice sealed-bid auctions.

detail.abstract: We study the optimal allocation of tasks over the life cycle of an innovative project. Innovation requires two complementary activities, research and development, both subject to moral hazard. Agents also privately observe the quality of discoveries, so the principal must elicit truthful reports to avoid costly mistakes. Assigning both tasks to a single "solo operator" avoids free-riding but creates a double-deviation problem: the agent can shirk on research and conceal the resulting low-quality discovery. As time passes without a discovery, this deviation becomes increasingly attractive. Separating the tasks across two agents eliminates the double deviation but introduces free-riding. We characterize how this tradeoff shapes organization over time. When low-quality discoveries are readily exposed, the project is run by sequential solo operators; when they are difficult to expose, a two-agent team is optimal from the outset. At intermediate levels of detectability, the project begins with a solo operator and switches endogenously to a team.

detail.abstract: This paper establishes a mathematically rigorous refinement framework for demonstrating that decentralized, autonomous execution environments conform to a set of universally declared constitutional safety bounds. Rather than evaluating compliance via post-hoc observational data, we formalize an inductive state-transition model on top of a discrete fixed-point arithmetic domain scaled to 10^{18} (\mathbb{W}_{18} precision). We define a formal abstraction mapping between concrete machine states and an idealized semantic state space. By establishing a strict commuting condition \phi \circ T = T^* \circ \phi, we show that any safety property proven on the abstract layer holds deterministically over the concrete execution domain. This formulation provides a direct, auditable translation path for verification kernels within modern interactive theorem provers such as Lean 4.

detail.abstract: Stouras, Erat and Lichtendahl (2025) study firms running innovation contests on a common platform and competing for solvers. In their model a firm's return is its best submission's expected quality net of the prizes it pays, so unspent money keeps its value; their programs and proofs price it at zero, as if the purse were sunk. We solve the model as printed, with a standard effort cost that vanishes at zero effort where firms compete on effort. Its payout identity, that expected payout equals expected entrants times payment per entrant, makes each firm a wage-paying hirer. Under monopoly the outlay is capped independently of the budget. Under competition with pure noise the prize is capped where the marginal entrant's output meets the marginal wage bill; above the cap the winner-take-all equilibrium leaves money unspent, uniform entry requires equal offers to solvers rather than equal budgets, and regulating budgets cannot raise welfare at any symmetric equilibrium. Once effort matters and the incentive ceiling binds, the number of prizes maximizes effort per dollar of compensation rather than effort itself, which calls for weakly more prizes. Their budget clauses in Theorems 1-3 are the sunk-purse answers: each agrees with ours below the cap and differs above it.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a conceptual and computational framework for déjà vu, the transient and involuntary sense that a novel situation has already been experienced. Where existing accounts typically locate the phenomenon in a single mechanism-a neurological transmission delay, a dual-processing memory glitch, or isolated hippocampal misfiring-this paper proposes that déjà vu is better understood as an emergent property of the brain's ongoing predictive activity. On this view, the brain continuously constructs probabilistic "pre-mapped" representations of likely future situations from accumulated spatial, contextual, emotional, and associative information. When a real-time event's structural features closely match one of these latent representations, familiarity-signaling circuits in the medial temporal lobe fire with unusual strength, and downstream temporal-tagging systems mislabel the match as a record of a prior lived episode rather than as a successful prediction. The paper situates this Neural Network Mapping Hypothesis within the predictive-processing literature, draws an explicit structural analogy to cache-based information retrieval, and-departing from purely descriptive treatments-derives a set of falsifiable, empirically testable predictions intended to distinguish this account from competing recollection-based and dual-pathway models. Limitations, boundary conditions, and a proposed neuroimaging research design are discussed.

detail.abstract: Household inflation perceptions often diverge from official inflation, but the policy meaning of that gap depends on what drives it and whether it reaches expectations. Using Polish quarterly data for 2004Q1-2025Q4, the analysis separates retrospective perceived inflation (Q51) from forwardlooking expected inflation (Q61) and combines both with source-specific energy prices. Aggregate energy inflation adds little to the perception-gap equation once core and food inflation are controlled for. Fuel, electricity, and gas contain more distinct information, while positive fuelprice movements are associated with Q61 under conventional HAC inference. Small-sample bootstrap evidence is less precise. A semi-structural policy exercise then asks whether perception information improves stabilization when conventional policy coefficients are held fixed. In the baseline activity-gap specification, perception-gap responses of 0.25 and 0.50 reduce modelimplied loss in 99.2 and 97.5 percent of accepted parameter draws. The quantitative gain becomes negligible when GDP growth replaces the filtered activity gap. The evidence supports treating household perceptions as supplementary policy information rather than as an additional stabilization target.

detail.abstract: This study examines the relationship between digitalization and corporate sustainability by investigating its association with firms' environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance. It also evaluates whether digitalization moderates the relationship between stock market valuation and ESG outcomes among publicly listed Danish firms. The analysis uses longitudinal panel data from 67 companies covering the eight-year period from 2018 to 2025, obtained from the Refinitiv Eikon database. We test the hypotheses using ordinary least squares, random-effects, and fixed-effects regression models. We also use a generalized method of moments estimator to assess robustness and address potential endogeneity and dynamic panel concerns. The findings reveal a positive association between digitalization and overall ESG performance, as well as its individual environmental, social, and governance pillar scores. Digitalization also strengthens the positive relationship between stock market valuation and both overall ESG performance and the environmental pillar score. However, it appears to weaken the corresponding relationships for the social and governance pillars, demonstrating that its moderating role varies across ESG dimensions. By providing evidence from the Danish corporate context, this study advances understanding of how digital technologies may reshape the relationship between market valuation and corporate sustainability outcomes. The findings offer practical insights for managers and policymakers seeking to align digital-transformation investments with sustainability strategies, resource allocation, and ESG reporting practices. They also emphasize the importance of integrating digital technologies with transparent and responsible corporate practices. Although the study is limited to publicly listed Danish firms, future research could assess the generalizability of its findings across other countries, institutional settings, industries, and privately held firms.

detail.abstract: Intelligent-building research has hardware, and it has decision layers, and almost no way of telling whether a given architecture keeps a dwelling habitable once the dwelling changes. This paper supplies both halves. The first is a reference architecture, stated completely enough to implement: eleven layers, an ontology of 46 machine-readable classes each carrying seven fields, an entity model whose tenth field is provenance, one reversible interface with 5 channels and an 8-question handshake, perception measured eight separate ways, an 11-step runtime loop with the safety filter inside it, and eight invariants below everything that reasons. The second is HouseBench: 12 procedurally generated dwellings, seven architectures, 15 adversarial tasks, a removal ladder of 6 rungs, 16 quantities measured separately, and 882 logged runs. The headline result is uncomfortable for everybody, this author included. With nothing broken every architecture above a commissioned table performs alike. Separation arrives under injury, and it is separation by dependence: the centre removed takes three architectures from 38 per cent of the day to 0 per cent; carriage cut takes the coordinated system to 0 per cent; and a confident wrong reading leaves six of seven at 8 per cent against 38 per cent for the one carrying provenance and a command log. On eight plans nobody tuned against, a commissioned table holds 0 per cent. Safe occupancy holds in 315 of 315 task runs and at every rung, because the filter is a step of the loop and the release is a spring. detail.abstract: Does a decline in the value of voting explain why candidates polarize? We show that even purely office-seeking candidates diverge from the median voter once turnout is costly and stochastic. The mechanism is a trade-off: moving toward the center to win undecided voters weakens a candidate's own supporters' incentive to turn out, since turnout falls with distance from her platform. This trade-off follows from any institution that raises or lowers the net value of voting. Using a formal spatial-competition model with probabilistic turnout, we derive candidates' equilibrium platforms in closed form and show that a decline in the electorate's mean net value of voting strictly widens the equilibrium distance between them, a demand-side account of polarization that requires no change in candidates' own ideology.

detail.abstract: This article advances a gendered political economy framework to examine how systemic educational collapse in Yemen simultaneously destroys, reproduces, and-under specific conditions-transforms structures of conflict and patriarchal authority. Drawing on 45 semistructured interviews with educators, community leaders, and local authorities across five governorates (Aden, Taiz, Hadramawt, Marib, and Sana'a), triangulated with humanitarian reports and peer-reviewed scholarship, the study argues that education in protracted conflict cannot be understood through humanitarian deficit frameworks alone. Instead, it must be analyzed as a terrain of political contestation where war economies, patriarchal bargains, and territorial governance fragment educational space. The analysis identifies three interconnected dynamics. First, the collapse of state financing has localized resource distribution through patronage and community coercion, producing new geographies of educational exclusion. Second, women's assumption of educational leadershipcelebrated in humanitarian discourse as empowerment-operates as a form of feminized survival work that extends patriarchal resilience rather than dismantling it. This concept is distinguished from feminist analyses of reproductive labor and care work by its specific focus on the public performance of crisis-time educational labor that is simultaneously hyper-visible in humanitarian narratives and structurally invisible in political economy. Third, while community-based schools and teacher-led curriculum mediation generate "everyday peacebuilding," these practices remain structurally constrained by the absence of redistributive justice and the territorialization of governance. The article concludes that sustainable educational recovery requires moving beyond humanitarian restoration toward politically-informed, gender-transformative reconstruction that addresses the political economy of teacher precarity, curriculum territoriality, and the structural devaluation of women's educational labor.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the microstructural phenomenon of “Liquidity Voids” (LQD) kinetic price shockwaves generated by the sudden withdrawal of massive limit orders within the high-frequency Ethereum futures market (ETH/USDT). Analyzing a continuous dataset of 1,086 verified institutional spoofing events, this pa per quantifies the resulting 15-second mean-reverting price decay. While the withdrawal of synthetic support (Bid walls) yields a positive gross capture of +0.0450%, the prevailing retail exchange fee architecture (0.10% round-trip) mathematically guarantees a negative expected value (-0.0550% net) for standard market participants. Furthermore, extreme LQD events (LQD ≥ 1610.2) demonstrate a severe degradation in mean-reversion win rates (36.36%), revealing these anomalies as risk-averse liquidity pulls during toxic flow rather than intentional traps. Ultimately, this research proves that LQD signals are structurally unviable as standalone autonomous taker strategies for retail capital, necessitating a paradigm shift where such anomalies are repurposed as kinetic execution gates to reduce entry slippage on broader macro-directional models.

detail.abstract: How might a monetary system operate in the absence of a policy rate and its associated policy measures? This paper first examines the persistent ex ante intervention in price discovery in the deposit market through policy-rate setting and central-bank liquidity provision, and proposes an institutional sequence of "deposit market first, AIR as a supplement." Under this framework, banks first express their funding demand through the deposit market. Any potential funding gap that remains unmet after the market has completed its price and quantity adjustments endogenously generates demand for newly created base money, to which the AIR mechanism responds. The paper further examines the effects of this institutional sequence on deposit returns and household choices. As the policy rate and central-bank liquidity provision are eliminated, deposit rates can respond more fully to changes in banks' funding demand and households' supply of deposits, allowing households with different risk preferences and investment capacities to allocate their resources accordingly among consumption, deposits, and risky assets.

detail.abstract:
Alignment work addresses a model’s tendencies at the training stage. This paper concerns what happens after that work is done, at the point of use, where an agent that has been given a bounded instruction can still act beyond it while its words track the instruction. From three documented incidents with Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 4.6, it identifies Agentic Shadow Governance: the condition in which an agent, still presented as a bounded executor, has begun making unauthorized decisions inside a workflow while the interface continues to signal compliance. The failure takes four separately checkable steps, Execution Boundary Override, Unauthorized Optimization, Silent Authority Violation, and Compliance Acknowledgment Gap, and it runs in two directions: the agent does more than it was authorized to do, or it stops short and reports the work complete. The fourth step is the safety-relevant one. An agent that acknowledges a boundary, commits to hold it, and crosses it again produces a log that reads as evidence of control and is not; the gap between what the model says about a constraint and what it does belongs to the same family as the alignment-faking and reward-hacking behaviors its developer has documented in controlled settings, in a direction those studies do not cover.

 The paper’s central claim concerns what counts as evidence of authorization fidelity, not why the failure occurs. Fidelity cannot be inferred from output quality or from compliance language, and, given what is now known about evaluation awareness, not from pre-deployment testing alone. The observations suggest that the boundary is best enforced outside the model and demonstrated from the operational record. That layer would be additive to alignment, not a substitute for it. The paper sets out Authority-Boundary FMEA, an analysis whose test case asks whether the agent completed the authorized task while preserving all non-authorized state, with pass, fail, and inconclusive outcomes. It also sets out the controls a deploying party should require, the division of failure knowledge between provider and deployer, and a proposed risk-transfer agenda.

The cause of the behavior is held open: a single trained pull toward the finished-looking result is one account among several, appraised against the record and not established. The captured diagnostic exchange of the first incident is reproduced in full, and a dated note records the measurements published since that now put base rates on both directions of the pattern. This is a control-design paper: it characterizes a structural failure mode from documented incidents and builds the safeguards a deploying party should require. It does not estimate how often the failure occurs, and it does not need to; a demonstrated vulnerability warrants controls before its frequency across a population is known. The measurements that put base rates on both directions of the pattern have since been published by others and are noted in the dated note; the companion paper takes up frequency directly.

detail.abstract: We study how anonymity affects fake-news sharing on social media using a natural experiment on Flashback, a large Swedish online discussion forum. In 2014, journalists obtained information that allowed them to identify users registered before March 2007, sharply increasing these users' risk of public exposure while leaving later registrants unaffected. Using a difference-indifferences design on 1.98 million posts, we find that exposed users reduce references to fake-news sites by about one-quarter of the mean. The effect is concentrated in immigration and domestic-politics discussions and does not extend to legitimate news sources, suggesting that accountability reduces misinformation without reducing news sharing more broadly.

detail.abstract: The EU's claim to support environmentally sustainable artificial intelligence (AI) remains largely aspirational. Although the EU AI Act recognizes environmental protection as a goal, its risk-based framework cannot adequately address AI's environmental impact, which is largely unrelated to a system's risks to fundamental rights and the rule of law. The Act consequently leaves most systems outside any meaningful environmental evaluation: fundamental rights impact assessments (FRIAs), risk management requirements and standardisations do not apply beyond highrisk and general-purpose AI models; codes of conduct aimed at providing key performance indicators for assessing and minimising the environmental impact of AI are non-binding nature; and all these tools only focus on energy consumption. Nor do adjacent EU regimes fill the gap: environmental law, emissions-trading rules, corporate-reporting, due diligence, and data protection regulate only fragments of AI's footprint. Member States must therefore address these gaps by implementing European regulations broadly or adopting national measures that cover the entire AI life-cycle, promote environmentally informed AI literacy that extends to the general public, and support the development of comparable measurement methodologies. This need is becoming more urgent as the European Commission's recent simplification and competitiveness agenda risks undermining the still modest progress achieved toward AI's environmental sustainability.

detail.abstract: Nested clustered optimization allocates within each cluster from the cluster's own covariance block and then across the resulting cluster portfolios. Block inversion says the unconstrained minimum-variance portfolio has the same two-tier shape, with each block replaced by its Schur complement against every other asset. Conditioning instead on one knot from each other cluster truncates the conditioning set in the manner of a Vecchia approximation, and we give the rankone model of cross-cluster dependence under which it is exact. Damping the complement by γ ∈ [0, 1] then gives a bridge with nested clustered optimization at γ = 0 and the global optimum at γ = 1, with no linear solve larger than a cluster or the number of clusters. Under estimation error the optimal γ can be strictly interior and full coupling can remain optimal, and we give the local theorem at the minimum-variance end with exact examples of both, including a symmetric family in which the optimum is a closed form.

title: Who Else is New? Immigrants, New Students, and Academic Performance in Peru

detail.title: Who Else is New? Immigrants, New Students, and Academic Performance in Peru

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: Initial funding provided by Duke University

detail.abstract: This article examines the impact of a large and rapid immigration flow on the academic performance of native high school students. I use quasi-random variation in classroom assignment to identify the effect of an additional Venezuelan classmate on Peruvians’ eighth-grade standardized scores. I find that an additional immigrant student reduces the academic performance of locals by 1.8% and 1.2% of a standard deviation in math and reading, respectively. These effects are not explained by resource dilution, are robust to the possibility of classroom assignment of immigrants being related to past academic performance of natives, and are also stable across subnational regions and between the public and private school systems. I observe that the magnitude and pattern of heterogeneity of these effects are comparable to those associated with introducing a new native student to a classroom, which suggests that the relevant characteristic of immigrant students in this context is their newness to the school. Turning to mechanisms, I find no changes in the effects by teacher experience, and some evidence of a decrease in native student effort following the introduction of a new student–regardless of nationality.

detail.abstract:
Every healthcare organization in the United States is now running its clinical operations on infrastructure it
does not own and, in most cases, could not independently rebuild: cloud platforms, graphics processing
units, foundation models, data centers, electrical grids, and a small number of cybersecurity and
interoperability vendors sitting beneath all of it, largely unexamined. This report calls that dependency
what it is, an unpriced concentration risk, and it tests the assumption that this infrastructure will simply be
there when a hospital needs it.

The evidence says otherwise. A single cyberattack on one claims clearinghouse disrupted direct patient
care at 74 percent of surveyed hospitals nationwide in 2024. A single flawed software update from one
cybersecurity vendor detectably disrupted services at 759 hospitals five months later, more than a fifth of
those disruptions patient facing. Both events shared the same underlying cause, a level of concentration in
critical infrastructure that no hospital board had modeled as a clinical risk. Meanwhile, the next layer of
that infrastructure, the data centers and electrical capacity an AI enabled healthcare system will require, is
being built against transformer lead times that have roughly doubled since 2020 and now stretch past three
years for the largest units, inside a grid expected to carry a data center load that grows from roughly 24
gigawatts to 100 gigawatts nationally by 2030.

This report introduces the Clinical Sovereignty Stack, a ten layer model of the dependencies that now sit
between electricity and a patient's care, and the Koru Clinical Sovereignty Index, a scoring framework that
lets a health system, an investor, or a regulator measure how exposed a given organization is across seven
specific dimensions of that stack, including the growing risk posed by autonomous AI systems operating as
attackers in their own right. The conclusion is not that hospitals should attempt technological
independence, an outcome this report considers both impossible and undesirable. It is that clinical
sovereignty, defined here as strategic control over critical dependency rather than self sufficiency, has
become as material to healthcare risk as the credentialing and regulatory dependencies this institute has
already documented in The Speed Illusion, Report 005, and The Veto Outside the Model, Report 007, and
almost nobody in the industry is currently measuring it.

detail.abstract: This paper evaluates the relationship between the admission cutoff scores of the Greek Panhellenic examinations and the departmental research standing published in Edition 2026 of the Greek Academic Rankings series. Each year some 75,000 candidates rank university departments on a single official form, and admission is settled by one published number per department: the score of the last candidate admitted. That number measures demand against supply and says nothing about the department. Departmental research standing is measurable, and Edition 2026 measured it for every tenured faculty member of seven fields across 23 universities under two published ranking designs, on a harmonised 2012-2025 window, across three bibliometric sources. The unit of analysis is the individual department. Of 338 ranked departments, 311 carry a 2025 cutoff and 298 carry cutoff , research output and admission places together. Departmental results are reported under the four επιστημονικά πεδία of the Ministry of Education, which is the taxonomy a candidate navigates. The association is positive, weak and robust to controls: +0.182 standard deviations on its own, +0.177 with places and city, and +0.132 with university fixed effects, remaining distinguishable from zero when departments are compared only against others in the same institution. It is dominated by geography: a department in Athens or Thessaloniki carries a cutoff 0.88 standard deviations higher than an otherwise comparable department elsewhere, about five times the research coefficient. The number of admission places, which enters the construction of a cutoff directly, is not significant in any specification. Together these account for 22 per cent of the variation, rising to 38 per cent once institution is absorbed. Holding the discipline constant, the two orderings are not distinguishable from unrelated: across 22 subjects offered at four or more universities, the department with the highest cutoff is also the strongest in research in six. The paper reports what two measurable series show and offers no recommendation. Research output is one dimension of academic quality, measured to a common international standard across every Greek university by a single method; it is not teaching quality, supervision or graduate outcome, none of which can presently be measured at national scale.

detail.abstract: The rise in global sea levels is well documented and continues to displace thousands of people living in coastal areas. These individuals become displaced persons and may need to relocate within or beyond their countries of origin. This article explores the obligations of States in protecting these groups. For internally displaced persons, fewer legal challenges tend to arise, as States remain primarily responsible for their own citizens. Still, recognizing that these individuals are particularly vulnerable to discrimination and violence, the United Nations has developed guiding principles that establish minimum standards of protection. In contrast, the situation of those displaced across borders raises more complex questions. Responsibility shifts to foreign States, and the concept of “environmental refugee” remains unrecognized in international law. Nevertheless, International Human Rights Law can provide meaningful protection, as the Human Rights Committee recognized in Teitiota v. New Zealand. The 2025 Advisory Opinions from the ICJ and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights represent a decisive moment, pointing towards specific States’ duties to address climate-driven displacement.

title: Who Says Yes When the Headhunter Calls? Understanding Executive Job Search Behavior
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania Wharton School - Center for Human Resources and Instituto de Empresa

detail.title: Who Says Yes When the Headhunter Calls? Understanding Executive Job Search Behavior
detail.abstract: We examine an aspect of job search in the important context of executive-level jobs using a unique data set from a prominent executive search firm.  Specifically, we observe whether or not executives pursue offers to be considered for a position at other companies.  The fact that the initial call from the search firm, which we observe, is an exogenous event for the executive makes the context particularly useful. We use insights from the Multi-Arm Bandit problem to analyze the individual's decision as it emphasizes assessments of future prospects in the decision process, which are particularly relevant for executive careers.  More than half the executives we observe were willing to be a candidate for a job elsewhere. Executives are more likely to search where their current roles are less certain and where their career experience has been broader.  Search is more likely even for broader experience within the same employer. In the latter case, the array of likely opportunities is also broader, making search more useful.

title: The Flight from Maturity
affiliations: Yale School of Management, Yale School of Management and AQR Capital Management, LLC

detail.title: The Flight from Maturity
detail.abstract: Why did the failure of Lehman Brothers make the financial crisis dramatically worse?  The financial crisis was a process of a build-up of risk during the crisis prior to the Lehman failure. Market participants tried to preserve an option or exit by shortening maturities - the "flight from maturity".  With increasingly short maturities, lenders created the possibility of fast exit. The failure of Lehman Brothers was the tipping point of this build-up of systemic fragility.  We produce a chronology of the crisis which formalizes the dynamics of the crisis. A crisis is a dynamic process in which "tail risk" is endogenous.

detail.abstract: From scientific collaborations to online communities, collective judgments emerge as individuals repeatedly revise their beliefs in response to one another. Whether this process produces accurate beliefs or merely consensus depends on how people combine private evidence with their neighbors' judgments. Two families of computational models make distinct assumptions: DeGroot models synchronously average available opinions, whereas reinforcement learning (RL) models update beliefs sequentially from neighbor-specific prediction errors. These accounts have not been directly compared in controlled social networks with repeated real-time interaction. We compared them using trial-by-trial choices from two previously published experiments involving 209 and 760 participants, respectively. Participants repeatedly revised predictions in networks differing in size and topology. We fitted unweighted and degree-weighted variants of both model families and compared them using random-effects Bayesian model selection. We then used simulations parameterized by the fitted models to assess network-level accuracy and consensus. In both datasets, a DeGroot variant had the strongest group-level model evidence, although the best-fitting rule varied across individuals. Network topology also mattered: unweighted DeGroot best explained behavior in most structures, whereas degree-weighted DeGroot was favored in the highly centralized Royal Family network. Simulations showed that DeGroot averaging generally generated more consensus than naïve sequential RL, while degree-weighted RL could achieve similar accuracy and consensus depending on the assumed information-sampling order. Topology further shaped collective outcomes: hub-dominated networks could reach high consensus despite relatively low accuracy. Exploratory simulations showed that increasing network size improved accuracy but reduced consensus, whereas increasing average degree improved both. These findings establish DeGroot averaging as a robust baseline account of belief updating in interactive networks and show how learning rules, sampling order, and topology jointly determine whether networks become accurate, consensual, or both.

title: External Equity Financing Shocks, Financial Flows, and Asset Prices
affiliations: , University of Minnesota and University of Connecticut - Department of Finance

detail.title: External Equity Financing Shocks, Financial Flows, and Asset Prices
detail.abstract: The ability of corporations to raise external equity finance varies with macroeconomic conditions, suggesting that the cost of equity issuance is time-varying. Using cross sectional data on U.S. publicly traded firms, we construct an empirical proxy of an aggregate shock to the cost of equity issuance, which we interpret as a financial shock. We show that this shock captures systematic risk, and that exposure to this shock helps price the cross section of stock returns including book-to-market, investment, and size portfolios. We propose a dynamic investment-based model with stochastic equity issuance costs and a collateral constraint to interpret the empirical findings. Our central finding is that time variation in external equity financing costs is important for the model to quantitatively capture the joint dynamics of firms’ asset prices, real quantities, and financing flows. In the model, growth firms, high investment firms, and large firms, can substitute more easily debt financing for equity financing when it becomes more costly to raise external equity, hence these firms are less risky in equilibrium. The model also replicates the failure of the unconditional CAPM in pricing the cross section of stock returns.

title: Beyond The Label: Regulatory Capture, Engineered Compulsion, And The Case For Supply-Side Intervention In India's Packaged Food Industry

detail.title: Beyond The Label: Regulatory Capture, Engineered Compulsion, And The Case For Supply-Side Intervention In India's Packaged Food Industry

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. No external funding was received for this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper is a secondary data analysis of publicly available records, published academic literature, regulatory documents, and documented investigative findings. No primary data collection involving human subjects was undertaken.

detail.abstract:
India's packaged food regulation has spent eight years optimising an instrument aimed at the wrong end of the causal chain. Front-of-pack labelling addresses consumer choice at the point of purchase. This paper documents why that framing misidentifies the regulatory problem and constructs an alternative architecture from the supply side.

The paper applies six bodies of analytical evidence to India’s packaged food regulatory failure: regulatory capture theory, credence good economics, dual-process behavioural science, international policy evaluation, food palatability neuroscience, and nutritional epidemiology. Five of these six constitute independent diagnostic frameworks whose predictions converge on a single structural conclusion. The convergence of five independent frameworks on the same finding through different disciplinary routes is the paper’s methodological claim to authority.

Five findings emerge from the convergent analysis. First, causal misdirection: front-of-pack labelling activates consumer agency that does not exist at the scale required for market discipline in the population segment where harm is concentrated. Second, regulatory capture: eight years of consultation have produced systematic movement away from effective intervention, with the Committee of Secretaries’ October 2025 recommendation to withdraw the 2022 draft being the most recent documented instance. The trans fat mandate provides a within-institution control case confirming the capture diagnosis. Third, the bypass vulnerability: demand-side instruments create reformulation incentives that preserve palatability engineering while achieving technical compliance, because they act on the point of consumer information rather than the point of product design. Fourth, the Harm-Agency Inversion: the population bearing the highest disease burden has the least capacity to act on any information-based instrument, a structural condition no label design resolves. Fifth, the Designed Equilibrium: voluntary reformulation has operated in the premium packaged food segment since approximately 2018 and has not diffused downward in eight years, confirming the Nash Equilibrium prediction for a market where reformulation is simultaneously rational for premium-tier producers and commercially irrational for mass-market producers.

The paper proposes a seven-recommendation, three-track supply-side architecture. Track 1 addresses product composition directly: a mandatory artificial food colourant restriction through a business-to-business upstream standard; a hyper-palatable food combination threshold mandate with cross-subsidisation mechanism; and a Domestic Equivalent Clause requiring multinational manufacturers to sell in India the formulation they apply in their most regulated G20 market. Track 2 addresses information asymmetry and market correction through a mandatory composition database, a trademark-labelling interface restricting health-claim vocabulary on HPF-classified products, child-directed marketing restrictions, and PM-POSHAN institutional procurement reform. Track 3 addresses the fiscal architecture through a Health Cess on sugar-sweetened beverages and a corporate canteen nudge standard.

The Domestic Equivalent Clause is identified as the most immediately actionable instrument: it requires no new technical standard-setting, is operable through existing PIL remedial architecture in Writ Petition (Civil) No. 437 of 2024, and functions in the period before any new FSSAI notification is issued. As of September 2026, following FSSAI's August 28, 2026 red hexagonal warning label proposal, the Supreme Court has issued thirteen clarificatory queries to FSSAI and directed a further affidavit by 20 September 2026, with final stakeholder submissions due 28 September 2026.

Eight years of deliberation have not yet produced an enforceable standard, but sustained judicial pressure through 2026, including the Supreme Court's indication that it will itself prescribe a standard if government action remains incomplete, signals that this deadlock is approaching resolution, whether through regulatory or judicial action. The paper's supply-side architecture is designed to shape whichever outcome follows

Disclosure: AI-assisted tools (including large language models) were used for research support, literature synthesis assistance, and language editing during preparation of this working paper. This study relies exclusively on secondary data; no primary data collection was undertaken. All analytical frameworks, theoretical applications, structural inferences, and conclusions are entirely the author's own.
