detail.abstract: The academic literature in recent years is full of articles and research focussing on the linkages between building entrepreneurial ecosystems and economic development. Entrepreneurial activities can be found throughout the whole economic value chain, including subsistence entrepreneurs, innovative entrepreneurs, social entrepreneurs, and growth-oriented entrepreneurs. The research shows that Entrepreneurial Ecosystems and the Entrepreneurial Support Organisations play a critical role in entrepreneurial success across the value chain as they provide the necessary infrastructure, access to knowledge, and network for entrepreneurial success as evidenced by academic research and successive Global Entrepreneurship Monitor Reports that give of the continued rise of startup businesses and entrepreneurial activity on the African continent. The focus of this article is to demonstrate the importance of sustainable entrepreneurial ecosystems in the Central African sub region called CEMAC. In order to achieve the above, a thorough literature review is conducted on the dependant and independent variables under study namely, entrepreneurial ecosystems, sustainable development, and the CEMAC sub region. Associated to the literature review, an empirical study was conducted among 100 citizens of the CEMAC sub region, a sample of peoples acquainted with the topic of entrepreneurship development through entrepreneurship ecosystems. The findings explain that some key organisations are designed to stimulate and actively support entrepreneurial activity and include organisations such as accelerators, incubators, co-working spaces, and other related programmes aimed to support entrepreneurs. In fine, the ultimate objective of the contribution is to look how localised growth entrepreneurs as well as social and environment focused entrepreneurs in one part of the CEMAC sub region could be scaled up and repeat in other parts of the CEMAC sub region.

detail.abstract:
This report examines Kenya’s trade-policy architecture between July 2023 and July 2026, focusing on the interaction between tariff protection, temporary trade relief, duty-remission arrangements and administrative mechanisms governing market access. It characterises the observed policy configuration as managed openness: a system in which a meaningfully protective tariff structure coexists with selective, temporary and often permission-based access to lower-cost imports and production inputs.

Drawing on Kenyan and East African Community legal instruments, WTO tariff and notification data, World Bank and WITS indicators, Global Trade Alert records, official statistics and judicial decisions, the report assesses tariffs, food-security measures, industrial-input relief, non-tariff measures, competitiveness, regional integration and trade-policy governance. The evidence shows that Kenya retains significant protection in selected sectors while using targeted exemptions, duty remission, waivers and other administrative mechanisms to respond to food-supply, industrial and competitiveness pressures. However, the report does not find sufficient evidence to conclude that these instruments represent a structural policy shift or an intensification relative to the pre-2023 period.

The report identifies predictability, transparency and evidence-based administration as central policy challenges. It recommends a whole-of-government trade-measures transparency framework, a consolidated national trade-measures register, systematic review of temporary relief measures, stronger WTO and EAC coordination, and improved measurement of cumulative border and administrative trade costs.

title: Family Structure, Male Migration and Child Outcomes: Evidence from India
affiliations: Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Kanpur, , Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Kanpur and

detail.title: Family Structure, Male Migration and Child Outcomes: Evidence from India

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Authors have no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding has been recieved for this work.

detail.abstract: We investigate the effects of family structure on male migration and child outcomes. Using the Indian Human Development Survey conducted in 2011-12 and an instrumental variable approach, we find that, first, males who live in joint families are more likely to migrate compared to their counterparts in nuclear families. Second, children belonging to these joint households tend to have better educational outcomes. The presence of a male patriarch provides a sense of security and support within a joint family, thereby facilitating male migration. Furthermore, these promising child educational outcomes are plausibly driven by increased migratory income, better women's well-being, and closer maternal attention towards children in joint families.

title: Fiscal Space and the Public-Private Financing Framework of Renewable Electricity in India

detail.title: Fiscal Space and the Public-Private Financing Framework of Renewable Electricity in India

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This study is simply influenced by mere passionate curiosity, the study for ever increasing sector of energy and renewables, especially exponentially in India itself. Previous studies have not yet included energy economics with that of public and private financing explicitly but my paper has done so. The increasing fiscal debts and spaces certainly shapes different financing for the sectors but does it also influence renewable sector? The reason was to study how changes in macroeconomic variables affect the expenditure and outcomes in the energy sector and the role of private participation. I would be humbly honored if this study even helps some of the specialists in this field. This is my first research paper and I am keen and curious to learn more and share with the ever intelligent growing world.

keywords: Public and Private Finance / Energy Economics fiscal space

detail.abstract: India's renewable-electricity transition is financed through a combination of Union and state policies, public financial institutions, public-sector procurement mechanisms and private project development. This study examines how fiscal space and public-support mechanisms relate to the evolving allocation of financing functions and private participation in India's renewable-electricity transition over FY2016-17 to FY2024-25. Drawing on secondary data, it combines a national trend review, a comparison of four states-Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka-and an institutional map of Union schemes, IREDA, REC and SECI facilitated procurement (Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, n.d.-a; Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency, 2024; Rural Electrification Corporation, 2025; Solar Energy Corporation of India, 2025). Renewable-energy capacity additions excluding large hydropower rose from 11,466.81 MW in FY2016–17 to 28,723.65 MW in FY2024–25 (Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, n.d.-a). Over the same period, public financial intermediation expanded: IREDA sanctions climbed from ₹10,199.01 crore to ₹47,453.11 crore, and REC’s renewable-energy sanctions reached ₹1,05,258.87 crore in FY2024–25 (Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency, 2024, 2025; Rural Electrification Corporation, 2025). None of these figures are treated as interchangeable with budget expenditure or private investment. Taken together, the evidence points to a division of functions: public actors supply policy, procurement, credit and risk-mitigation mechanisms, while private developers carry out most of the on-the-ground project execution. The four-state comparison is illustrative only and does not establish a causal link between fiscal space and renewable-energy outcomes (Eichengreen & Gupta, 2025). What follows is a descriptive framework, along with a note on what data future panel based causal work would need.

title: The Use and Misuse of Patent Data: Issues for Corporate Finance and Beyond
affiliations: Harvard Business School - Finance Unit and Stanford University

detail.title: The Use and Misuse of Patent Data: Issues for Corporate Finance and Beyond
detail.abstract: Patents and citations are powerful tools for understanding innovative activity inside the firm, and are increasingly use in corporate finance research. But due to the complexities of patent data collection and the changing spatial and industry composition of innovative firms, biases may be introduced. We highlight several patent-level biases induced by truncation of reported patent awards and citations, affecting estimates of time trends and patterns across technology classes and regions. We then introduce measures of patent and citation biases. When aggregated at the firm level, these survive popular methods of adjustment and are correlated with firm-level characteristics. We show that these issues can lead to problematic – and ex ante predictable – inferences, using several examples from prominent streams of finance literature that use patent data. We suggest a number of concrete steps that researchers can employ to avoid biased inferences.

title: Measuring the Effects of Firm Uncertainty on Economic Activity: New Evidence from One Million Documents
affiliations: University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - School of Global Policy & Strategy and University of British Columbia (UBC)

detail.title: Measuring the Effects of Firm Uncertainty on Economic Activity: New Evidence from One Million Documents
detail.abstract: We construct a new measure of firm-level uncertainty from analyzing the text of mandatory reports filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. Using firm and establishment level panel data on investment margins and employment dynamics, we find our uncertainty measure has large effects on investment even after controlling for industry and time-varying shocks. Periods of high firm uncertainty (1) reduce investment rates by 0.5% and attenuate the response to positive sales shocks by about half and (2) reduce employment growth rates by 1.4% and the response to positive sales shocks by 30%. Firms are less responsive to demand shocks at the firm level and across establishments within the firm. Consistent with “wait and see” dynamics, uncertainty affects new investment activity, e.g. plant births and acquisition, more than disinvestment margins.

title: Rethinking Agricultural Innovation in the Brazilian Amazon: Native Seed Collector Networks and SDG 2.4

detail.title: Rethinking Agricultural Innovation in the Brazilian Amazon: Native Seed Collector Networks and SDG 2.4

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interests.
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: This policy report examines how grassroots innovation can contribute to Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) target 2.4 in the Brazilian Amazon, using the indicator framework of SDG 2.4.1 to assess the dimensions of sustainable agriculture addressed by Native Seed Collector Networks (NSCNs)-forms of grassroots innovation rooted in Indigenous and local knowledge. The perspective adopted, drawing on political ecology theory, argues that the dominant productivist framework of agricultural innovation in Brazil, centered on industrial and export-oriented models, has contributed to the marginalization of Indigenous and locally embedded systems of knowledge, despite evidence of their contributions to conservation, livelihoods, food security, and climate change mitigation and adaptation. The case study of the Associação Rede de Sementes do Xingu (ARSX) is therefore presented to show the transformative potential of NSCNs across the three dimensions of scaling deep, scaling out and scaling up, and illustrates the structural constraints affecting these initiatives, including limited access to markets, land insecurity, and a National System of Innovation (NSI) that tends to privilege large scale agribusiness. Three possible policy pathways for Brazil's Ministry of Agriculture, Livestock and Food Supply (MAPA) are identified and evaluated through the scaling framework: state-led integration, support for network autonomy, and hybrid co-governance. The analysis suggests that the hybrid co-governance pathway, while institutionally challenging, may offer a balanced route to reconcile scaling with the preservation of local governance and epistemic diversity. Four recommendations are developed in conclusion, addressing co-management with Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities (IPLCs), integration of Indigenous knowledge into national policy, land rights enforcement, and reform of existing funding mechanisms. The central thesis presented is that unlocking grassroots potential is primarily a matter of equitably redistributing institutional authority.

title: Public-Safety Externalities of Power Outages: Evidence from the United States
affiliations: Georgia Institute of Technology

detail.title: Public-Safety Externalities of Power Outages: Evidence from the United States
detail.abstract: As climate change intensifies weather extremes and electricity demand grows, power grid failures are becoming more consequential. This paper provides the first national-scale estimates of the relationship between power outages and crime. I construct a county-day dataset merging 15-minute outage records with incident-level crime reports across 1,256 U.S. counties from 2018 through 2023. Using high-dimensional fixed effects and weather controls, I compare reported crime across outage-intensity levels relative to days with no recorded outages. Reported theft is 0.57-0.92% higher during outages, while reported assault is 0.71-0.81% lower. The positive property-crime association is concentrated at residences. Mobility data show lower residential presence and increased activity at retail, workplace, and transit locations, consistent with a possible “flight from home” mechanism: lower residential presence may weaken informal guardianship while reducing opportunities for close-contact interactions that may precede assault. Distributed-lag models indicate that the positive theft association persists in one outage-intensity range, whereas the contemporaneous negative assault association does not. Reporting checks using 911 calls and arrest rates do not show a broad collapse in reporting or police activity. Under a causal interpretation of the estimates, an illustrative calculation implies approximately 17.8 million USD in annual theft-related costs within the estimation sample.

title: The Flight to Affordability: Effects of Pandemic Rent Increases on Renters By Geography
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Independent, Independent, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Independent and Independent

detail.title: The Flight to Affordability: Effects of Pandemic Rent Increases on Renters By Geography

publicationDetails.detailsText: Finance and Economics Discussion Series, issue 2026-062, 2026[10.17016/FEDS.2026.062]

publicationDetails.journalName: Board of Governors: Finance & Economics Discussion Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: In the pandemic era, people moved from high-density, expensive areas to more affordable areas, putting upward pressure on local housing prices. We examine the geographic distribution of rent growth during this time and its effects on renters. We use administrative new lease data from RealPage and household-level data on rent and income from the American Community Survey. We analyze rents and incomes using Public Use Microdata Areas grouped in two ways: by prepandemic rent levels and by pre-pandemic rent-to-income ratios. Rents grew more in areas with lower pre-pandemic rents but not in areas with lower rent-to-income ratios, consistent with higher-income remote workers moving away from high rent areas to more affordable areas. Lower-income households experienced larger increases in rent relative to their income compared to the median renter. However, area-level rent-to-income ratios reflect both compositional changes in renter populations from mobility and changes in local rents. We highlight the need for future work to track affordability for the same households over time to fully understand pandemic era affordability trends.

title: Bayesian probability-of-default calibration with benchmark uncertainty and cohort dependence

detail.title: Bayesian probability-of-default calibration with benchmark uncertainty and cohort dependence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: no conflict of interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: No approval was needed
declarations.funderStatement: No funding

detail.abstract: Probability-of-default (PD) calibration for low-default portfolios must use sparse observations without understating the uncertainty created by common economic conditions. This paper studies benchmark uncertainty and cohort dependence in a controlled 2 × 2 family of Bayesian models. The fitted models are evaluated against a heterogeneous two-factor simulation that none of them nests. Across 500 known-truth replications, the fixed-benchmark correlated model attains 94.0-97.0% interval coverage across seven grades, whereas procedures based on independent defaults attain 14.0-40.2%. Correlated specifications gain about 720 expected log predictive density units in joint leave-one-cohort-out comparisons, although prediction does not distinguish the fixed-and uncertain-benchmark variants. Native pooled binomial and Jeffreys diagnostics reject 37.0-40.4% under dependent nulls. Following independent cutoff calibration, a directed likelihood-ratio statistic has 58.4% and 100% power against 20% and 50% PD understatement, with evaluated null rejection rates of 6.8-7.2%. A signed Shapley decomposition describes how the two model features change an illustrative capital measure. These components are sensitivity diagnostics, not booked margin of conservatism. The evidence is simulation-based and is not a validation of any bank portfolio.

title: Partisan Politics and Annual Shareholder Meeting Formats
affiliations: Villanova University and New York University (NYU) - Stern School of Business

detail.title: Partisan Politics and Annual Shareholder Meeting Formats
detail.abstract: We study companies’ decisions about holding annual shareholder meetings on-line during the Covid pandemic, and returning to classical in-person meetings post-pandemic. Among S&P 1500 companies, the frequency of virtual meetings shot up from less than 10 percent to more than 80 percent in the first year of the pandemic, with only gradual reversion to in-person meetings since then. Partisan politics has significant associations with these decisions. In-person meetings are more likely for companies that have Republican CEOs, and for companies with headquarters located in jurisdictions that vote Republican.  Corporate democracy therefore seems to have been swept up by the tides of contemporary political feuds.

title: Collusion, Mergers, and Related Antitrust Issues
affiliations: UCLA and University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) - Department of Economics

detail.title: Collusion, Mergers, and Related Antitrust Issues
detail.abstract: This survey examines recent developments in economic research relating to antitrust, paying specific attention to research in the areas of collusion and merger enforcement.   Research relating to both collusion and mergers has made significant advances in the last twenty years. With respect to collusion, this includes important theoretical and empirical work on the sustainability, structure, and impact of collusive schemes. With respect to mergers, this includes important work on the impact of enforcement institutions, both theoretical and empirical work on unilateral effects, and theoretical work on the selection of which mergers get proposed to antitrust agencies and optimal policy in the face of that selection. A feature of recent research is the increasing complementarity between empirical work (ranging from observational studies to model-based measurement) and theoretical work in advancing our understanding of collusive and merger-related phenomena.

title: Consumption-Dependent Risk Aversion in an Incomplete-Markets Economy
affiliations: University of Edinburgh - School of Economics

detail.title: Consumption-Dependent Risk Aversion in an Incomplete-Markets Economy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or non-financial interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently.

detail.abstract: Consumption experience may change how households evaluate future risk. This paper studies that feedback in a Bewley-Huggett economy with persistent income risk and a risk-free bond in zero net supply. Consumption shortfalls update a memory state that can induce either caution or greater risk tolerance. Each temporal self evaluates continuation consumption using its current risk index while anticipating successors' choices. A restricted Epstein-Zin criterion holds intertemporal substitution and discounting fixed. We characterise the three-period intrapersonal equilibrium and provide conditional existence and uniqueness results for its stationary extension. Illustrative computations show opposite return effects under caution and risk tolerance, and policy and distributional patterns distinct from a bounded habit benchmark. Constant risk indices that closely match the clearing return leave stationary asset-distribution discrepancies among the candidates examined. These findings indicate that aggregate price matching can conceal differences in household financial positions. The numerical evidence remains subject to off-grid approximation error and incomplete validation of the matching search.

title: Transferable Skills? Founders as Venture Capitalists
affiliations: Harvard Business School - Finance Unit and Georgetown University - McDonough School of Business

detail.title: Transferable Skills? Founders as Venture Capitalists
detail.abstract: In this paper we explore whether or not the experience as a founder of a venture capital-backed startup influences the performance of founders who become venture capitalists (VCs).  We find that nearly 7% of VCs were previously founders of a venture-backed startup. Having a successful exit and being male and white increase the probability that a founder transitions into a venture capital career. Successful founder-VCs have investment success rates that are 6.5 percentage points higher than professional VCs while unsuccessful founder-VCs have investment success rates that are 4 percentage points lower than professional VCs. While successful founder-VCs do get higher quality deal flow than professional or unsuccessful founder-VCs, observably higher deal quality does not explain the entire difference in performance. Using an instrumental variables approach to separate unobservable deal quality from value-add, we find that the outperformance of successful founder-VCs is consistent with them adding more value post-investment.

title: Data-Driven Minimax-Regret Portfolio Optimization under Tail-Risk Ambiguity
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST)

detail.title: Data-Driven Minimax-Regret Portfolio Optimization under Tail-Risk Ambiguity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No Declaration of Interest
declarations.funderStatement: Not applied

detail.abstract: We study data-driven portfolio choice under Expected Shortfall when a short training sample can distort a plug-in optimizer and when competing tail-risk engines disagree on which feasible portfolios are safer. Checking only the level of Value-at-Risk or Expected Shortfall can miss this disagreement: a common additive shift leaves every ranking unchanged, yet a relative distortion can change the optimizer. We form a training-score mix of the engines, independently audit relative Expected Shortfall differences on a frozen audit library, and project that mix onto the resulting admissible set of engine mixtures. The implemented rule interpolates, with a parameter locked in advance, between that validated mix and worst-case admissible regret. We prove a high-probability bound on true Expected Shortfall regret that separates model tolerance, validation error, coverage error, and optimization error. An empty admissible set, under the stated validation model, yields a level-$\beta$ rejection of the engine library at the prescribed tolerance, rather than a solver failure. For a small finite library the rule is a linear program obtained from the extreme points of the admissible set. We do not claim a polynomial dual reformulation in general, and we do not place a Wasserstein ball around return laws.

title: Green Tariff Asymmetries and Sustainability-Oriented Trade Reallocation in Developing Economies: Evidence on Environmental Goods Matched within HS4 Product Families, 2002 to 2023
affiliations: and National Economic University

detail.title: Green Tariff Asymmetries and Sustainability-Oriented Trade Reallocation in Developing Economies: Evidence on Environmental Goods Matched within HS4 Product Families, 2002 to 2023

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no conflicts of interest related to this work.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Developing economies often rely on international trade to access environmental technologies, but average tariffs do not show whether green goods are treated more or less favourably than similar products. This study measures green tariff asymmetry within HS4 product families and examines whether it is associated with sustainabilityoriented trade reallocation. We combine CEPII BACI bilateral HS6 trade, WTO MFN tariffs, the APEC list of environmental goods, official HS concordances, and historical World Bank income classifications for 2002-2023. The models include pair fixed effects together with importer by year and exporter by year fixed effects, so the estimates come from changes within continuing bilateral relationships. Among importers classified as developing economies, a 1 percentage point increase in the difference between control and green tariffs is associated with 1.97%-2.10% higher trade in environmental goods relative to matched controls. The relationship appears for imports from both developing and high income suppliers. Economies in the lower middle income group have the largest point estimates, although formal differences across income groups are not robust. The positive relationship also remains under alternative product mappings and checks of timing, sample composition, extreme tariff values, and predetermined product baskets. The findings suggest that relative tariff design is one policy margin that can shape access to environmental technologies, but they do not imply that tariff reform alone causes environmental or welfare gains.

title: Cash Transfers and the Indian Household: Liquidity, Labour Supply, and Financial Resilience
affiliations: Wageningen University & Research, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Cash Transfers and the Indian Household: Liquidity, Labour Supply, and Financial Resilience

detail.abstract: India now delivers unconditional cash transfers (UCTs) at a scale without precedent: seven flagship national and state programmes budget roughly Rs 1.7 lakh crore for 2026-27 and reach well over ten crore beneficiaries among farmers and women. What should these transfers be expected to do to Indian households? This paper, the first in a series, develops a unified conceptual framework for that question. We organise the possible effects of UCTs across six outcome domains and develop a basic model of labour force participation under three constraints that bind simultaneously: rationed working capital, a casual labour market that does not clear, and social norms that tax women's market work. The model yields a discrete-choice formulation over six activities and a decomposition of the labour supply response into income, liquidity, and norms channels, with labour rationing entering as the conditioning variable that sets how much each can do, while a single shadow price of liquidity ties the labour predictions to household financial resilience, so that outcome domains discipline one another. Thirteen graded hypotheses, mapped to Indian datasets and quasi-experimental designs, define the research programme the series executes. A closing section carries the same channels into design: the cadence, size, and reliability of a transfer, who receives it, and how widely it is paid.

title: The Rise of Market Power and the Macroeconomic Implications
affiliations: Princeton University - Department of Economics and University College London - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Rise of Market Power and the Macroeconomic Implications
detail.abstract: We document the evolution of markups based on firm-level data for the US economy since 1950. Initially, markups are stable, even slightly decreasing. In 1980, average markups start to rise from 18% above marginal cost to 67% now. There is no strong pattern across industries, though markups tend to be higher, across all sectors of the economy, in smaller firms and most of the increase is due to an increase within industry. We do see a notable change in the distribution of markups with the increase exclusively due to a sharp increase in high markup firms. We then evaluate the macroeconomic implications of an increase in average market power, which can account for a number of secular trends in the last 3 decades: 1. decrease in labor share, 2. increase in capital share, 3. decrease in low skill wages, 4. decrease in labor force participation, 5. decrease in labor flows, 6. decrease in migration rates, 7. slowdown in aggregate output.

title: THE COST OF TRUST: DIGITAL FINANCIAL FRAUD, FINANCIAL RISK AND A MITIGATION FRAMEWORK IN NEPAL

detail.title: THE COST OF TRUST: DIGITAL FINANCIAL FRAUD, FINANCIAL RISK AND A MITIGATION FRAMEWORK IN NEPAL

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that they do not have any personal, professional, financial or other relationships with any of the individuals, organisations, institutions or companies, which, if any, could be deemed to have had an influence on the research, analysis, findings, conclusions, presented in this paper. The author does not have any relevant financial or non-financial conflicts of interest to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: This research paper has been written by the author and the author has been responsible for developing the research idea, literature review, research methodology, as well as analysis, interpretation of the findings and preparation of this manuscript. The author has read and approved the final version of this manuscript and accepts responsibility of its content.

detail.abstract: The use of Digital Financial Services (DFS) such as mobile, internet, wallet, card and QR payments has changed the functions of the banks and other financial institutions for individuals and firms in Nepal. However, it has led to the creation of new avenues of committing digital financial crimes which can be done remotely, fast and at multiple banking outlets. Instead of looking at cybercrimes committed through digital financial services, the study looks at the trends of digital financial fraudulence in Nepal. It addresses the risks of unauthorized transactions, phishing activities, theft of one-time passwords (OTPs), social engineering and account takeoffs and the fraudulent transfer of money through digital channels pose to the economy. The paper evaluates DFS-related frauds using the secondary information collected from Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB), Financial Intelligence Unit-Nepal (FIU-Nepal), and Nepal Police Cyber Bureau and other reliable sources. It also uses the results of a survey to look at the customer exposure, reporting, and perceptions of digital financial fraud in Nepal. The results of the analysis reveal that the rate of DFS penetration in the economy is rising fast. Specifically, the number of wallet users increased by 18.94 million people (from 4.72 million to 23.46 million) between the mid-July 2023 and mid-July of 2024. Similarly, the number of mobile banking users rose by 3.29 million (from 21.36 million to 24.65 million) during the same period. In view of the fact that fraudsters can move the money fast, customer awareness may not be enough to address the problem. The paper recommends the need for multi-factor authentication, monitoring and analyzing the transactions, use of transaction alerts, and limiting the big transactions as a way of protecting the customers. It emphasizes the need for enhanced customer due diligence, laxity in transaction processing by the banks and financial institutions, and collaboration among the law-enforcement agencies to address the challenges. Lastly, the paper recommends the development of a financial fraud-risk management framework to prevent, respond and mitigate digital financial fraud in Nepal.

title: Measuring Gender Attitudes Toward Men and Women
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, Harvard University, Stanford University - Department of Economics and University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Measuring Gender Attitudes Toward Men and Women
detail.abstract:
Gender-neutral attitudes judge a behavior the same way regardless of whether a man or a woman does it. Yet surveys of gender attitudes typically ask respondents to evaluate statements about men's or women's behaviors in isolation, never eliciting how the same behavior is evaluated when assigned to the other gender. Such responses therefore cannot reveal whether respondents perceive society as holding gender-neutral views. We introduce paired (role-reversed) elicitation, which varies the gender assigned to otherwise identical behaviors. In a representative sample of Americans, responses to standard statements suggest that few respondents perceive society as holding traditional views toward women. In isolation, this may be seen as evidence that society has moved past gender roles that confine choices. The paired elicitation, however, reveals a gender-neutrality gap: only about half of respondents report the same beliefs across the standard and role-reversed statements, even though these statements only vary in terms of which gender is assigned to which behavior. Thus, a substantial portion of respondents believe that the social acceptability of different actions depends on gender. Paired responses also uncover substantial heterogeneity and reveal broader underlying beliefs driving responses, such as beliefs about work and family rather than gender-specific views.

title: Social Interactions and Lottery Stock Mania
affiliations: Georgetown University - McDonough School of Business, University of Southern California - Marshall School of Business - Finance and Business Economics Department, City University of New York, Baruch College - Zicklin School of Business - Department of Economics and Finance, Fordham University - Gabelli School of Business and Hong Kong Baptist University (HKBU)

detail.title: Social Interactions and Lottery Stock Mania
detail.abstract: We find that social interactions are associated with stocks becoming more lottery-like and with greater investor overoptimism about the lottery characteristic. Heightened social media activity about a stock predicts extreme daily price run-ups—lottery events. Lottery event stocks subject to more extensive social media discussions subsequently experience greater retail buying pressure—particularly from Robinhood users—followed by lower returns. Moreover, lottery stocks of firms headquartered in more socially connected counties experience lower subsequent returns. Using staggered adoption of state-level social media privacy laws for identification, our findings support theories where social interactions incite investor excitement and asset price bubbles.

title: Digital (Killer?) Acquisitions
affiliations: Boston University - Markets, Public Policy, and Law, University of Toronto and Boston University - Questrom School of Business

detail.title: Digital (Killer?) Acquisitions
detail.abstract:
This paper examines innovation outcomes before and after 1,200 startup acquisitions by eight major technology firms. Linking patent and workforce data to these deals, we document four main findings. First, most acquired startups hold no patents, but those with patents tend to operate in technology areas where the acquirer already has a presence and that see further acquisition activity. Second, innovation typically rises before an acquisition, continues afterward only where further acquisitions follow, and falls back once acquisition activity ends. We propose a stylized model in which beliefs about commercial viability drive both startup entry and acquisitions to explain how these patterns arise through selection rather than effects of the deals. Third, acquired patents receive significantly more citations after the acquisition than comparable patents, not only from the acquirer but also from firms that hire the targets’ employees. Fourth, although 31% of employees and 23% of inventors depart within a year, inventors who stay go on to patent substantially more, while stayers and leavers were equally productive beforehand. In the aggregate, we find little evidence that acquisitions by digital incumbents suppress innovation, even though serial acquisitions go hand in hand with growing patent consolidation.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: The Impact of Fertility on Mothers’ Remote Work
affiliations: Washington State University and Washington State University

detail.title: The Impact of Fertility on Mothers’ Remote Work
detail.abstract:
This paper estimates the causal effect of fertility on mothers’ work arrangements, with a particular focus on remote work. Using harmonized individual-level data from the American Community Survey (ACS) for the period 2003--2024, we exploit exogenous variation in fertility generated by the sex composition of the first two children and twin births at the second parity. We find that fertility significantly reduces labor force participation across our sample period, consistent with existing evidence, but its effects on remote work are nuanced. Prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, an additional child increases the likelihood of working remotely. However, these effects turn negative after 2020 when remote work became common. We show that these patterns are not driven by changing selection into teleworkable occupations nor by changes in the observable characteristics of compliers over time. The limited feasibility or attractiveness of remote work for many women, combined with changes in the nature of remote work over time, are more likely explanations. Taken together, these findings suggest that remote work, in its current form, has limited potential to meaningfully reduce child penalties for higher-order births.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: Incentivizing Self-Protection From Wildfires
affiliations: University of British Columbia (UBC), University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - Department of Economics, Oregon State University and

detail.title: Incentivizing Self-Protection From Wildfires
detail.abstract:
Losses from natural disasters can be mitigated through investments in property protection, yet adoption of low-cost risk-reducing measures remains low. In wildfire-exposed areas, managing vegetation and other fuels next to homes decreases structure vulnerability, but few properties comply with best practices despite widespread outreach efforts. We report on two randomized field experiments that incentivized thousands of Oregon homeowners to participate in pre-existing fire department programs to reduce wildfire risk. Across both experiments, financial incentives of $100 to $500 resulted in up to 12% of homeowners scheduling free defensible space assessments, while information-only approaches achieved assessment takeup rates of 3% at most. Responses to subsidies are largest among owners of more valuable homes, while baseline wildfire risk does not predict responsiveness. On-the-ground and remotely-sensed measures of vegetation provide noisy estimates of treatment effects on endline vegetation. Finally, we consider the extent to which the estimated behavioral elasticities from these experiments might shed light on potential homeowner responses to pricing of wildfire risk reductions in home insurance premiums, a practice that is becoming more common due to technological and regulatory changes.

title: The Evolving Marriage Gap in Children’s Outcomes: Family Structure and Young Adult Outcomes Revisited
affiliations: Department of Economics, Wellesley College and University of Notre Dame

detail.title: The Evolving Marriage Gap in Children’s Outcomes: Family Structure and Young Adult Outcomes Revisited
detail.abstract:
Much of the existing research on the relationship between family structure and children’s outcomes has focused on average effects. Kearney and Levine (2017) instead proposed a heterogeneous framework in which the gap in outcomes between children of married and unmarried parents varies according to the resource context, namely a mother’s own resources, the net resources that a partner would contribute, and the outcome-specific returns to those resources. Using data from the 2013 Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID), they found evidence consistent with the model’s predictions. We revisit this question using the 2023 PSID to examine how these relationships have changed over the past decade. We find that the association between childhood family structure and young adult poverty has greatly diminished, whereas the association with college completion persists and is concentrated among children of mothers with higher levels of education. These findings suggest that although the economic circumstances of single mothers and their children have generally improved in recent decades, disparities in household resources and higher-order educational outcomes by family structure remain.

title: Expectations and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
affiliations: Northwestern University,  and Boston University - Department of Finance & Economics

detail.title: Expectations and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
detail.abstract:
This paper studies the relationship between subjective expectations and the term structure of interest rates. Departing from rational expectations, we allow market participants to hold arbitrary beliefs about future interest rates, and derive the condition that expected and realized interest rates must satisfy irrespective of how expectations are formed. We use this condition to decompose the sensitivity of long-term yields to the short-term interest rate into contributions from expectations and risk premia, without imposing any assumption on expectation formation. We find that, for short- and medium-maturity bonds, this sensitivity is driven primarily by movements in expectations rather than risk premia. We then study the sensitivity of expectations themselves and document systematic wedges between the response of long-term yield expectations and that of expectations of shorter-maturity yields over the same window. We argue that these wedges reflect structural inconsistency in subjective expectations, in the sense that expectations across maturities and forecast horizons are inconsistent with the equilibrium restrictions that link different interest rates.

title: Borrowing in the Shadow of China
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis, University of Notre Dame and University of Minnesota

detail.title: Borrowing in the Shadow of China
detail.abstract:
China's rise as a major lender to emerging economies since the early 2000s has introduced a unique form of lender power: borrowers cannot default on the subsidized loans they receive, but may still face sudden rollover demands outside their control. We argue this distinctive structure—bilateral rollover risk without default risk—disciplines recipient countries' borrowing on international markets. In a quantitative long-term sovereign debt model, we show that such rollover-prone nondefaultable Chinese loans expose market debt to dilution risk: governments may need to tap international lenders when repayment to China comes due, and therefore choose to deleverage from private markets when Chinese inflows arrive. Market debt and bond yield dynamics in the data are consistent with this “disciplining effect.” We then use the model to study two geopolitical scenarios: a bloc-formation exercise in which China offers take-it-or-leave-it loans to induce the borrower's exit from international debt markets, and an optimal exposure-to-China problem under the risk of a permanent and sudden retrenchment of Chinese funding. Together, these results show how official finance à la China can simultaneously improve market borrowing conditions and become a new destabilizing force to the global sovereign debt architecture as geopolitical alliances shift.

title: Money and Power: Historical Lessons for Stablecoins and U.S. Dollar Dominance
affiliations: Rutgers University, New Brunswick - Department of Economics and Princeton University

detail.title: Money and Power: Historical Lessons for Stablecoins and U.S. Dollar Dominance
detail.abstract:
This paper uses the history of private money to assess the conditions under which stablecoins could function safely at scale and what their growth may imply for U.S. monetary power. Historical systems of private money in the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, Sweden, and Switzerland show that par circulation depended on institutional arrangements rather than payment technology. Drawing on the monetary history of private money, convertibility, and international currencies, the paper identifies five foundations for scalable private money: credible convertibility, high-quality and transparent backing, a uniform regulatory perimeter, par clearing infrastructure, and credible crisis management and loss allocation. Stablecoins may improve settlement speed, programmability, and cross-border access, but they do not remove these requirements. Applying this framework to contemporary stablecoins and the GENIUS Act, the paper finds that the Act addresses several of these foundations more fully than others, with crisis management and cross-border coordination less fully developed. Dollar stablecoins could extend the reach of dollar settlement, but historical experience reviewed here suggests that whether this strengthens the dollar system depends both on the institutional framework supporting stablecoins and on the deeper foundations of U.S. monetary dominance: confidence in U.S. institutions, fiscal capacity, monetary credibility, and the rule of law.

title: Diversification as a Process: Geographic Expansion and the Formation of National Insurers
affiliations: California Institute of Technology (Caltech)

detail.title: Diversification as a Process: Geographic Expansion and the Formation of National Insurers
detail.abstract:
Large financial intermediaries are more stable than small ones, and the largest are also the most geographically diversified. Whether that breadth is a source of stability or a byproduct of scale is difficult to establish, since intermediaries diversify by growing large. I examine how the diversified intermediary is assembled, using a newly digitized firm-by-state panel of the near-universe of U.S. life insurers from 1888 to 1940, the largest nonbank institutional investors of the period. Over these decades, the number of insurers per state more than quadrupled and within-state concentration declined by half, yet a small number of geographically extensive insurers retained a stable share of national premiums. I decompose firm-level outcomes into the insurer’s underwriting level and the composition of its book. Insurers entered new states before attaining scale, each entry constituting a small and favorably selected position with the convex payoff of a real option. The most successful decile of entries generated half of a cohort’s premium. Expansion was costly on two margins: a broad insurer earned less per dollar of coverage and paid 15.1 percent more in claims than an equally large insurer writing in the same state and year. The pricing cost is attributable to the composition of a broad insurer’s book, the claims cost to the insurer itself. A comparison across firms understates the claims cost, since the markets a broad insurer adds exhibit favorable claims experience of their own. Stability, by contrast, is attributable to scale, since breadth’s advantages in volatility and survival vanish conditional on size. Risk pooling was bounded: approximately nine tenths of an insurer’s loss-ratio variance was common to its markets. Diversification was the product of costly expansion, and the stability attributed to it is the scale that expansion produced.

title: Advertising Claims, Pricing, and Customer Evidence
affiliations: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management

detail.title: Advertising Claims, Pricing, and Customer Evidence
detail.abstract:
Why might firms make different claims in advertising both with respect to themselves and to rivals? I study how claims direct consumers to different customer experiences, and how prices change the available evidence. Attributing successes to the advertiser requires a low price when its product is superior; attributing failures to the rival supports a higher price. Focussing on a single strategic advertiser, the model shows that the claim that attracts the most customers to a superior product never maximises profit. The optimal campaign raises advertiser profit but lowers consumer surplus relative to fully informed choice, and reduces total welfare whenever product reliabilities differ. When both firms choose claims and prices, competition can sustain a mix of positive and negative claims with price dispersion, restoring claims that a lone advertiser would reject. A rival's pricing response alone can make failure attribution optimal by weakening incentives to undercut. Allowing the rival to advertise can lower both prices and shift customers towards it if the incumbent retains its previous claim; allowing the incumbent to change its claim can eliminate this additional effect. Advertising, therefore, changes not only persuasion but also pricing incentives, making its market consequences different from its effects at fixed prices.

title: Planning for Retirement? The Importance of Time Preferences
affiliations: North Carolina State University - Poole College of Management, North Carolina State University, Ohio University-Voinovich School of Leadership and Public Affairs, University of Wyoming - College of Business - Department of Economics and Finance and North Carolina State University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Planning for Retirement? The Importance of Time Preferences
detail.abstract: Ensuring retirement income security is a priority for individuals, employers, and policymakers. Using merged administrative and survey data for public sector workers in North Carolina, we explore how workers’ characteristics and preferences are associated with planning and saving for retirement. We then assess the “quality” of a retirement plan and whether retirement behavior is consistent with these plans.   The findings indicate that the way that individuals discount future consumption is associated with the extent of their retirement planning and preparedness.  We find that individuals who engage in retirement planning are better prepared to meet their retirement goals upon leaving their career jobs.

title: Integration Without Decentralization: The Financial Geography of U.S. Life Insurance, 1880–1940
affiliations: California Institute of Technology (Caltech)

detail.title: Integration Without Decentralization: The Financial Geography of U.S. Life Insurance, 1880–1940
detail.abstract:
This paper studies the transformation of American life insurance, the largest contractual savings institution in the United States before Social Security. As the market for insurance became national, did control over the savings it collected disperse with it? Using a newly digitized annual firm-by-state panel of premiums and losses covering nearly every U.S. life insurer from 1888 to 1940, I distinguish the geography of collection from the geography of control: where premiums were paid, and where the firms receiving them were domiciled. The industry was remade over these six decades. Real premium income rose more than twentyfold, the number of active insurers grew sixfold, incorporation shifted decisively from the Northeast toward the Midwest and South, and within-state concentration fell by nearly half. Control was rearranged, not dispersed. Chartering domestic insurers raised local retention almost entirely at the extensive margin. Across regions, this closed a large gap, as the Northeast retained nearly eleven times as much of its premium as the South in the 1890s and only twice as much by the 1930s, with nine-tenths of the convergence coming from Southern states acquiring domestic sectors where they had none. The national total held: firms domiciled where premium was raised collected just under a quarter of it in the 1890s and just over a fifth in the 1930s, even as household participation converged steadily across states. Legal permission to operate nationally sufficed to integrate the market in which insurance was sold, but not to disperse control over the investable cash it collected.

title: Cooler Laws, Safer Workers: Evaluating California’s Heat Standard and Injury Reduction
affiliations: Workers Compensation Research Institute, Tufts University and

detail.title: Cooler Laws, Safer Workers: Evaluating California’s Heat Standard and Injury Reduction
detail.abstract:
A growing body of research shows that excessive heat increases the frequency of heat-related injuries at work. While interest in mitigating occupational risks from excessive heat is high, there is little evidence on whether legislation targeting heat exposure can reduce such injuries. Using a triple-differences approach and administrative data from workers’ compensation systems, we evaluate California’s heat standard – adopted in 2005 - and find that the standard substantially reduces the frequency of work injuries in the construction, agriculture, and transportation industries. The effects increase with outside temperatures and are larger among younger workers. Our findings have clear implications for workplace safety and contribute to ongoing policy debates.

title: Compound Delay: The Causes and Consequences of Later Grandmotherhood
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) - Department of Economics and University of Southern California

detail.title: Compound Delay: The Causes and Consequences of Later Grandmotherhood
detail.abstract:
We show how fertility delays compound across generations to raise age at first grandmotherhood. Under the 1960 first-birth schedule median grandmotherhood came at 44. Under the 2024 schedule it is 57, cutting the healthy years with grandchildren from 28 to 15. Longer life does not make up the loss of years when the grandmother is healthy enough to supply money and care. Delay is most pronounced among the college-educated, with reproductive-control access accounting for over half the fall in grandmotherhood by age 55 among White college graduates. When a daughter times her first birth to maximize her own payoff, the loss her choice imposes on her mother is external to her calculation. We call this the Rotten Adult Kid Problem. Delay raises both the price of a grandmother's care and wealth per grandchild.

title: The Returns to International Migration in a Free Mobility Setting: Evidence from Austria and Germany
affiliations: Central European University (CEU), University of California, Berkeley - Department of Economics, Government of the Federal Republic of Germany - Institute for Employment Research (IAB), University of Linz, Otto von Guericke University Magdeburg and Johannes Kepler University Linz - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Returns to International Migration in a Free Mobility Setting: Evidence from Austria and Germany
detail.abstract:
How big are the gains to international migration? How do they vary across migrants? We study these questions using linked administrative data for Austria and Germany, focusing on migrants who were steadily employed 2-4 years before their move and using their previous co-workers as a comparison group for a difference-in-differences design. We combine data from the origin and destination countries for 5 years after the move, allowing us to assess the gains for those who remain in the destination and those who return. On average, migrants from Austria to Germany experience an immediate and persistent rise of around 13% in their daily wage relative to their matched co-workers, while migrants from Germany to Austria gain about 4%. The higher returns for Austrians are mainly driven by higher average wages in Germany, rather than by differential selection of migrants. Consistent with a dynamic learning model, the returns to migration are largest for migrants who remain in the destination country, smaller for those who return after 1-4 years, and zero or even slightly negative for those who return in less than a year. They are also larger for migrants who follow established cross-border networks between workplaces. To help interpret our findings we conduct a parallel analysis of domestic migrants who move to a larger city (Vienna or one of the 5 largest cities in Germany). “Big city” movers experience gains in wages of about 5% for Austrians and 10% for Germans. Again the gains are largest for those who remain in the destination city, with smaller effects for those who move on.

title: Can Early Exposure to the Teaching Profession Increase Teacher Supply and Diversity? New Evidence on the Teacher Pipeline
affiliations: Old Dominion University and Brown University

detail.title: Can Early Exposure to the Teaching Profession Increase Teacher Supply and Diversity? New Evidence on the Teacher Pipeline
detail.abstract:
We examine whether early exposure to the teaching career has the potential to expand the size and diversity of new teacher supply. Exploiting the staggered expansion of high school education courses across Texas, we find little evidence that these courses increased new teacher supply or diversity despite course takers being substantially more diverse than the teacher workforce. High school education course takers who become teachers are similarly effective and more likely to be retained than their peers. Most course takers drop out of the teacher pipeline prior to college enrollment where racial gaps in 4-year college going serve as major barriers. Our findings suggest that early exposure without support to increase college going is unlikely to increase teacher supply or diversity.

title: When Tax Shields Shrink: Interest Deductibility Limitations and Corporate Innovation
affiliations: Fordham University, , Fordham University and Virginia Tech - Pamplin College of Business

detail.title: When Tax Shields Shrink: Interest Deductibility Limitations and Corporate Innovation
detail.abstract:
We investigate how limiting interest deductibility under the 2017 TCJA shapes corporate innovation. Using alternative identification strategies, we show that, relative to unaffected firms, affected firms experience significant declines in patenting and narrow the technological scope of their patent portfolios. This contraction is concentrated in exploitative patents, the type of innovation most naturally supported by debt financing. By weakening firms’ ability to finance innovation with long-term debt, interest limitations reveal a novel channel linking taxation to innovation, with the debt tax shield serving as an implicit subsidy. Cross-country evidence from the staggered implementation of interest limitation rules confirms negative effects.

title: Measuring and Projecting U.S. Investment in Semiconductor Manufacturing Capacity
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and Dartmouth College

detail.title: Measuring and Projecting U.S. Investment in Semiconductor Manufacturing Capacity
detail.abstract:
We consider official and alternative data sources for measuring and projecting the role of U.S. manufacturing in the global semiconductor manufacturing industry. We find that the government sources we consider face significant limitations for tracking semiconductor fab investment in real time: they use industry and product categories that are too broad and come with substantial publication lags. We then analyze project-level alternative data from Semiconductor Equipment and Materials International (SEMI), which provides quarterly tracking of individual fab projects with greater timeliness and specificity. Comparing SEMI data with official statistics through 2023, we find broad consistency in investment levels, validating SEMI as a credible supplement to official statistics. This work provides both a practical guide for tracking real-time trends in semiconductor manufacturing and a case study in synthesizing government and alternative data sources.

title: Governing Global Externalities: Investor Voice Amid Fragmented Policy
affiliations: Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR), University of Washington - Michael G. Foster School of Business, Boston College, Carroll School of Management and Imperial College Business School

detail.title: Governing Global Externalities: Investor Voice Amid Fragmented Policy
detail.abstract:
We study whether investor voice can help address global externalities under fragmented regulation. In our setting, a multinational firm generates externalities across jurisdictions, national regulators face political frictions that can impede corrective regulation, and policy differences create scope for regulatory arbitrage and production leakage. We compare two channels of investor influence: corporate stewardship, which affects firms’ global operations, and policy advocacy, which affects local regulation. Both channels can help address global externalities, but their relative effectiveness depends on political frictions abroad. When these frictions are severe enough to prevent foreign regulation, leakage weakens policy advocacy but strengthens stewardship. When foreign regulation is politically feasible, however, stewardship can crowd out foreign regulation and reinforce policy miscoordination, while local policy advocacy can crowd in foreign regulation and reduce externalities abroad.

title: Risk Premia, Firm Insurance, and Endogenous Labor Income Risk
affiliations: Washington University in St. Louis - John M. Olin Business School, Kellogg School of Management - Department of Finance and University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - University of California, San Diego

detail.title: Risk Premia, Firm Insurance, and Endogenous Labor Income Risk
detail.abstract:
We study how aggregate financial conditions shape firm insurance and, through it, labor income risk. In a directed search model with dynamic wage contracts and two-sided limited commitment, firm insurance against idiosyncratic shocks erodes when risk premia rise. Using U.S. administrative data, we document new evidence supporting the model: pass-through of firm shocks to earnings rises in bad times, especially for lower-paid workers near the separation margin. The model reproduces many untargeted time-series and cross-sectional features of earnings risk and implies substantial welfare costs of idiosyncratic risk, high private discount rates on human capital, and large gains from recession-contingent transfers.

title: Regulating Entrepreneurship: The Case of Capital Requirements
affiliations: BI Norwegian Business School, BI Norwegian Business School, University of Texas at Austin - Department of Finance and BI Norwegian Business School

detail.title: Regulating Entrepreneurship: The Case of Capital Requirements
detail.abstract:
Governments have long imposed minimum equity requirements on new corporations. Opponents view them as barriers to entry while proponents argue that they protect stakeholders from financially unviable businesses. We study this quantity-quality trade-off using a Norwegian reform and comprehensive data linking entrepreneurs to their firms. A 70% reduction in required capital nearly doubled entrepreneurial entry, with no deterioration in survival, profitability, productivity, or interest-bearing leverage and no differences in founders’ ex-ante income, liquidity, or ability. These results suggest capital requirements restrict entrepreneurship without screening on quality or liquidity. Rather, we highlight returns-to-scale heterogeneity as an important determinant of the observed entry response.

title: Benchmark Interest Rates When the Government is Risky
affiliations: McGill University, UCLA Anderson, University of Southern California - Marshall School of Business and Johns Hopkins University - Carey Business School

detail.title: Benchmark Interest Rates When the Government is Risky
detail.abstract: Since the Global Financial Crisis, rates on interest rate swaps have fallen below maturity matched U.S. Treasury rates across different maturities. Swap rates represent future uncollateralized borrowing between banks. Treasuries should be expensive and produce yields that are lower than those of maturity matched swap rates, as they are deemed to have superior liquidity and to be safe, so this is a surprising development. We show, by no-arbitrage, that the U.S. sovereign default risk explains the negative swap spreads over Treasuries. This view is supported by a quantitative equilibrium model that jointly accounts for macroeconomic fundamentals and the term structures of interest and U.S. credit default swap rates. We account for interbank credit risk, liquidity effects, and cost of collateralization in the model. Thus, the sovereign risk explanation complements others based on frictions such as balance sheet constraints, convenience yield, and hedging demand.

title: Unbundling Labor
affiliations: University of Melbourne - Department of Economics and Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis

detail.title: Unbundling Labor
detail.abstract:
Why is there so much wage inequality within occupations? Why has the overall level of within-occupation wage inequality risen? Why is the rise concentrated in cognitive-intensive occupations, while inequality has fallen in manual-intensive ones? To answer these questions we develop a general equilibrium model with heterogeneous workers who supply multiple skills jointly, as an indivisible bundle. This bundling friction allows a given skill to be priced differently in different occupations. We find in US data that differences in skill prices, not worker composition, explain why within-occupation inequality is higher in more cognitively intensive occupations and account for about a third of the rise in within-occupation inequality from 1980 to 2010. We show that a uniform increase in the productivity of cognitive skill can drive inequality up in cognitive-intensive occupations and down in manual ones, just as in the data.

title: The Macroeconomic Effect of Stimulus Checks: Evidence from Postwar Veterans’ Payments
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), Northwestern University and London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE)

detail.title: The Macroeconomic Effect of Stimulus Checks: Evidence from Postwar Veterans’ Payments
detail.abstract:
Do stimulus checks—one-off, deficit-financed lump-sum payments to households—boost the economy? We study a natural experiment: payments to U.S. veterans after World War II that mimic stimulus checks but were plausibly exogenous to the economy. These payments led to a temporary increase in transfers and a persistent, hump-shaped increase in consumption. The transfer multiplier—the cumulative response of consumption to transfers—reaches 1 after six months and exceeds 2 after a year. The standard heterogeneous-agent New Keynesian model cannot match the hump-shaped consumption response. A version with imperfect expectations—with households underreacting on impact but overreacting at longer horizons—can match our estimates.

title: The Remains of the Trade: The U.S.–China Trade War and its Aftermath
affiliations: Harvard University - Department of Economics, Harvard University and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: The Remains of the Trade: The U.S.–China Trade War and its Aftermath
detail.abstract:
We study how the U.S.-China trade war has reshaped global trade patterns, creating significant spillovers to third countries. Using recent tariff policy changes and monthly international trade flow data, we document a redirection of Chinese exports away from the U.S. market and toward third countries. To interpret the impact of these reallocations on third countries, we introduce a taxonomy that separates four exposure margins - export competition, import competition, consumer gains, and sourcing gains - and construct theoretically-derived indices that map countries into these channels. Recent work often proxies such exposure with trade-basket similarity. We show why this can be problematic: similarity measures are symmetric and omit the size of product-specific shocks, Chinese market penetration, substitution elasticities, and incidence weights. Our model-based indices therefore generate country rankings that differ substantially from conventional similarity measures.

title: Risk Management in Financial Institutions
affiliations: Duke University, Duke University - Fuqua School of Business and

detail.title: Risk Management in Financial Institutions
detail.abstract: The authors have retracted this paper and the subsequent version that was published in the April 2020 issue of The Journal of Finance (JF). A replication study that will be, or has, been published in the JF finds that the replication code provided in the supplementary information section of the article does not reproduce some of the central findings reported in the article. Upon reexamination of the work, the authors confirmed that the replication code does not fully reproduce the published results and were unable to provide revised code that does. Therefore, the authors conclude that the published results are not reliable and that the responsible course of action is to retract the article. Further information may be found at https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/jofi.13064. The authors deeply regret the damage this caused to the scholarly community. The specific contributions of the authors to the article were as follows: the first and second author provided the theoretical hypothesis; all three authors jointly designed the empirical approach and identification strategy; the third author constructed and handled the data, implemented the empirical analysis, and provided the empirical results as well as the replication data and code. The third author states that the original data and code that produced the published results were lost. The first and second author were not notified of the loss of the original data and code at the time it occurred and had no prior knowledge of the issues with the replication data and code provided to the journal.

title: Migration, Identity and Political Economy in a Globalizing World
affiliations: Stanford University and Harvard Business School

detail.title: Migration, Identity and Political Economy in a Globalizing World
detail.abstract:
We discuss how immigration affects identity, with implications for politics. We build on key insights from social psychology and their formalization in economics to derive predictions about how immigration changes both self-identification and categorization of others into groups. These immigration-induced identity changes can explain two recent political transformations that have characterized many Western democracies: the rise of right-wing populism and the realignment of voters and parties along a socio-cultural, rather than economic, dimension of political conflict. We also discuss how immigration can reshape group boundaries and political cleavages, depending on the characteristics of immigrants, host populations, and the local context. We highlight open questions and possible directions for future research.

title: Using Policy Functions to Estimate Merger Impacts: An Application to JetBlue-Spirit
affiliations: Columbia University, Cornerstone Research and U.S. Department of Justice - Economic Analysis Group

detail.title: Using Policy Functions to Estimate Merger Impacts: An Application to JetBlue-Spirit
detail.abstract:
Analyses of impacts of potential mergers in differentiated product markets often rely on non-transparent identification and strong conduct assumptions. We propose a simpler alternative: using quasi-exogenous variation in market structure to estimate equilibrium pricing policy functions. When price can appropriately capture consumer welfare, this methodology may require fewer assumptions than a structural equilibrium approach, including allowing variation in conduct. We apply this methodology to the JetBlue–Spirit merger, estimating policy functions using entry events. Our counterfactual price simulations account for changes in JetBlue’s capacity and Sprit’s elimination. The merger would cause $2.6 billion in annual harm under our preferred specification.

title: Cross-Border Common Ownership and the Gains from Trade in Employment

detail.title: Cross-Border Common Ownership and the Gains from Trade in Employment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: Does cross-border common ownership reverse the employment gains from trade, and who bears the loss? I develop a two-country general-equilibrium oligopoly model in which trade integration and ownership integration vary separately. Trade integration raises employment, while cross-border common ownership lowers it. The effect depends on ownership structure. Under reciprocal cross-holding, where each firm's owners also hold stakes in its foreign rivals, employment is U-shaped with an interior minimum. Under a single common owner, a structure that better reflects how today's asset managers hold equity, employment is lowest at full integration. Holding common ownership among domestic firms fixed, employment falls below autarky only when firms internalize foreign rivals' profits more heavily than domestic firms' profits, a threshold independent of labor supply and technology. When ownership differs across countries, the country whose firms internalize rivals' profits more heavily employs less. I then calibrate the model to measured profit weights. I find that trade integration raises employment by about 15 percent, while cross-border ownership at the observed level reduces that gain by less than one percentage point. Workers' losses exceed owners' gains.

The author is affiliated with Algol Ventures, a proprietary trading operation, but this study uses only publicly available secondary market index data and was not commissioned, funded, or influenced by any trading, investment, or business activity.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study uses only publicly available, anonymized secondary market data (S&P 500 and Nifty 50 index-level daily returns) and does not involve human participants, patients, or personal data requiring ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: This paper extends the empirical framework of Christopher (2026), which documents a 49% contagion intensification between the S&P 500 and Nifty 50 during joint high-volatility regimes using GJR-GARCH and rolling-threshold regime classification, along two dimensions: replacing the univariate GARCH specification with a jointly-estimated multivariate stochastic volatility (MSV) model, and replacing the fixed three-regime classification with a data-driven layer combining an infinite Hidden Markov Model (iHMM) with an ensemble machine-learning classifier. A full Bayesian implementation-a Gibbs/FFBS-estimated MSV with ancillaritysufficiency interweaving, and an iHMM estimated via truncated Dirichlet-process, hierarchical Dirichlet process, and beam-sampling approximations-finds a posterior mean correlation of 0.824 between the two markets' latent volatility innovations, and a contagion-intensification estimate ranging from-49.5% to +295.7% depending on estimator, regime-partition choice, sample period, and bias-correction. This sensitivity is itself a central finding: correlation-based estimates prove too methodology-dependent to report as a single magnitude, whereas the biasimmune Bayesian volatility-innovation correlation remains stable under subsample and prior perturbation. Freed from a fixed state-count ceiling, beam sampling recovers 11-12 active regimes versus 14-15 under truncated alternatives. Full derivations and convergence diagnostics are provided in the appendices.
