detail.abstract: We introduce a test of whether a benchmark uniformly dominates competing methods when forecasting a panel of series, and apply it to three FRED-MD applications: policy-relevant variables, the eight categories, and the full panel. Against alternatives from univariate methods to machine learning, the factor-model benchmark proves difficult to beat uniformly. Results vary across categories: at short and long horizons, dominance is not rejected for output and money but is rejected for labour markets, housing, and interest rates. The test traces each rejection to the series and methods responsible. These findings highlight the value of uniform forecast evaluation across series.

title: Optimizing Water Transfer Networks and Drought Mitigation: A Multi-Layered Engineering and Compounding Socio-Economic Framework

detail.abstract: Water resource management in tropical regions often faces a distinct climatic divide, where wet zones contend with seasonal surpluses while arid zones suffer from chronic water shortages and agricultural vulnerability. This theoretical and numerical research paper introduces a practical, multi-layered engineering framework designed to mitigate severe droughts through the optimization of large-scale water transfer systems. By blending advanced computational fluid dynamics (CFD) with hydraulic modeling of complex tunnel and open-channel networks, this study examines how water flows, loses energy, and surges across changing terrains. Beyond engineering metrics, the research conceptualizes the human and economic impact-demonstrating how optimized water routing can safeguard crop yields across seasonal shifts and alleviate regional public health and environmental challenges in vulnerable communities. Ultimately, this study provides a robust theoretical roadmap for policymakers and civil engineers aiming to design resilient, equitable water management systems under changing climatic conditions, using secondary literature and mathematical modeling principles.

title: The Duty of Environmental Care: Reframing Fiduciary Responsibility in Higher Education Governance
affiliations: University of Taipei

detail.title: The Duty of Environmental Care: Reframing Fiduciary Responsibility in Higher Education Governance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declared no potential conflicts of interest with respect to the research, authorship, and/or publication of this article.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethical approval is not required.
declarations.funderStatement: The author reported that no funding is associated with the work featured in this article.

detail.abstract: This article conceptualizes and analyzes the Duty of Environmental Care (DEC) as a developing legal and governance framework for embedding sustainability in higher education institutions. DEC reframes the fiduciary duty and responsibility to regard sustainability as a fiduciary obligation rather than a voluntary commitment in line with the UN Sustainable Development Goals, particularly SDG 4 (Quality Education) and SDG 13 (Climate Action). Drawing on theories of sustainability governance, stakeholder accountability, and fiduciary care responsibility, the research develops normative and comparative frameworks to integrate environmental care into institutional decision-making and oversight. Through a comparative, cross-jurisdictional analysis of higher education governance models, the study identifies legal, administrative, and policy opportunities to codify and operationalize DEC. The results indicate that institutions seeking DEC-oriented frameworks improve accountability, legitimacy, and sustainability outcomes. The article will contribute to sustainability research by deepening understanding of a new fiduciary paradigm that connects ethical responsibility, legal obligations, and environmental stewardship, adding a practical, knowledge-based framework to embed sustainability in the governance and management of higher education.

title: Fiscal Populism and Monetary Policy Rules
affiliations: Georgetown University, International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF) and Columbia University - Graduate School of Arts and Sciences - Department of Economics

detail.title: Fiscal Populism and Monetary Policy Rules
detail.abstract:
We explore the historical link between populist regimes, fiscal monetization, and inflation, and how these links affect monetary policy in the 21st century. Using data for a large set of advanced economies and emerging markets since 1960, we show that, historically, left-leaning populist regimes are linked to increases in central bank lending to the central government, a gauge of deficit monetization. In turn, central bank lending is associated with marked increases in inflation. We show that past exposure to populism that relied on deficit monetization affects the conduct of monetary policy today. Countries with a history of deficit monetization and left-wing populist regimes systematically respond more strongly to deviations of inflation expectations from target. This effect persists even after controlling for the direct effect of past inflation on monetary policy rules. In the context of the literature of experienced learning, this novel finding sheds light on the persistence of past populist policies—central banks operating under the shadow of past populist regimes that relied on inflation-prone deficit monetization continue today needing to send stronger signals of their independence and commitment to price stability to effectively anchor inflation expectations.

title: Responses to Extreme Price Changes: Evidence from the Residential Demand for Natural Gas
affiliations: Department of Agricultural & Resource Economics, Charles University, Charles University Prague and Department of Agricultural & Resource Economics

detail.title: Responses to Extreme Price Changes: Evidence from the Residential Demand for Natural Gas
detail.abstract:
We examine the response of residential customers to an extreme price change – namely that imposed by the government in the Republic of Georgia during the pandemic lockdown in the winter of 2020 and early 2021. As of November 2020, the government paid the gas bill directly to the utility, effectively making gas free, as long as consumption was below or exactly 200 m3/month. The policy was lifted at the end of February 2021. We use quasi-experimental causal methods based on a control group comprised of permanent residents of an area along the North-South pipeline, who receive gas for free (up to the generous allowance of 700 m3/month) every winter, while the treatment group is comprised of households living in areas with similar climates and similar population density who received gas for free only during the pandemic free gas months. Controlling for the weather, the ATT of the policy is a 2-7% increase in gas consumption (in the treatment group compared to the control group). Back-of-the-envelope calculations suggest a price elasticity of demand of -6.5% to -11%.

title: Well-Being Salience in Corporate Disclosures and Worker Health
affiliations: University of Southern Denmark, Brown University and University of Southern Denmark

detail.title: Well-Being Salience in Corporate Disclosures and Worker Health
detail.abstract:
We study how firms’ orientation toward employee well-being shapes the health of their workers. Because this orientation is not directly observable, we measure it from the language Danish firms use in their public disclosures, applying language models to construct a firm-level well-being salience score. We link this score to population-wide administrative registers of health and sickness absence over 2013–2022, and exploit workers’ mobility between firms to estimate how workers respond to a change in the salience of their employer. We find an asymmetry: workers who move to higher-salience firms take substantially more sickness absence, while their use of health care does not change. Because worsening health would raise both, the absence response suggests a behavioral change rather than deteriorating health. Broadly, our results show that firms shape not only worker health but how workers act on it, and that the language of routine corporate disclosure can reveal economically meaningful features of the workplace that administrative data leave unrecorded.

detail.abstract: Achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 requires not only deep emissions reductions but also the deployment of carbon capture, transport, and storage (CCTS) technologies-yet public acceptance remains a critical barrier to implementation. This study examines public preferences for CO2 transport options in Switzerland, with the aim of informing communication strategies and infrastructure planning for CCTS projects. Using a representative survey of 3,000 German-speaking Swiss residents, we implement a randomised experiment in which participants evaluate one of six CO2 transport options. Pipeline transport, particularly via repurposed existing infrastructure, receives the strongest public support, followed by rail and electric lorry transport. Providing information about existing CO2 transport practices in Switzerland significantly increases support, whereas safety regulation information has no measurable effect. These findings suggest that CCTS project developers and policymakers should prioritise the assessment and communication of existing pipeline networks and systematically incorporate information about current CO2 transport practices into public engagement strategies. The results offer actionable guidance for the social feasibility of CCTS deployment in Switzerland and comparable European contexts.

title: Information Gaps and Price Efficiency: The Role of Social Media
affiliations: University of Memphis - Finance

detail.title: Information Gaps and Price Efficiency: The Role of Social Media

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No competing interests.

detail.abstract: We study how information availability affects price efficiency using natural disasters and delayed official damage reporting. When affected locations receive no traditional-media coverage, municipal bond yields exhibit an initial relative response followed by a predictable correction as more precise information becomes available. These corrections are substantially attenuated when decentralized local social information is available. Traditional media provide a clearer signal of subsequently realized damages, but decentralized information improves price discovery when traditional information is limited. Our results show that the value of an information source depends not only on its precision, but also on the information set available in its absence.

title: Two Rulebooks: Which AI Transparency Measures Canada Can Keep
affiliations: New York Law School

detail.title: Two Rulebooks: Which AI Transparency Measures Canada Can Keep

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.funderStatement: non-funded

detail.abstract:
Canada's 2026 consultation on artificial intelligence transparency operates under two simultaneous rulebooks: a domestic rulebook that asks what Parliament and regulators may require, and a trade rulebook that asks how those requirements affect digital products, services, investment, and protected information. The central claim is that most desired transparency measures remain legally available under existing trade obligations if they are structured through four instrument types: appropriation, advantage condition, procurement condition, and standing obligation.

This paper maps each consultation area against CUSMA Chapters 19 and 20, together with the relevant provisions of Chapters 15, 16, 18, and 32, and identifies the description-is-not-access principle as the key to the design space: a regulator may require accounts of a system, its inputs, outputs, and operation without requiring source code, weights, or corpus access.

The analysis treats institutional capacity and enforcement as part of legal design rather than as later implementation detail. It examines why Canada's AI safety institute, established as a research body rather than by statute, had to request access to a foreign developer's safety protocols in 2026 rather than compel it, and why no entry in Canada's Annex II schedule of reservations would support the local presence requirement on which comparable enforcement regimes depend.

It concludes with seventeen recommendations sequenced by a single principle: build the institution, then write the obligation. Canada can preserve regulatory space most effectively by constructing the bodies, standards, records, and expertise that its transparency rules will require before turning to the obligations themselves.

title: Omitted Variable Bias in Difference-in-Differences Designs
affiliations: University of Washington, Emory University, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Department of Economics and University of Washington - Department of Statistics

detail.title: Omitted Variable Bias in Difference-in-Differences Designs

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: National Science Foundation Grant No. MMS-2417955.

detail.abstract: We study the omitted variable bias (OVB) problem in canonical difference-indifferences (DiD) designs when unobserved confounding induces departures from the parallel trends assumption. Our results provide a novel characterization of the OVB formula for the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT), which is of independent interest. We show how the ATT bias is mainly governed by the strength of confounding in the treatment assignment mechanism and provide alternative ways of quantifying this strength, such as (i) changes in the average odds of treatment among the treated, (ii) confounding imbalance between treated and control units, or (iii) variation explained in treatment odds among the untreated. Building on these results, we offer sensitivity statistics for routine reporting, describing the minimum strength of confounding required to overturn the conclusions of a DiD study, as well as formal bounds on the strength of confounders based on comparisons to observed covariates or pre-trends. Finally, we provide flexible and efficient statistical inference methods for the bounds on ATT, which can leverage modern machine learning algorithms for estimation. We demonstrate the utility of our approach in an empirical example that estimates the effects of minimum wage on teen employment.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a new series of National Transfer Accounts for France covering the period 1979-2019 and leverages it to analyze the evolution of consumption and its sources of financing across ages, including age profiles of labour income, transfers and saving for each year. Three main results are documented. First, the age profile of consumption has shifted markedly since the late 2000s: while consumption growth decelerated across most age groups after the global financial crisis, it continued to increase for individuals aged 65 and over. Second, the origin of funds used for consumption has evolved across age groups, with younger individuals becoming increasingly dependent on public transfers, while the role of individual resources has increased at older ages. Third, the rise in seniors’ consumption does not reflect an improvement in their relative income position but is associated with a decline in their relative saving behaviour. These results point to substantial transformations in the generational structure of the French economy over four decades

title: Business-Level Expectations and Uncertainty
affiliations: , University of Chicago, U.S. Census Bureau - Center for Economic Studies, Charles River Associates (CRA),  and Tel Aviv University

detail.title: Business-Level Expectations and Uncertainty
detail.abstract: The Census Bureau’s 2015 Management and Organizational Practices Survey (MOPS) utilized innovative methodology to collect five-point forecast distributions over own future shipments, employment, and capital and materials expenditures for 35,000 U.S. manufacturing plants. First and second moments of these plant-level forecast distributions covary strongly with first and second moments, respectively, of historical outcomes. The first moment of the distribution provides a measure of business’ expectations for future outcomes, while the second moment provides a measure of business’ subjective uncertainty over those outcomes. This subjective uncertainty measure correlates positively with financial risk measures. Drawing on the Annual Survey of Manufactures and the Census of Manufactures for the corresponding realizations, we find that subjective expectations are highly predictive of actual outcomes and, in fact, more predictive than statistical models fit to historical data. When respondents express greater subjective uncertainty about future outcomes at their plants, their forecasts are less accurate. However, managers supply overly precise forecast distributions in that implied confidence intervals for sales growth rates are much narrower than the distribution of actual outcomes. Finally, we develop evidence that greater use of predictive computing and structured management practices at the plant and a more decentralized decision-making process (across plants in the same firm) are associated with better forecast accuracy.

title: Understanding Variation in Emotional Maltreatment Reports in the United States: A Cluster Analysis of State Policy
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Understanding Variation in Emotional Maltreatment Reports in the United States: A Cluster Analysis of State Policy
detail.abstract: Background: Emotional maltreatment reports (EMR) are less examined than physical or sexual abuse, despite being 6.26% of child first entry maltreatment reports from 2013-2021, and often being reported along with other types of maltreatment. Objective: This study examines how EMR rates differ across policy clusters defined by evidentiary standard, required diagnosis, and parental intent.Participant and Setting: 51 U.S. jurisdictions, and children represented in the Report and Placement Integrated Data Set (RAPIDS) from 2013 to 2021. Methods: Hierarchical cluster analysis with three EMR policy variables was used to classify jurisdictions into policy clusters. RAPIDS data were aggregated to state-year levels to calculate EMR rates. Regression analyses and planned contrast test were conducted.Results: Of the total 1,831,443 first entries maltreatment reports from 2013-2021, exclusive EMR accounted for 27,538 (1.50%) compared with physical abuse (n = 149,623; 8.17%), sexual abuse (n = 30,830; 1.68%), and neglect (n = 930,814; 50.82%). A three-cluster solution showed the best fit: Intent Required cluster (10 states); No Intent but Preponderance Evidence Required cluster (27 states); Low Requirements cluster (14 states). Regression analyses showed no obvious differences in EMR rates across clusters. However, the planned contrast showed that the Intent Required cluster had significantly lower non-exclusive EMR rates than the combined No Intent but Preponderance Evidence Required cluster and the Low Requirements clusters. Conclusions: These findings show a need to advocate for clearer, more consistent definitions of EM across states to facilitate more accurate identification and more effective prevention efforts.

title: Law in a Thousand Characters Punishment, Adjudication and Commentary in the Qianziwen

detail.title: Law in a Thousand Characters Punishment, Adjudication and Commentary in the Qianziwen

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded

detail.abstract: The Qianziwen (千字文) places praise of restrained law beside the apprehension and execution of wrongdoers, while recalling an exemplary official through the sweet-pear tree associated with his adjudication. This article examines the legal reasoning made available by these passages and their explanation in an annotated edition preserved at Waseda University Library. Reading that witness alongside the Hanshu, Shiji and recorded Liang legislation reveals several distinctions obscured by a simple opposition between moral government and punishment. Legal simplicity can accompany severe sanctions; a commentator's account of penal excess can depart from the biography of its named exemplar; and the description of persons as offenders can presuppose the identification that legal procedure must establish. Comparison with the Tanglü shuyi, the Jijiupian and the Youxue qionglin shows that moral explanation and procedural knowledge occupy overlapping textual forms. An Old Uighur translation further illustrates how legal meaning can emerge outside an expected Chinese vocabulary. The article argues that the primer offers resources for evaluating coercion whose legal implications depend on the explanatory text brought to bear. Its evidence concerns particular representations and interpretations of authority, with consequences for how elementary texts should be used in legal history.

title: Is Uncle Sam Inducing the Elderly to Retire?
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley - Department of Economics, Boston University - Department of Economics, Economic Security Planning and Boston University

detail.title: Is Uncle Sam Inducing the Elderly to Retire?
detail.abstract: Many, if not most, Baby Boomers appear at risk of suffering a major decline in their living standard in retirement. With federal and state government finances far too encumbered to significantly raise Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid benefits, Boomers must look to their own devices to rescue their retirements, namely working harder and longer. However, the incentive of Boomers to earn more is significantly limited by a plethora of explicit federal and state taxes and implicit taxes arising from the loss of federal and state benefits as one earns more. Of particular concern is Medicaid and Social Security’s complex Earnings Test and clawback of disability benefits. This study measures the work disincentives confronting those age 50 to 79 from the entire array of explicit and implicit fiscal work disincentives. Specifically, the paper runs older respondents in the Federal Reserve’s 2013 Survey of Consumer Finances through The Fiscal Analyzer -- a software tool designed, in part, to calculate remaining lifetime marginal net tax rates. We find that working longer, say an extra five years, can raise older workers’ sustainable living standards. But the impact is far smaller than suggested in the literature in large part because of high net taxation of labor earnings. We also find that many Baby Boomers now face or will face high and, in very many cases, extremely high work disincentives arising from the hodgepodge design of our fiscal system. A third finding is that the marginal net tax rate associated with a significant increase in earnings, say $20,000 per year, arising from taking a full-time or part-time job (which could a second job), can, for many elderly, be dramatically higher than that associated with earning a relatively small, say $1,000 per year, extra amount of money. This is due to the various income thresholds in our fiscal system. We also examine the elimination of all transfer program asset and income testing. This dramatically lowers marginal net tax rates facing the poor. Another key finding is the enormous dispersion in effective marginal remaining lifetime net tax rates facing seeming identical households, i.e., households with the same age and resource level. Finally, we find that traditional, current-year (i.e., static) marginal tax calculations relating this year’s extra taxes to this year’s extra income are woefully off target when it comes to properly measuring the elderly’s disincentives to work. Our findings suggest that Uncle Sam is, indeed, inducing the elderly to retire.

title: Rational Attention Allocation Over the Business Cycle
affiliations: Imperial College London - Accounting, Finance, and Macroeconomics, Columbia University Graduate School of Business and Columbia University - Columbia Business School

detail.title: Rational Attention Allocation Over the Business Cycle
detail.abstract: The question of whether and how mutual fund managers provide valuable services for their clients motivates one of the largest literatures in finance. One candidate explanation is that funds process information about future asset values and use that information to invest in high-valued assets. But formal theories are scarce because information choice models with many assets are difficult to solve as well as difficult to test. This paper tackles both problems by developing a new attention allocation model that uses the state of the business cycle to predict information choices, which in turn, predict observable patterns of portfolio investments and returns. The predictions about fund portfolios’ covariance with payoff shocks, cross-fund portfolio and return dispersion, and their excess returns are all supported by the data. These findings offer new evidence that some investment managers have skill and that attention is allocated rationally.

title: The Protective Effects of a Healthy Spouse: Medicare as the Family Member of Last Resort
affiliations: University of California, San Diego (UCSD), Boston University, University of Toronto and Harvard Medical School - Department of Health Care Policy

detail.title: The Protective Effects of a Healthy Spouse: Medicare as the Family Member of Last Resort
detail.abstract: We study the value of informal care from a spouse and how access to such care shapes optimal insurance coverage for long-term care. Using Medicare claims and a novel spousal crosswalk, we examine how the sudden incapacitation of a spouse affects their partner's use of formal care. A spouse's health shock increases their partner's probability of a nursing-home stay by 30%. We document significant negative health effects for the partner, but provide evidence that their increase in nursing-home stays is largely driven by substitution from informal care to formal care. When their partners are incapacitated, Medicare recipients become less sensitive to the price of formal care, consistent with a higher valuation of that care and reduced moral hazard. We develop a framework to interpret these findings. The framework translates differences in the level and price elasticity of demand for formal care into a lower-bound estimate of the value of informal care provided by a spouse. It also suggests that optimal insurance for long-term care should be designed at the household level with more generous coverage for those who do not have access to informal care.

title: Political Polarization and Inventor Productivity: Evidence from Local Television Markets in the US

detail.title: Political Polarization and Inventor Productivity: Evidence from Local Television Markets in the US

declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by institutional research funds from Peking University HSBC Business School (PHBS). The author received no external grant funding and declares no conflicts of interest.

detail.abstract: Innovation depends on collaboration across people with different perspectives, yet little is known about whether political polarization disrupts this process. We study how the partisan homogenization of local television affects inventor productivity by exploiting the staggered expansion of the Sinclair Broadcast Group (SBG) across U.S. media markets between 2003 and 2023. Comparing inventors at the same firm in the same year who live in different media markets, we find that SBG entry makes inventors' collaboration networks more ideologically homogeneous and leads to persistent declines in inventive output. Patent applications fall by 1.6% and forward citations by 5.8%, indicating that partisan media affects the quality of invention more than its quantity. The effects are concentrated entirely among inventors with high pre-treatment exposure to ideologically diverse collaborators while inventors with homogeneous networks are unaffected. The failure to form new collaborations explains the decline in invention more than the deterioration of existing collaborations. After SBG entry, the formation of new ideologically distant ties falls more than three times as much as the formation of ideologically similar ties. Partisan media reduces innovation by narrowing the pool of collaborators from whom inventors draw new ideas. We thank Brian Uzzi, Yanzhi Wang, and seminar participants at the Taiwan Symposium on Innovation Economics and Entrepreneurship. All errors are our own.

title: Institutional Investors and Proxy Voting on Compensation Plans: The Impact of the 2003 Mutual Fund Voting Disclosure Regulation
affiliations: University of Notre Dame and Yale Law School

detail.title: Institutional Investors and Proxy Voting on Compensation Plans: The Impact of the 2003 Mutual Fund Voting Disclosure Regulation
detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact on shareholder voting of the mutual fund voting disclosure regulation adopted by the SEC in 2003, using a paired sample of management proposals on executive equity incentive compensation plans submitted before and after the rule change. While voting support for management has decreased over time, we find no evidence that mutual funds' support for management declined after the rule change, as expected by advocates of disclosure. In fact, we find evidence of increased support for management by mutual funds after the change. There is some evidence that firms sponsoring such proposals both before and after the rule change differ from those sponsoring a proposal only before the change. For example, firms are more likely to sponsor a proposal both before and after the rule change if they have higher mutual fund ownership. Such endogeneity could partly explain our findings of increased support after the rule.

title: Analysis of Marketing Strategy Dynamics in the Sachet Economy Phenomenon: A Theoretical Review of Market Penetration, Consumer Behavior, and Environmental Sustainability Dilemmas in Indonesian Traditional Retail

detail.title: Analysis of Marketing Strategy Dynamics in the Sachet Economy Phenomenon: A Theoretical Review of Market Penetration, Consumer Behavior, and Environmental Sustainability Dilemmas in Indonesian Traditional Retail

declarations.declarationOfInterest: no

detail.abstract: The sachet economy phenomenon is growing widely in developing countries, including Indonesia, as consumer needs for products with low nominal prices, practical, and in accordance with daily spending patterns. On the producer side, sachet packaging is a market penetration instrument that allows Fast-Moving Consumer Goods (FMCG) products to reach consumers through traditional retail networks. However, the success of the economy is faced with environmental problems due to the dominance of multilayer plastic packaging that is difficult to recycle. This conceptual paper aims to analyze the dynamics of the sachet economy through the integration of marketing strategy theory, consumer behavior, and environmental sustainability. The writing uses a descriptive qualitative approach through a review of narrative literature on relevant national and international research. The results of the synthesis show that the sustainability of the sachet economy is formed from the interaction between producers' market penetration strategies, financial affordability, practicality, trialability, and characteristics of traditional retail distribution. At the same time, the attitude-behavior gap, the limitations of waste management infrastructure, and the characteristics of multilayer materials reinforce the sustainability dilemma. Therefore, the transformation of the sachet economy requires a combination of mono-material innovations, take-back systems, waste banks, waste treatment technology, and refill schemes that still consider consumer affordability.

detail.abstract: The standard Katz-Bonacich centrality characterization of equilibrium in linear network games with strategic complementarities requires small spillovers. We show that, with bounded actions and strictly positive autarkic optima, an exact characterization remains available without this restriction. The unique equilibrium is the componentwise lower envelope of the equilibria of auxiliary linear games satisfying the usual small-spillover condition, each of which has the familiar Katz-Bonacich form. The formula is expressed directly in the primitives and yields comparative statics with respect to autarkic optima. Large spillovers thus do not overturn the Katz-Bonacich logic; they make the subnetwork on which centrality is evaluated endogenous.

title: A Hypothesis of Regulatory Capture in Japan: Parallel Non-Disclosure by a Securities Supervisor and the National Police in a Whistleblower Case Involving the NTT Group

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the reporting person to whom the privately submitted reply was addressed, and the petitioner and requester in Exhibits 52 and 53. The author holds no position designed to benefit from any market reaction to this paper, and furnishes it as a contribution to the public record.
declarations.funderStatement: The author receives no funding for this work.

detail.abstract: Regulatory capture is usually inferred from outcomes. This paper asks whether it can be inferred from procedure. A whistleblower report concerning the termination of a remote VPN connection to the systems of NTT DATA JAPAN CORPORATION, an NTT Group systems integrator, without an explanation being given to its user, drew a substantive reply through the NTT Group’s ethics helpline 232 days after the report. Nothing in the record indicates that the termination was a security incident or that it affected any client. The content of that reply is excluded from this public paper because of the author’s confidentiality and contractual obligations, and is addressed only in a private submission to the addressees. The reporting person’s subsequent petitions to the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC) and to the National Police Agency (NPA) were then met, when their handling records were requested under the Information Disclosure Act, by a common procedural pattern applied by both agencies: the request, which named the petitioner, was treated as one about “information concerning an individual”; each agency signalled a refusal to confirm or deny the existence of any record; the requester was referred to a non-public personal-information procedure; and a pre-printed form offering withdrawal was enclosed with a fixed arrival deadline. Each reply came 15–16 days after its request, and the SESC’s letter was dated the day before the NPA’s deadline of 18 September 2026, so that the two response windows were open at the same time. Neither petition concerns NTT DOCOMO Financial Group or its subsidiaries, and their filing is not evidence that any law was broken. The feature that, in the author’s view, makes this parallelism worth examining as a hypothesis of capture is documentary: the Chairman of NTT DOCOMO Financial Group, the NTT Group’s new financial holding company, is a former Commissioner of the Financial Services Agency, the office from which the SESC’s disclosure powers are delegated; nothing here suggests that the appointment breached any rule. The paper does not allege that any act was deliberate or that any individual engaged in misconduct; its subject is the opacity of the governance-response process. It separates what is documented from what is alleged and what is inferred, acknowledges the innocent explanations, and places the hypothesis before the SEC, ESMA and the FCA for examination.

title: The Silver Age of Mercenaries: How Population Decline Drove a Return to Mercenary Armies

detail.title: The Silver Age of Mercenaries: How Population Decline Drove a Return to Mercenary Armies

detail.abstract: This paper coins the term "Silver Age of Mercenaries" to describe the resurgence of mercenary employment in Europe from 1618 to 1714. It argues that population decline during the crisis of the seventeenth century raised the relative price of domestically sourced military labor, increasing rulers' incentives to hire foreign mercenaries as a substitute for domestic soldiers beyond what regime popularity alone can explain. I extend the model developed by Leeson and Piano (2021) by incorporating demographic contraction, operationalized as a shrinking recruitment base, as an independent driver of mercenary reliance. This extension explains why mercenary reliance recurs across distinct historical eras, rather than varying only with a ruler's political security. I test this prediction using a natural experiment from the Republic of Venice. Two outlying Mediterranean island possessions, Cyprus and Crete, came under siege by the Ottoman Empire in the Fourth (1570-1573) and Fifth (1645-1669) Venetian-Ottoman Wars. Venice's population, however, never recovered from the plague of 1575-77 and did not exceed its pre-plague peak again until 1951, leaving its recruitment base sharply diminished by the time of the Fifth War. Consistent with the model, the mercenary share of Venice's besieged garrisons rose from roughly 38 percent in the Fourth War to over 90 percent in the Fifth. The findings suggest that demographic contraction is an independent driver of mercenary reliance, distinct from regime insecurity, with implications for states facing similar pressures today, including Russia and Ukraine.

detail.abstract: How do cross-border lending responses to U.S. monetary-policy surprises differ across lender systems with different dollar orientations? Using bilateral BIS Locational Banking Statistics for 17 lender systems and 16 Pacific Basin borrowers during 2005Q1-2025Q4, we estimate same-borrower, same-quarter differences in lending responses. The interaction between a standardized high-frequency U.S. monetary surprise and lagged lender dollar-funding exposure is positive (2.717; lender-level wild-cluster p = 0.003), implying a 1.01percentage-point larger quarterly flow response at the 75th than the 25th exposure percentile. The result survives extensive fixed-effect, sample, measurement, and lender-characteristic checks and rejects a simple monotonic funding-fragility benchmark. Diagnostics show that approximately 97% of exposure variation is between lender systems. We therefore interpret dollar orientation as a marker of structural dollar-market integration: the evidence establishes a robust cross-lender difference in monetary-shock sensitivity while not isolating dollar funding as the causal mechanism. The findings reveal persistent lender heterogeneity in international monetary transmission.

detail.abstract: This paper studies a continuous-time consumption-portfolio choice problem in which an investor has preferences for certain risky assets ("asset tastes"). A prominent recent example is the preference for green over brown assets. In a framework with a riskfree bond and two risky assets, one favored and one non-favored, we derive solutions for finite and infinite horizons. The risky assets are exposed to both diffusive and jump risk. The model can be interpreted as a dynamic resource-allocation problem under uncertainty in which alternatives differ in their financial and nonfinancial attributes. We establish existence and uniqueness of the solutions and provide verification theorems for optimality. Our model generates two key effects that shape optimal portfolio demand: Preferences for a particular asset increase exposure to that asset, which we call the preference effect. At the same time, demand for the non-favored asset is crowded out, generating a substitution effect. While the directions of these effects are intuitive, their magnitudes depend critically on market characteristics. In particular, the sensitivity ("beta") of the favored asset to the non-favored asset determines the strength of the crowding-out effect. The total risky share increases when this sensitivity is below one and decreases when it exceeds one. Portfolio outcomes are thus jointly determined by preference-based features, such as the strength of asset tastes, and market-based features, such as the comovement between favored and non-favored assets. A numerical calibration based on U.S. data for green and brown stocks illustrates the theoretical results and highlights their quantitative implications.

detail.title: Residence for Corporate Income Tax Purposes - General Report

publicationDetails.detailsText: International Fiscal Association 2025 Lisbon Congress | cahiers volume 109

detail.abstract:
Residence is one of the most fundamental legal concepts for taxation. This general report aims to provide a better understanding of the function, meaning and role performed by the concept in modern corporate income tax systems. A comprehensive assessment of the branch reports reveals a complex normative landscape shaped by globalisation and digitalisation and evolving legal concepts under a mist of indeterminacy. Regarding domestic law, there is considerable diversity, with divergent jurisdictional approaches, encompassing the interplay of incorporation, governance and other criteria and with a clear trend of expanding the scope of the concept. At the income tax treaty level, while most treaties still adhere to place of effective management as a tie-breaker, there is a progressive shift to the mutual agreement procedure (hereinafter MAP), which should be regarded with concern. Such a mechanism, as it prevents taxpayers from anticipating the tax consequences of their (often genuine and needed) behaviour, is particularly worrisome, taking into account that residence is often a trigger for worldwide taxation.

The general report underscores the need for enhanced international cooperation and legislative reforms to address the challenges emphasised by globalisation and digitalisation, advocating for a nuanced balance between sovereignty and global tax fairness.

detail.abstract: Post-combustion carbon capture systems are conventionally optimized to maximize the percentage of CO2 captured from a flue-gas stream, an objective that can mask a system's true climate value once the energy penalty, embodied carbon of solvent and equipment, water use, and total resource footprint required to achieve that capture rate are accounted for. This paper proposes NET-CAPTURE-X, a framework that reframes the optimization objective from raw capture percentage to net lifetime CO2 avoided per unit of total resource burden, encompassing energy, cost, embodied carbon, physical footprint, and water. The framework is restricted in scope to amine-based post-combustion capture, explicitly excluding direct air capture, pre-combustion and oxy-fuel pathways, and downstream transport, storage, and utilization logistics, which are proposed as separate future extensions. Methodologically, the framework applies a Codd-style relational schema to structure the variable-dependency space of the capture process, a Pareto screening step to identify the small number of dominant variables (regeneration duty, heat integration, solvent degradation, absorber mass-transfer efficiency, and solvent loading) responsible for the majority of net-avoidance variance, a Goldbach-conjecture-inspired heuristic for pairing complementary interventions across these dominant variables, a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) layer for adaptive predictive control, and a LEED AP BD+C-aligned whole-system validation step. The paper is explicit that the Goldbach-inspired pairing heuristic is a design convenience for structuring intervention combinations and carries no claimed physical or thermodynamic basis in the capture process itself.

title: Private Equity and Industry Performance
affiliations: Harvard University - Business School (HBS), Harvard Business School - Finance Unit, Dartmouth College - Tuck School of Business and Swedish House of Finance

detail.title: Private Equity and Industry Performance
detail.abstract: The growth of the private equity industry has spurred concerns about its potential impact on the economy more generally. This analysis looks across nations and industries to assess the impact of private equity on industry performance. Industries where PE funds have invested in the past five years have grown more quickly in terms of productivity and employment. There are few significant differences between industries with limited and high private equity activity. It is hard to find support for claims that economic activity in industries with private equity backing is more exposed to aggregate shocks. The results using lagged private equity investments suggest that the results are not driven by reverse causality. These patterns are not driven solely by common law nations such as the United Kingdom and United States, but also hold in Continental Europe.

detail.abstract: This article develops conditional predictability as a methodological component of the Theory of Dynamic Adaptive Warfare (TDAW). Strategic analysis routinely oscillates between overconfidence and fatalism: either analysts imply that conflict can be predicted with excessive precision, or they treat uncertainty as a reason to avoid explicit forecasts. The article argues for a third position. Conditional predictability treats forecasts as transparent, revisable judgments about relative plausibility under specified assumptions. It makes three contributions. First, it distinguishes forecasting from deterministic prediction by combining game-theoretic interdependence, bargaining theory, and research on calibrated geopolitical judgment. Second, it proposes a structured variable architecture covering intent, capability, vulnerability, opportunity, legal and political cost, expected response, adaptation, and signal reliability. Third, it introduces an updating protocol that separates observations from interpretations, requires dated assessments, records disconfirming evidence, and prevents legal permissibility from being mistaken for behavioral probability. International law enters the framework as a source of incentives, constraints, and expected third-party reactions, not as a mechanical predictor of compliance. The method is designed for qualitative and semi-structured use in crisis analysis, early warning, and comparative case research. Its purpose is to improve reasoning under uncertainty while preserving humility about low-probability shocks, deception, and strategic adaptation.

detail.abstract: We study the impact of skilled immigrants on the employment structures of U.S. firms using matched employer-employee data. Unlike most previous work, we use the firm as the lens of analysis to account for a greater level of heterogeneity and the fact that many skilled immigrant admissions are driven by firms themselves (e.g., the H-1B visa). OLS and IV specifications find rising overall employment of skilled workers with increased skilled immigrant employment by firm. Employment expansion is greater for younger natives than their older counterparts, and departure rates for older workers appear higher for those in STEM occupations compared to younger worker.

detail.abstract: This article examines how existing scientific and legal institutions could govern a scientifically credible discovery of extraterrestrial life or intelligence. The paper deliberately excludes unidentified anomalous phenomena, unverified visitation claims, and speculative narratives unsupported by reproducible evidence. Its starting point is that astrobiology and international space governance already contain important fragments of a post-detection architecture: life-detection frameworks, planetary-protection rules, the Outer Space Treaty, COSPAR policy, the International Academy of Astronautics' 2026 SETI principles, frequency-protection pathways referenced by the IAA principles, and United Nations mechanisms for international coordination. The article makes three contributions. First, it develops a legal-scientific taxonomy that distinguishes remote biosignatures, in situ biological evidence, returned extraterrestrial material, and verified technosignatures because each generates different legal and governance questions. Second, it maps the existing fragmented institutional architecture and identifies the gap between scientific verification and collective decision authority. Third, it proposes a staged Post-Detection Governance Framework covering independent verification, evidence classification, planetaryprotection review, international notification, data preservation, risk assessment, coordinated public communication, and any decision concerning reply. The article argues that a credible framework should emerge from existing institutions rather than from fictional assumptions about extraterrestrial actors. The deeper legal problem is not whether international law already recognizes extraterrestrial legal personality; it is whether humanity has procedures for governing its own conduct when evidence of life beyond Earth becomes scientifically credible.

title: State Responsibility for Private Space Activities: Authorization, Continuing Supervision and Orbital Risk

detail.title: State Responsibility for Private Space Activities: Authorization, Continuing Supervision and Orbital Risk

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial, professional, personal, or institutional interests that could have influenced the research, analysis, interpretation, or conclusions presented in this manuscript.

detail.abstract: This article examines how international law allocates responsibility and risk when private entities conduct space activities. Commercial launch providers, satellite operators, on-orbit servicing companies, remotesensing firms, and future resource-utilization ventures increasingly perform functions once dominated by States, yet the core treaty architecture remains State-centered. The article makes three contributions. First, it separates three legal questions that are often conflated: international responsibility for national space activities under Article VI of the Outer Space Treaty, attribution of private conduct to a State under the general law of State responsibility, and liability for damage caused by space objects under the Liability Convention. Second, it conceptualizes 'continuing supervision' as a regulatory cycle extending from licensing and technical conditions through monitoring, incident reporting, modification, end-of-life obligations, and enforcement. Third, it proposes a risk-tiered supervision matrix in which regulatory intensity increases with operational proximity, autonomy, destructive potential, data sensitivity, and externality. The article relies on the Outer Space Treaty, Liability and Registration Conventions, the International Law Commission's Articles on State Responsibility, United Nations guidance on national space legislation, and emerging standards for rendezvous and proximity operations. It argues that Article VI should not be treated as a slogan or as automatic attribution of every private act to the State. Its contemporary significance lies in requiring States to build credible regulatory capacity for private activities whose externalities can propagate across the shared orbital environment.

detail.title: What Do Survey Data Tell Us about US Businesses?
detail.abstract: This paper examines the reliability of survey data on business incomes, valuations, and rates of return, which are key inputs for studies of wealth inequality and entrepreneurial choice. We compare survey responses of business owners with available data from administrative tax records, brokered private business sales, and publicly traded company filings and document problems due to nonrepresentative samples and measurement errors across several surveys, subsamples, and years. We find that the discrepancies are economically relevant for the statistics of interest. We investigate reasons for these discrepancies and propose corrections for future survey designs.

detail.title: Exit After Exit

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None

publicationDetails.detailsText: U of Penn Law School, Public Law Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School, Public Law & Legal Theory Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Business law and finance scholarship has long treated the initial public offering (IPO) as a clean exit for venture capital. Under the prevailing account, venture capitalists supply capital and governance in the private phase, exit shortly after the IPO, and yield their position to public markets and dispersed shareholders. This assumption underlies doctrinal frameworks and contemporary debates about firms staying private longer and going public with dual-class stock.

This Article shows that this exit paradigm no longer reflects how many venture-backed startups transition to the public markets. Using a dataset of U.S. venture-backed IPOs, we document sustained venture capital ownership, voting power, and board involvement well beyond the lock-up period. Venture capitalists frequently remain significant governance actors during a company’s early public life, often participating in governance with founders or, in some cases, replacing founders as primary stewards of growth firms. Further, we find that retained VC voting power is positively associated with same-year shareholder returns.

Building on these findings, the Article theorizes venture capital’s role in post-IPO firms as a governance institution that mediates the shift from private to public markets. Continued VC involvement can provide transitional governance while also supporting privately ordered founder-led arrangements. This perspective reframes concerns about minority controllers by showing how contingent, coalition-based control arrangements complicate the assumption of unilateral founder control. It also suggests that the debate over dual-class sunset provisions focuses too heavily on a fixed passage of time and overlooks the governance shift that occurs as venture capital involvement unwinds and founder control consolidates. We contribute a new account of venture capital’s post-IPO role, with implications for corporate doctrine, securities regulation, and governance design for newly public firms.

title: Contracting for Decision-Relevant Beliefs

detail.title: Contracting for Decision-Relevant Beliefs

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA

detail.abstract: Forecasts guide decisions, but an expert who privately values the decision may misreport beliefs to influence it. We study contracts that jointly elicit the expert's belief about a verifiable state and her stake in a binary action. When agents with different stakes can hold the same belief, exact belief-only IC forces the action to ignore the report. Joint screening permits responsiveness but may require implementation rent. For thresholds, minimum implementation rent equals the distribution-weighted positive curvature of the belief-dependent cutoff. Optimal threshold design is rentadjusted concavification. We give sufficient conditions for unrestricted threshold optimality and, beyond them, bounds and a direct optimality certificate.

detail.abstract: This paper shows that U.S. consumption growth comoves with household wealth primarily when the wealth-to-income ratio lies below a slow-moving benchmark. We estimate a Bayesian state-space model that decomposes the wealth-to-income ratio into a stochastic trend and a gap with regime-dependent drift and volatility, while allowing consumption to load differently on positive and negative gaps. A 0.10 log-point shortfall is associated with a 0.49 percentage point decline in quarterly consumption growth, whereas the positive-gap coefficient is indistinguishable from zero. Allowing gap dynamics to switch between normal and stressed states substantially sharpens inference relative to a homogeneous model. A Financial Accounts decomposition shows that revaluation accounts for 78 percent of the variance in quarterly net-worth changes, compared with 19 percent for net investment.

detail.abstract: This article analyzes disinformation as a repeated strategic game rather than as a collection of isolated false statements. The central problem is why actors continue to produce and distribute misleading or fabricated content even when platforms, regulators, journalists, and audiences possess correction mechanisms. The article argues that persistence is often rational from the manipulator's perspective when production costs are low, attribution is difficult, engagement rewards are immediate, correction is slow, and sanctions are uncertain. It makes three contributions. First, it develops a repeated-game model in which manipulators, platforms, regulators, and audiences adapt to one another over time. Second, it identifies an attribution-cost asymmetry: defenders often bear substantial verification and procedural costs before responding, while manipulators can externalize the cost of correction and rapidly change accounts, narratives, or channels. Third, it proposes a payoff-shifting governance framework focused on provenance, friction, detection, transparency, and proportional sanctions rather than indiscriminate content control. The analysis draws on game theory, empirical misinformation research, platformgovernance literature, and the Theory of Dynamic Adaptive Warfare (TDAW). It concludes that durable resilience requires changing the incentives and architecture of manipulation while preserving room for error, satire, opinion, and legitimate political persuasion.

detail.abstract: This article develops a framework for assessing escalation risk in outer space without treating ambiguous technical activity as proof of hostile intent or legal violation. Contemporary space security involves reversible and non-reversible counterspace capabilities, electronic warfare, cyber operations, rendezvous and proximity operations, remote sensing, and dependence on commercial infrastructure. Many of the same capabilities can serve benign, commercial, intelligence, defensive, or offensive functions. The article makes three contributions. First, it proposes an Orbital Escalation Warning Framework (OEWF) that evaluates behavior through converging indicators of capability, proximity, pattern, reversibility, target dependence, concurrent cyber/electromagnetic activity, political signaling, and attribution confidence. Second, it establishes a 'warning-legality firewall': analysts may identify rising strategic risk before the evidence is sufficient to characterize conduct as a threat or use of force, armed attack, or attack under international humanitarian law. Third, it develops an Orbital Escalation Ladder from routine competition through ambiguous interference, coercive disruption, destructive action, and space-enabled armed conflict. The framework draws on international space law, the UN Charter, the Woomera Manual, ISO 24330 on rendezvous and proximity operations, open-source counterspace assessments, and the Theory of Dynamic Adaptive Warfare (TDAW). It argues that the most reliable warning comes from patterns across domains, not from a single satellite maneuver or technical anomaly.

title: Filtering and Smoothing with Score-Driven Models

detail.title: Filtering and Smoothing with Score-Driven Models

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No potential conflict of interest was reported by the authors
declarations.funderStatement: Italian Ministry MUR (PRIN2020) European Program scheme “INFRAIA-01-2018-2019: Research and Innovation action”

detail.abstract: Score-driven models are, by construction, purely predictive filters. When such models are read as filters for an underlying latent process, rather than as data generating processes, this is a restriction rather than a feature, because the contemporaneous and the future observations also carry information on the current state. Starting from the observation that the Kalman filter and smoother recursions for linear Gaussian models can be written in terms of the score of the conditional log-likelihood, and that the predictive step then takes the form of a score-driven recursion, we generalize score-driven models along this direction by deriving an update filter and a smoother, which exploit the contemporaneous observation and the whole sample respectively, together with the corresponding conditional variances. In extensive Monte Carlo analyses the update filter lowers the mean square error of the predictive filter by 3.5% to 8.8%, and the smoother by 32% to 44%, with the ordering holding in every replication; confidence bands built on the associated conditional variances attain their nominal coverage, whereas bands that ignore filtering uncertainty capture less than a third of it. Empirically, we demonstrate the benefits of employing score-driven models as filters rather than as purely predictive processes, showing that the resulting smoothed estimates align more closely with realized quantities than their predictive counterparts.

title: The Productivity J-Curve: How Intangibles Complement General Purpose Technologies
affiliations: National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER), University of Pennsylvania - Operations & Information Management Department and University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: The Productivity J-Curve: How Intangibles Complement General Purpose Technologies
detail.abstract: General purpose technologies (GPTs) such as AI enable and require significant complementary investments, including co-invention of new processes, products, business models and human capital. These complementary investments are often intangible and poorly measured in the national accounts, even when they create valuable assets for the firm. We develop a model that shows how this leads to an underestimation of productivity growth in the early years of a new GPT, and how later, when the benefits of intangible investments are harvested, productivity growth will be overestimated. Our model generates a Productivity J-Curve that can explain the productivity slowdowns often accompanying the advent of GPTs, as well as the increase in productivity later. We use our model to analyze empirically the historical roles of intangibles tied to R&D, software, and computer hardware. We find substantial and ongoing Productivity J-Curve effects for software in particular and computer hardware to a lesser extent. Our adjusted measure TFP is 11.3% higher than official measures at the end of 2004, and 15.9% higher than official measures at the end of 2017. We then assess how AI-related intangible capital may be currently affecting measured productivity and find the effects are small but growing.

affiliations: Independent

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Not applicable

detail.abstract:
On 18 August 2026 the Syrian Arab Republic adopted a new Electronic Payment and Transfer System by Decision 1124, repealing the 2019 framework that preceded it. This paper examines what the instrument does and does not do, and situates it within the wider reintegration of Syria's financial sector following the restoration of dollar clearing, the return of international card acceptance and the resumption of multilateral technical engagement.

The central argument is that Decision 1124 is a licensing and conduct rulebook rather than an infrastructure programme. It establishes a three-tier market covering payment service providers, electronic money issuers and payment system operators, holds operators to the CPMI-IOSCO Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures, mandates segregated safeguarding of customer funds, and creates a regulatory sandbox and a licensed agent model. It reserves the national settlement and clearing systems to the central bank without specifying them, and gives existing providers six months to conform.

The paper identifies gaps in financial inclusion, anti-money laundering anchoring and data localisation, and considers whether the framework could support designating an incumbent provider as national infrastructure. A September 2026 postscript records the regulator's public framing of the decision and the unexplained suspension of a major international remittance channel.

title: Bank competition and credit risk: the conditioning role of capital

detail.title: Bank competition and credit risk: the conditioning role of capital
detail.abstract: This paper examines how bank capital conditions the effect of competition on credit risk in lending markets, informing the debate on banking competition, deregulation, and risk-based supervision. Using ECB supervisory data for 146 euro area banks across 19 countries over 2020Q2–2025Q3, we analyze whether this relationship depends on banks’ regulatory capital positions. We find that greater market power is associated with higher subsequent credit risk, while stronger capitalization is associated with lower risk. Crucially, competition reduces credit risk primarily for well-capitalized banks, whereas the effect is weak or absent for banks with lower capital ratios. By aligning the measurement of competition and risk with the pricing-based mechanism, the paper provides a direct empirical test of the borrower-risk channel and offers an explanation for mixed evidence in the competition–risk literature. The results highlight the importance of considering the interaction between competition and prudential capital requirements when assessing financial stability.

detail.abstract: Digital interfaces increasingly allow consumers to render marketplace options onto representations of themselves. We propose self-standard reweighting: self-visualization increases the decision weight placed on congruity with the self-standard active during choice, rather than uniformly increasing favorability toward an option. We distinguish this mechanism from generic self-association and uncertainty reduction. Descriptive field evidence from 10,000 completed AI hairstyle-generation events shows broad but structured self-directed exploration, motivating a distinction between public attention and what consumers are willing to visualize on themselves. We then specify three confirmatory studies. The first compares public search attention with consequential self-directed trial under equal exposure. The second randomizes consumers to self versus appearance-matched-other visualization and tests whether pre-treatment self-congruity becomes more predictive of consequential choice under self-visualization, while an independent process sample separates self-diagnosticity from uncertainty reduction. The third manipulates actual- versus ideal-self choice goals to test whether reweighting is specific to the active self-standard. The framework contributes to research on self-congruity, identity-based choice, and virtual product experience.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether and how the peer information environment – generated by peer firms' disclosures and by the information intermediaries covering them – affects the CEO's delegation of decision rights to division managers (DMs). Using an international survey dataset, I measure within-firm delegation of decision-making over capital investment, human capital investment, investment in new products, and sales. I find that CEOs delegate more to managers of divisions in country-industries with richer peer information environments. Cross-sectional tests highlight three underlying channels. Specifically, the results suggest that peer information (i) helps the CEO acquire information to reduce potential information disadvantages relative to DMs (CEO learning), (ii) mitigates CEO-DM agency frictions (agency mitigation), and (iii) provides DMs with relevant information to make better decisions (DM learning). While CEO learning reduces delegation, agency mitigation and DM learning increase it. These findings provide evidence that information about peers influences the internal organization of firms.

detail.abstract: Using exogenous variation generated by the creation of the Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM) in the euro area, we find that relative to firms borrowing from banks subject to national supervision, firms borrowing from banks subject to supranational supervision reduce their share of intangible assets. This effect does not pre-date the supervisory reform and it does not obtain in non-SSM jurisdictions. The reallocation of investment away from intangible assets is stronger for small and young firms and appears to be driven by a short-term reduction in lending and a persistent increase in collateral standards.

title: Specialized Investments and Firms’ Boundaries: Evidence from Textual Analysis of Patents
affiliations: University of British Columbia - Sauder School of Business, Ohio State University (OSU) - Department of Finance,  and Ohio State University (OSU) - Department of Finance

detail.title: Specialized Investments and Firms’ Boundaries: Evidence from Textual Analysis of Patents
detail.abstract: Inducing firms to make specialized investments through bilateral contracts can be challenging because of potential hold- up problems. Such contracting difficulties have long been argued to be an important reason for acquisitions. To evaluate the extent to which this motivation leads to mergers, we perform a textual analysis of the patents filed by the same lead inventors of the target firms before and after the mergers. We find that patents of inventors from target firms become 28.9% to 46.8% more specific to those of acquirers’ inventors following completed mergers, benchmarked against patents filed by targets and a group of counterfactual acquirers. This pattern is stronger for vertical mergers that are likely to require specialized investments. There is no change in the specificity of patents for mergers that are announced but not consummated. Overall, we provide empirical evidence that contracting issues in motivating specialized investment can be a motive for acquisitions.

title: Corporate Acquisitions, Diversification, and the Firm's Lifecycle
affiliations: Kent State University and Ohio State University (OSU) - Department of Finance

detail.title: Corporate Acquisitions, Diversification, and the Firm's Lifecycle
detail.abstract: Lifecycle theories of mergers and diversification predict that firms make acquisitions and diversify when their internal growth opportunities become exhausted. Free cash flow theories make similar predictions. In contrast to these theories, we find that the acquisition rate of firms (defined as the number of acquisitions in an IPO cohort-year divided by the number of firms in that cohort-year) follows a u-shape through their lifecycle as public firms, with young and mature firms being equally acquisitive but more so than middle-aged firms. Firms that go public during the merger/IPO wave of the 1990s are significantly more acquisitive early in their public life than firms that go public at other times.  Young public firms have a lower acquisition rate of public firms than mature firms, but the opposite is true for acquisitions of private firms and subsidiaries. Strikingly, firms diversify early in their life and there is a 41% chance that a firm's first acquisition is a diversifying acquisition. The stock market reacts more favorably to acquisitions by young firms than to acquisitions by mature firms except for acquisitions of public firms paid for with stock. There is no evidence that the market reacts more adversely to diversifying acquisitions by young firms than to other acquisitions.

title: Input Diffusion and the Evolution of Production Networks
affiliations: Universitat Pompeu Fabra/CREI and University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) - Anderson School of Management

detail.title: Input Diffusion and the Evolution of Production Networks
detail.abstract: The adoption and diffusion of inputs in the production network is at the heart of technological progress. What determines which inputs are initially considered and eventually adopted by innovators? We examine the evolution of input linkages from a network perspective, starting from a stylized model of network formation. Producers direct their search for new inputs along vertical linkages, screening the network neighborhood of existing suppliers to identify potentially useful inputs. A subset of these is then adopted, following a tradeoff between the benefits from input variety and the costs of customizing new inputs. Guided by this framework, we document a novel stylized fact at both the sector and the firm level: producers are more likely to adopt inputs that are already used – directly or indirectly – by their current suppliers. In particular, using disaggregated input-output data, we show that initial network proximity of a sector in 1967 significantly increases the likelihood of adoption throughout the subsequent four decades. A one-standard deviation decrease in network distance is associated with an increase in the adoption probability by one third to one half. Similarly, U.S. firms are significantly more likely to develop new input linkages among their suppliers’ network neighborhood. Our results imply that the existing production network plays a crucial role in the diffusion of inputs and the evolution of technology.
